arguments.content:
ETS frontend design review

Overriding, Overloading
and Overload Resolution

Spec reading, current frontend flaws, and an incremental migration plan toward a single semantic model for classes, inheritance, and multiple interfaces.

Spec: 15_semantics.rst Frontend: ets2panda Focus: class + multiple interfaces
Executive summary

What I found

Some pieces exist

Parser, binder, checker, explicit overload AST nodes, call selection, and bridge lowering already exist.

But semantics are fragmented

Overriding, explicit overload aliases, inherited overload sets, interface conflicts, and bridge generation are solved in separate local mechanisms.

Target design

Introduce one source of truth: override graph + overload-set builder + resolved call target.

The most visible deficiency is false interface conflict detection when a concrete superclass method already implements methods from several interfaces.
Spec anchor

Overriding rules that matter here

  • Constructors do not participate in overriding.
  • Only accessible methods/accessors are override candidates.
  • Parameters are contravariant: derived parameter type must be a supertype of base parameter type.
  • Return type is covariant: derived return type must be a subtype of base return type.
  • Protected may become public; public cannot become protected/private.
  • A single derived method can override several inherited methods.
  • More than one method in the subtype overriding the same inherited method is a compile-time error.
Important: superclass methods can implement interface methods. Interface conflicts must be checked after accounting for concrete class/superclass implementations.
Spec anchor

Overloading rules that matter here

  • Overload resolution is first match, not best match.
  • Overload sets are ordered: textual order, explicit list order, then inheritance order.
  • Return types do not participate in overload resolution.
  • Implicit overload-equivalence ignores return type.
  • Explicit overload declaration can list a name that denotes an implicit overload group; it must expand to all candidates.
  • For class instance methods: own methods, then direct superclass overload set, then direct interfaces in implements order.
  • For interfaces: own methods, then direct superinterfaces in extends order.
Spec anchor

Type erasure and bridge methods

Effective signature type

Used by overload-equivalence and erasure-related override diagnostics. It is a spec-level concept and should not be approximated casually by assembler names.

Bridge methods

If a derived method overrides a base method but runtime/erased signatures differ, generate an inaccessible synthetic bridge that delegates to the real method.

class B<T extends Object> {
    foo(p: T) {}
}
class D extends B<string> {
    foo(p: string) {} // real method
    // compiler may need bridge foo(p: Object)
}
Current implementation map

Where the feature currently lives

AreaFiles / mechanisms
Parser / IRir/base/overloadDeclaration.h, parser/ETSparser*.cpp
Scope init / bindingcompiler/lowering/scopesInit/scopesInitPhase.cpp, varbinder/ETSBinder.cpp
Call resolutionchecker/ets/function.cpp, especially FirstMatchSignatures, MatchOrderSignatures
Object/member lookupchecker/types/ets/etsObjectType.cpp, synthetic method types from properties
Interface/class validationchecker/ets/object.cpp
Explicit overload checkschecker/ets/typeCheckingHelpers.cpp
LoweringoverloadMappingLowering.cpp, genericBridgesLowering.cpp, overrideBridgesLowering.cpp
Main architectural flaw

There is no single source of truth

Property lookup→ Synthetic variables→ Call signatures→ Local override checks→ Bridge phases rediscover relations
The same semantic question — “does this method override that one?” — is answered in several places with slightly different logic.
  • Override checks mutate state while asking compatibility questions.
  • Overload sets are built as side effects of property lookup.
  • Bridge lowering scans supertypes again instead of consuming checker-produced override facts.
Concrete false rejection

Superclass method implements multiple interfaces

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }

interface I1 { foo(): string }
interface I2 { foo(): string }

class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}

Correct semantics

C2 inherits concrete C1.foo. That method is override-compatible with both I1.foo and I2.foo. No conflict.

Deficiency

Interface collision detection can compare I1.foo and I2.foo before accounting for concrete class/superclass implementations.

Flaw #1

Overload-equivalence is mixed with other checks

Spec-level overload-equivalence is not the same as signature identity or assembly descriptor equality.

function foo(x: number): string { return "" }
function foo(x: number): number { return 1 }
// Should be CTE: return type does not distinguish overloads.
  • Current logic uses paths around CheckIdenticalOverloads, SignatureIsIdenticalTo, and assembly signatures.
  • Return type can leak into decisions where the spec says it must be ignored.
Needed: a dedicated AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature*, Signature*) helper that compares effective parameter signature types and ignores return type.
Flaw #2

Effective signature type is not first-class

The spec uses effective signature types for overload-equivalence and erasure-conflict diagnostics.

interface Base {
    m(a: Array<string>): void
}
interface Derived extends Base {
    m(a: Array<number>): void
    // CTE: not override-compatible, but erasure/effective signatures collide
}
  • Current code often uses normal type relation or assembler type strings.
  • That is not a clear implementation of the spec's effective signature type mapping.
Flaw #3

Explicit overloads mishandle implicit overload groups

function foo(x: number) {}
function foo(x: string) {}
function bar(x: boolean) {}

overload baz { foo, bar }
// baz's set should be: foo(number), foo(string), bar(boolean)
  • Current validation can reject listed overloaded names.
  • Several paths use CallSignatures().front(), keeping only the first signature.
  • Spec says the listed name expands to all implicit overload candidates in declaration order.
Casual front() in overload-related code is a design smell unless there is an explicit exactly-one-signature assertion.
Flaw #4

Overload sets are hidden in property lookup

Current ETSObjectType::GetProperty can create synthetic variables and assemble signatures.

Problem

Lookup, overload-set construction, inheritance ordering, explicit overload expansion, and duplicate suppression become entangled.

Better

Lookup should find declarations. A checker-owned overload-set builder should build ordered semantic candidates.

OverloadSet BuildClassInstanceMethodSet(ETSObjectType *type, Name name);
OverloadSet BuildInterfaceMethodSet(ETSObjectType *type, Name name);
OverloadSet BuildConstructorSet(ETSObjectType *type);
Flaw #5

Override validation is scattered

Current areaIssue
checker/ets/function.cppMethod override checks and mutations while checking individual methods.
checker/ets/object.cppInterface collision, abstract implementation, optional property checks.
genericBridgesLowering.cppRediscovers generic bridge needs.
overrideBridgesLowering.cppRediscovers non-identical override bridge needs.
Needed: one override analyzer that produces explicit override edges, then diagnostics/lowering consume those edges.
Flaw #6

Explicit overload inheritance is checked too weakly

Spec requires inherited explicit overload aliases from multiple interfaces to be reconciled by a new explicit overload declaration including all methods.

interface I1 { overload foo { f1, f2 } }
interface I2 { overload foo { f3, f4 } }

class C implements I1, I2 {
    // CTE unless C declares overload foo including all inherited methods
}
  • Current checks are largely name-list based.
  • If no local overload declaration exists, conflict can be missed or mishandled.
  • Correct check must compare resolved methods/signatures, not just identifier text.
Flaw #7

Bridge generation is not checker-driven

Bridge generation currently scans classes/supertypes independently.

  • Checker and lowering can disagree about what overrides what.
  • Bridge requirement logic can become narrower than the spec.
  • Duplicate bridge avoidance is harder without a normalized override graph.
Better: checker computes OverrideEdge { derived, base }; lowering asks each edge whether its effective/ABI signature requires a bridge.
Correct design

Three semantic products

1. Override graph

derivedSignature → baseSignature(s). Used for diagnostics, implementation validation, duplicate suppression, and bridge creation.

2. Overload sets

Ordered vector<OverloadCandidate>, built from declarations, explicit aliases, and supertypes in spec order.

3. Resolved call target

Each call stores selected signature plus selected function/method/constructor target for lowering and codegen.

Declarations→ Signatures→ Override graph→ Overload sets→ Resolved calls→ Lowering / bridges
Correct design

Override graph

struct OverrideEdge {
    Signature *derived;
    Signature *base;
    OverrideKind kind;      // class, interface, implementation
    bool requiresBridge;
};
  • Computed after own members and supertypes are resolved.
  • Pure compatibility checks first; mutation/marking second.
  • One method can have several base edges.
  • Detect duplicate overrides by grouping edges by base signature.
The false rejection case becomes explicit: C1.foo → I1.foo and C1.foo → I2.foo. Therefore no interface conflict remains.
Correct design

Overload set builder

struct OverloadCandidate {
    Signature *signature;
    varbinder::LocalVariable *variable;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    CandidateOrigin origin;
    size_t sourceOrder;
};
  • Build functions, static methods, instance methods, interface methods, constructors through one API family.
  • Explicit overload list entries expand to all candidates of the listed implicit group.
  • Own class/interface candidates precede inherited candidates.
  • Use the override graph to skip already-overridden inherited methods.
  • Do not rely on map iteration or property lookup side effects for ordering.
Correct design

Call resolution

  1. Build the overload set from the callee form and static receiver type.
  2. If explicit type arguments are present, filter incompatible generic candidates.
  3. Visit candidates in order.
  4. Pick the first candidate where arguments are valid.
  5. Do not use return type for overload selection.
  6. Store selected signature and selected declaration target on the call.
callExpr->SetSignature(selected.signature);
callExpr->SetResolvedCallTarget(selected.target);
Lowering should consume the resolved target instead of rediscovering it through Signature::OwnerVar() assumptions.
Correct design

Multiple interface implementation

For class C extends B implements I1, I2:

  1. Collect own and inherited concrete class methods: C, then B, then transitive superclasses.
  2. Collect interface requirements/defaults from direct interfaces in order.
  3. Create override/implementation edges from concrete class methods to interface methods.
  4. Remove satisfied interface requirements.
  5. Only unresolved defaults/abstracts can conflict.
Class/superclass methods win over interface defaults. This prevents false conflicts when a superclass already implements all interface requirements.
Correct design

Bridge generation

for (OverrideEdge edge : overrideGraph) {
    if (NeedsBridge(edge.base, edge.derived)) {
        GenerateBridge(edge.base, edge.derived);
    }
}
  • Bridge has the base/effective callable descriptor.
  • Bridge delegates to the real derived method.
  • Bridge is synthetic and excluded from source overload sets.
  • Deduplicate by effective/assembly descriptor.
  • No independent rediscovery of override relationships in lowering.
Migration plan

Phase 0: tests and characterization

  • Add positive test: superclass method implements same method from multiple interfaces.
  • Add negative test: conflicting defaults with no class/superclass implementation.
  • Add overload-equivalence tests where return type differs.
  • Add explicit overload tests where a listed name is an implicit overload group.
  • Add overload-set ordering tests with superclass + multiple interfaces.
Tests should come before broad refactoring. They lock down both current regressions and intended spec behavior.
Migration plan

Phase 1: local false-rejection fix

Fix the concrete superclass implementation case without a full rewrite.

if (classType is class &&
    HasCommonConcreteClassImplementation(classType, sigA, sigB)) {
    return; // no interface collision
}
  • Collect class/superclass concrete implementations before reporting interface conflicts.
  • Or pass implementation information into CheckInterfaceFunctions.
  • Keep this patch small and test-focused.
Migration plan

Phase 2: pure semantic helpers

bool IsOverrideCompatible(Signature *base, Signature *derived);
bool AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature *a, Signature *b);
bool HasConcreteClassImplementation(ETSObjectType *cls, Signature *iface);
bool HasCommonConcreteClassImplementation(ETSObjectType *cls, Signature *a, Signature *b);
  • Predicates must be pure: no SetOverride() inside compatibility checks.
  • Current behavior can still call old paths while new helpers are introduced.
  • This reduces duplication before deeper migration.
Migration plan

Phase 3: separate language and ABI concepts

Language-level

  • AreOverloadEquivalent
  • ignores return type
  • uses effective parameter signature types

ABI/lowering-level

  • HaveSameAssemblySignature
  • may include return depending on use
  • drives helper/bridge decisions
This prevents accidental source-language diagnostics from depending on backend descriptor details.
Migration plan

Phase 4: effective signature type

Type *EffectiveType(Type *type);
Type *EffectiveSignatureType(Type *type);
EffectiveSignature EffectiveSignatureOf(Signature *sig);
  1. Implement helper and tests.
  2. Use it for overload-equivalence.
  3. Use it for override erasure-conflict diagnostics.
  4. Later use it for bridge necessity checks.
Migration plan

Phase 5: explicit overload expansion

This should be one coherent patch, because validation, type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree.

  • Allow listed names that resolve to implicit overload groups.
  • Expand all signatures in source/listing order.
  • Stop using CallSignatures().front() in explicit overload construction.
  • Update OverloadMappingLowering to use the selected target robustly.
Do not partially implement this. A checker that sees many candidates and a lowering phase that handles only one candidate will break.
Migration plan

Phase 6: overload-set builder behind existing API

Introduce the new builder without immediately deleting old lookup paths.

ETSObjectType::CreateSyntheticVarFromEverySignature(...) {
    auto set = OverloadSetBuilder(checker).BuildInstanceMethodSet(...);
    return CreateSyntheticFunctionTypeFrom(set);
}
  • First centralize order and expansion logic.
  • Keep callers stable.
  • Later, call resolution can consume OverloadSet directly.
Migration plan

Phase 7: build the override graph

  1. Compute graph per class/interface but do not consume it yet.
  2. Compare graph output against existing diagnostics in debug/assert tests.
  3. Migrate override diagnostics to graph.
  4. Migrate duplicate override-of-same-base detection to graph.
  5. Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to graph.
  6. Migrate overload-set duplicate suppression to graph.
This is the main path toward one consistent semantic model.
Migration plan

Phase 8: graph-driven bridge generation

Replace rediscovery in bridge phases with override-edge consumption.

for (auto edge : classType->OverrideGraph()) {
    if (NeedsBridge(edge)) {
        CreateBridge(edge);
    }
}
  • Deduplicate by effective/assembly descriptor.
  • Disable old discovery in the same patch.
  • Keep bridge body generation machinery if useful, but change its input source.
Gradual vs atomic

Can be done gradually

  • Add characterization tests.
  • Add pure helper functions.
  • Fix superclass method satisfying multiple interfaces.
  • Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision.
  • Add effective signature type helper.
  • Introduce overload-set builder behind existing API.
  • Build override graph without consuming it.
  • Migrate diagnostics one by one to graph.
Gradual vs atomic

Should be done all at once

ChangeWhy atomic?
Explicit overload expansionValidation, type construction, resolution, and lowering must agree about candidate count/order.
Resolved call target representationChecker and lowering must switch together from owner-var assumptions to explicit target metadata.
Bridge generation sourceRunning old rediscovery and new graph-driven generation together risks duplicate or missing bridges.
Direct overload-set call resolutionMemberExpression, CallExpression, method references, and explicit overload lowering must be aligned.
Effective overload-equivalence across all declarationsFunctions, methods, interfaces, and constructors must use the same language rule.
Recommended implementation order

Practical sequence

  1. Tests + local fix for superclass method implementing multiple interfaces.
  2. Pure helpers for override compatibility and overload-equivalence.
  3. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision.
  4. Implement effective signature type and use it for overload-equivalence.
  5. Atomic explicit overload expansion patch.
  6. Introduce overload-set builder behind current APIs.
  7. Produce override graph but keep old behavior initially.
  8. Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to graph.
  9. Migrate overload-set duplicate suppression to graph.
  10. Atomic graph-driven bridge generation switch.
  11. Remove obsolete synthetic/ad-hoc overload paths.
Tests to protect design

Minimum coverage matrix

AreaTests
Multiple interfacesSuperclass method implements two interfaces; conflicting defaults without class method; diamond interface inheritance.
Override compatibilityContravariant params, covariant returns, access weakening, final method, duplicate override of same base method.
Overload-equivalenceSame params different return; generic erasure collisions; constructor overload-equivalence.
Overload orderTextual order; explicit list order; own before superclass before interfaces; implements/extends order.
Explicit overloadsListed implicit overload group expansion; inherited explicit overload from multiple interfaces; alias same as method name.
Runtime dispatchCall through superclass reference and interface reference; one method overriding several inherited signatures; bridge dispatch.
Conclusion

The end state

The frontend should stop rediscovering overload and override facts at each phase. It should compute them once, store them explicitly, and let call resolution and lowering consume them.

Predictable

Spec order and inheritance behavior become visible and testable.

Correct

Class inheritance and multiple interfaces share one override model.

Maintainable

Bridge generation, diagnostics, and overload resolution use the same facts.

1 / 1
Use ←/→, Space, Home/End

ETS frontend design review

Overriding, Overloading,
and Overload Resolution

A more detailed and explanatory slide deck covering what the spec requires, what the current frontend does, where it is fragile, and how to migrate gradually toward a correct design for inheritance and multiple interface implementation.

Spec source: 15_semantics.rst Bridge source: 20_implementation.rst Frontend: ets2panda Focus: classes + interfaces + overload sets
How to read this deck

Purpose and assumptions

This deck is not a patch proposal for one small bug only. It is a design review of a whole semantic area. The goal is to explain how overriding, overloading, overload resolution, class inheritance, and multiple interface implementation should fit together in the ETS frontend.

What this deck covers

  • Spec-derived behavior.
  • Current implementation structure.
  • Concrete deficiencies and why they matter.
  • A target design based on explicit semantic facts.
  • A staged migration plan.

Important assumption

“Compiler implementation” here means the ets2panda frontend pipeline: parser, scope init/binder, checker, lowering, and codegen handoff. The optimizing/backend compiler should not own source-language overload and override decisions.

Executive summary

The current frontend has pieces, but not one model

The current implementation is not empty or naive. It already parses explicit overload declarations, groups same-name methods, resolves calls by scanning signatures, validates many override cases, and creates bridge methods. The problem is that these pieces are not coordinated by one semantic representation.

Works for many simple cases

Simple same-name methods, ordinary class overrides, and many direct method calls are already handled.

Fragile for hard cases

Multiple interfaces, inherited explicit overload aliases, erasure collisions, and bridge requirements are handled by separate mechanisms that can disagree.

Needed end state

The checker should compute override edges and overload sets once. Lowering should consume those facts, not rediscover them.

Key idea: the frontend needs explicit semantic products: an override graph, spec-ordered overload sets, and resolved call targets.

Terminology

Glossary for the rest of the deck

TermMeaning in this discussion
SignatureType parameters, parameter types, return type, flags, owner method/function.
Override-compatibleSpec relation that allows a subtype method to override a supertype method.
Overload-equivalentSpec relation used to reject duplicate implicit overload declarations. It ignores return type.
Overload setOrdered list of callable candidates for a name. Resolution scans this list and picks the first valid candidate.
Explicit overload aliasA declaration such as overload foo { a, b } that gives a name and order to a set of callables.
Effective signature typeSpec-defined erased/effective type used for overload-equivalence and erasure-related diagnostics.
Bridge methodSynthetic method generated so runtime dispatch works when source-level overriding uses a different erased/ABI descriptor.
Spec overview

Overriding: what the checker must decide

Overriding is about runtime polymorphism. A method selected at compile time may be replaced at runtime by a more specific method from the actual object type. Therefore the checker must know exactly which methods override which inherited methods.

  • Constructors do not override.
  • Only accessible inherited methods and accessors are override candidates.
  • Private methods do not participate as inherited override targets.
  • Static methods are not instance override targets.
  • A method marked override must actually override something.
  • A subtype method may override several inherited methods.
  • Two different subtype methods must not override the same inherited method.

Overriding must be analyzed independently of overload resolution. Overload resolution chooses the compile-time signature; overriding determines the runtime implementation.

Spec overview

Override compatibility: parameter and return variance

For a derived method to override a base method, it must be safe to call the derived method wherever the base method was expected. This creates two variance directions.

Parameters: contravariant

If the base accepts Derived, the overriding method may accept Base. That is safe because every Derived is also a Base.

interface B { m(p: Derived): void }
interface D extends B { m(p: Base): void }

Return: covariant

If the base promises Base, the overriding method may return Derived. That is safe because the caller still receives a Base.

interface B { m(): Base }
interface D extends B { m(): Derived }

The checker should implement this as one pure relation helper. It should not be duplicated in interface validation, method checking, and bridge lowering.

Spec overview

Overloading: first-match compile-time dispatch

Overloading is different from overriding. Overloading is compile-time polymorphism by name. A call is resolved against an ordered set of candidates, and the first candidate that can be called is selected. Candidates after the first valid one are ignored.

  1. Build the overload set for the callee name.
  2. Preserve the order required by the spec.
  3. For each candidate, check whether the provided arguments can call it.
  4. Pick the first valid candidate.
  5. Do not use return type to select the overload.
function f1(p: number) {}
function f2(p: number | string) {}
function f3(p: string) {}

overload foo { f1, f2, f3 }
foo("x") // f2 wins; f3 is never considered
Spec overview

Overload-equivalence is not signature identity

Implicit overloads cannot contain two overload-equivalent signatures. The important subtlety is that the return type is irrelevant for overload-equivalence.

function foo(x: number): string { return "" }
function foo(x: number): number { return 1 }
// Should be compile-time error.
// Return type cannot distinguish overloads.

What to compare

  • same number of parameters;
  • effective signature type of each parameter.

What not to compare

  • return type;
  • method body;
  • source parameter names.

This deserves a dedicated helper, not reuse of ordinary signature identity.

Spec overview

Explicit overload declarations can expand implicit groups

An explicit overload declaration lists names, not necessarily single signatures. If a listed name denotes an implicit overload group, the group expands at that position.

function foo(x: number) {}
function foo(x: string) {}
function bar(x: boolean) {}

overload baz { foo, bar }

// baz's overload set should be:
// 1. foo(number)
// 2. foo(string)
// 3. bar(boolean)

This is one of the places where using CallSignatures().front() is incorrect. The implementation must preserve all signatures in order.

Spec overview

Class method overload-set order

For an instance method call, the static receiver type determines the overload set. The set is not just “all methods with that name”. It is ordered by specificity and source order.

  1. Add explicit/implicit methods declared in the current class.
  2. Append the direct superclass overload set.
  3. Append each direct superinterface overload set in implements order.
  4. Skip methods already represented by an earlier overriding candidate.
class D extends C implements I1, I2 {
    foo(x: boolean) {}
}
// overload set for D.foo:
// own D.foo candidates,
// then C.foo set,
// then I1.foo set,
// then I2.foo set
Spec overview

Overloading and overriding interact, but at different times

Compile-time overload resolution selects a signature using the static type. Runtime dispatch then uses the actual object type to find the overriding implementation for that selected signature.

class C1 {}
class C2 extends C1 {}

class A {
    foo(c: C2) { console.log("A.C2") }
    foo(c: C1) { console.log("A.C1") }
}
class B extends A {
    override foo(c: C2) { console.log("B.C2") }
}

let a: A = new B()
a.foo(new C2()) // overload selects A.foo(C2), runtime calls B.foo(C2)
a.foo(new C1()) // overload selects A.foo(C1), runtime calls A.foo(C1)

The frontend must preserve both facts: the selected compile-time signature and the override relation used for runtime dispatch/bridges.

Spec overview

Effective types and bridge methods

Effective signature types are needed when source types erase to broader runtime representations. If a derived method overrides a base method but the runtime descriptor differs, a synthetic bridge method may be required.

class B<T extends Object> {
    foo(p: T) {}
}
class D extends B<string> {
    foo(p: string) {}
    // compiler may need synthetic foo(p: Object)
    // bridge body casts p to string and calls foo(string)
}

Source semantics

D.foo(string) correctly overrides B.foo(T) after substitution.

Runtime need

A caller through B<string> may dispatch by the erased/base descriptor, so the derived class must contain a matching bridge.

Current implementation map

Where the feature currently lives

ResponsibilityCurrent frontend areaObservation
Syntaxparser/ETSparser*.cpp, ir/base/overloadDeclaration.*Explicit overload nodes and modifiers exist.
Same-name method groupingcompiler/lowering/scopesInit/scopesInitPhase.cppSame-name methods are grouped in MethodDefinition::Overloads().
Bindingvarbinder/ETSBinder.cppExplicit overload declarations become variables with OVERLOAD flag.
Call resolutionchecker/ets/function.cppFirst-match over signature vectors already exists.
Member lookupchecker/types/ets/etsObjectType.cppLookup may create synthetic variables/signature containers.
Class/interface validationchecker/ets/object.cppInterface collision and abstract implementation logic lives here.
LoweringoverloadMappingLowering.cpp, bridge phasesLowering rewrites overload aliases and generates bridge methods.
Current architecture

The current flow is implicit and side-effectful

AST declarations→ scope grouping→ property lookup→ synthetic function types→ call signature vector→ lowering rediscovery

Several operations that should be explicit semantic analysis are currently embedded in property lookup or in local checks. This makes behavior hard to predict because the result depends on which lookup flags and checker contexts were active when a property was requested.

The design smell is that asking for a property can also build an overload set, create a synthetic variable, and affect later call behavior.

Finding #1

No single source of truth for overriding

The same semantic relation — “derived method X overrides base method Y” — is calculated in several places for different purposes. That creates divergence risk.

Current style

  • Method checker decides some override facts.
  • Interface checker separately compares interface methods.
  • Bridge phases scan supertypes again.
  • Overload collection suppresses candidates with its own logic.

Consequence

  • Diagnostics and bridge generation can disagree.
  • Multiple-interface cases are fragile.
  • Hard to reason about one method overriding several inherited methods.
  • Hard to detect duplicate override-of-same-base uniformly.

The checker should compute override edges once and make every consumer use them.

Finding #2

Multiple interface conflicts can be checked too early

When a class implements several interfaces, an apparent conflict between interface methods may already be resolved by a concrete method in the class or superclass chain. The checker must account for the class hierarchy before reporting an interface conflict.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string }
interface I2 { foo(): string }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}

Correct interpretation

C1.foo implements both I1.foo and I2.foo. C2 inherits that implementation.

What goes wrong if rejected

The checker treats I1.foo and I2.foo as conflicting interface members before checking the class hierarchy implementation.

Even if a specific build accepts the abstract-interface variant, the same deficiency appears in related default-method cases if class methods should dominate interface defaults.

Finding #2 explained

Correct algorithm for class + multiple interfaces

  1. Collect concrete instance methods declared in the class.
  2. Collect concrete instance methods inherited from the superclass chain.
  3. Collect abstract/default methods from direct and indirect interfaces.
  4. For each interface method, check whether a concrete class/superclass method implements it.
  5. Remove satisfied interface requirements from the conflict set.
  6. Only report conflicts among unresolved interface defaults/requirements.
// For C2:
C1.foo -> I1.foo
C1.foo -> I2.foo

// Both requirements satisfied; no conflict remains.

This is naturally represented by an override/implementation graph.

Finding #3

Overload-equivalence is not cleanly implemented

Current logic around duplicate overloads mixes several concepts: signature identity, return type, assembly descriptor collision, and helper overload generation. This is dangerous because the spec has a simpler source-level rule.

Language-level question

Are these two declarations illegally overload-equivalent in source?

same parameter count
same effective parameter types
ignore return type

ABI-level question

Will these two methods collide in generated descriptors or require helper/bridge methods?

assembly type descriptors
possibly include return
backend/runtime constraints

These questions should not be answered by the same helper.

Finding #4

Effective signature type is not explicit

The spec gives effective type mapping rules. The implementation needs an actual helper that represents this mapping, otherwise the checker will keep using approximations such as ordinary subtyping or assembler type strings.

Type *EffectiveType(Type *type);
Type *EffectiveSignatureType(Type *type);
EffectiveSignature EffectiveSignatureOf(Signature *sig);
  • Use this helper for overload-equivalence.
  • Use it for “not override-compatible but erasure-compatible” diagnostics.
  • Use it later for bridge necessity decisions.

This reduces the risk that different subsystems implement slightly different erasure semantics.

Finding #5

Explicit overload declarations mishandle groups

Spec allows a listed name inside an explicit overload declaration to denote an implicit overload group. Current code can reject this or keep only the first signature.

function foo(x: number) {}
function foo(x: string) {}

overload callFoo { foo }
// should include both foo(number) and foo(string)

Current risk

Using CallSignatures().front() silently drops overload candidates.

Required behavior

Expand all call signatures of the listed overload group in declaration order.

Finding #6

Overload-set formation is too implicit

The checker should be able to answer “what is the overload set for this name and static receiver type?” without triggering a complex property lookup with synthetic variables and special flags.

OverloadSet BuildFunctionOverloadSet(scope, name);
OverloadSet BuildStaticMethodOverloadSet(classType, name);
OverloadSet BuildInstanceMethodOverloadSet(objectType, name);
OverloadSet BuildInterfaceMethodOverloadSet(interfaceType, name);
OverloadSet BuildConstructorOverloadSet(classType);

Once overload-set formation is explicit, ordering and inherited candidate skipping become testable.

Finding #7

Explicit overload inheritance is too name-based

The spec says that if explicit overloads are inherited from supertypes, a subtype declaration may need to include all inherited overloaded methods. This must be checked by resolved semantic targets, not just text names.

interface I1 { overload foo { f1, f2 } }
interface I2 { overload foo { f3, f4 } }

class C implements I1, I2 {
    // should need a new overload foo that includes all relevant methods
}
  • Name comparison is not enough because methods can be inherited, overridden, imported, or represented by overloaded groups.
  • If no local overload declaration exists, the checker must still detect conflicting inherited aliases.
Finding #8

Bridge generation rediscovers checker semantics

Generic and override bridge phases currently scan the class hierarchy again. That means bridge generation performs its own override analysis instead of using the checker's result.

Problem

  • Bridge phase may miss an override the checker accepted.
  • Bridge phase may generate a bridge for a relation the checker would reject.
  • Deduplication is harder.

Better

  • Checker records override edges.
  • Lowering asks each edge whether a bridge is needed.
  • Bridge generation becomes mechanical.
Target design

Three explicit semantic products

1. Override graph

Edges from derived signatures to base/interface signatures they override or implement.

2. Overload sets

Ordered vectors of call candidates built from declarations, explicit overload aliases, and inheritance.

3. Resolved call target

The concrete selected function/method/constructor target attached to every call expression.

Declarations→ Signatures→ Override graph→ Overload sets→ Resolved calls→ Lowering / bridges
Target design

Override graph in detail

struct OverrideEdge {
    Signature *derived;
    Signature *base;
    OverrideKind kind;      // class override, interface override, implementation
    bool requiresBridge;
};

The graph is computed once the type's own members and supertypes are known. It should be built by pure compatibility checks followed by explicit marking.

  • Diagnostics use the graph to report bad override, final override, access weakening, return mismatch, and type parameter issues.
  • Interface implementation validation uses the graph to know which requirements are satisfied.
  • Overload-set construction uses the graph to avoid adding overridden inherited methods twice.
  • Bridge generation uses the graph to know exactly which base descriptors must be supported.
Target design

Overload candidate representation

struct OverloadCandidate {
    Signature *signature;
    varbinder::LocalVariable *variable;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    CandidateOrigin origin; // own, explicit, superclass, interface
    size_t sourceOrder;
};

A candidate is more than a signature. Lowering needs to know which declaration was selected. Diagnostics may need the origin. Ordering must be stable and spec-derived.

This also avoids guessing selected targets later from Signature::OwnerVar(), which is fragile with synthetic/helper/imported signatures.

Target design

Resolved call target

After overload resolution, the call expression should store both the selected signature and the selected semantic target.

struct ResolvedCallTarget {
    Signature *signature;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    varbinder::Variable *variable;
    CallTargetKind kind; // function, instance method, static method, constructor
};

callExpr->SetSignature(target.signature);
callExpr->SetResolvedCallTarget(target);

Checker responsibility

Resolve overloads and choose a target using source-language semantics.

Lowering responsibility

Rewrite syntax according to the already selected target. Do not redo overload resolution.

Target design

Graph-driven bridge generation

for (OverrideEdge edge : classType->OverrideGraph()) {
    if (NeedsBridge(edge.base, edge.derived)) {
        GenerateBridge(edge.base, edge.derived);
    }
}

This makes bridge generation a mechanical consequence of checker semantics. The bridge phase no longer needs to ask “does this method override that method?” It only asks “does this already-known override edge need an ABI/runtime adapter?”

  • Deduplicate bridges by effective or assembly descriptor.
  • Mark generated methods as synthetic/bridge.
  • Exclude bridge methods from source overload sets.
  • Preserve existing bridge body generation machinery where it is correct.
Migration plan

Principle: do not rewrite everything at once

The current code is intertwined with many other frontend phases. A total rewrite would be risky. The safe strategy is to introduce better semantic primitives while keeping existing APIs alive, then migrate consumers one by one.

Good gradual changes

Add tests, helper predicates, local bug fixes, a builder behind old APIs, and an override graph initially used for validation/debug.

Atomic changes

Some changes must update checker + lowering together, especially explicit overload expansion and resolved call target representation.

Migration phase 0

Add characterization tests first

Before refactoring, write tests that describe both current failures and intended behavior. These tests become the safety net for each later phase.

AreaTests
Multiple interfacesSuperclass method satisfies two interface methods; class method dominates interface defaults if specified; conflicting defaults without class method.
Override compatibilityContravariant params, covariant returns, access weakening, final method override, duplicate override of same base.
Overload-equivalenceSame parameters with different returns; generic/effective type collisions; constructors.
Explicit overloadsListed implicit overload group expansion; alias same as method; inherited aliases from multiple interfaces.
Runtime dispatchCalls through superclass and interface references; bridge dispatch; one method overrides several inherited methods.
Migration phase 1

Local fix for class method satisfying multiple interfaces

This is the first practical patch because it addresses a concrete deficiency without forcing the whole redesign.

bool HasConcreteClassImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                    Signature *interfaceSig);

bool HasCommonConcreteClassImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                          Signature *a,
                                          Signature *b);

Before reporting a collision between two interface methods inherited by a class, check whether a concrete method in the class or its superclass chain implements both.

if (HasCommonConcreteClassImplementation(classType, sigA, sigB)) {
    return; // conflict resolved by class hierarchy
}
Migration phase 2

Extract pure semantic helpers

The next step is to make semantic relations explicit and side-effect-free. A predicate should not mutate the AST or mark a method as overriding while answering a yes/no question.

bool IsOverrideCompatible(Signature *base, Signature *derived);
bool AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature *a, Signature *b);
bool IsConcreteImplementationOf(Signature *impl, Signature *requirement);

Before

Compatibility checks can call SetOverride() as a side effect.

After

First compute compatibility. Then a separate analyzer records or marks the override relation.

Migration phase 3

Separate overload-equivalence from ABI collision

This is a cleanup with behavior impact. It prevents source-language diagnostics from depending on backend descriptor behavior.

// Source-language rule
bool AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature *a, Signature *b);

// Backend/helper/bridge rule
bool HaveSameAssemblySignature(Signature *a, Signature *b, bool includeReturn);

// Ambient/helper-specific rule
bool NeedHelperOverload(...);

Apply the language-level helper consistently to functions, methods, interfaces, and constructors.

Migration phase 4

Implement effective signature type

Start by implementing the helper without replacing every use immediately. Then migrate one consumer at a time.

  1. Implement EffectiveType and EffectiveSignatureType.
  2. Use it in AreOverloadEquivalent.
  3. Add erasure-collision override diagnostics.
  4. Use it in bridge necessity checks after override graph is available.

Do not confuse effective signature type with the assembler descriptor. They are related but serve different semantic layers.

Migration phase 5

Atomic explicit overload expansion patch

This change should be done all at once because validation, type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree about how many candidates an explicit overload alias has.

  • Allow listed names that resolve to implicit overload groups.
  • Expand all signatures of a listed group in source order.
  • Remove front()-only behavior from explicit overload construction.
  • Store selected target after resolution.
  • Update overload mapping lowering to consume the selected target.

A partial implementation is dangerous: the checker could resolve to a candidate that lowering cannot correctly rewrite.

Migration phase 6

Introduce overload-set builder behind existing APIs

Do not immediately delete synthetic property lookup behavior. Instead, make it delegate to the new builder first.

ETSObjectType::CreateSyntheticVarFromEverySignature(...) {
    auto set = OverloadSetBuilder(checker).BuildInstanceMethodSet(...);
    return CreateSyntheticFunctionTypeFrom(set);
}

This lets existing call sites keep working while overload set formation becomes centralized and testable.

Migration phase 7

Compute override graph, then migrate consumers

The override graph can be introduced before it is used for all decisions. Initially, compute it and compare it with old behavior in assertions/debug logs or focused tests.

  1. Build graph per class/interface.
  2. Use it for override keyword diagnostics.
  3. Use it for final/access/return diagnostics.
  4. Use it for duplicate override-of-same-base detection.
  5. Use it for interface implementation and conflict validation.
  6. Use it for inherited overload candidate suppression.
Migration phase 8

Atomic switch to graph-driven bridge generation

Once override graph consumers are stable, bridge generation should stop rediscovering overrides and consume graph edges instead.

  • Disable old bridge discovery in the same patch.
  • Generate bridges from override edges.
  • Deduplicate by effective/assembly descriptor.
  • Reuse bridge body builders where possible.
  • Add runtime dispatch tests for generated bridges.

Running old and new bridge discovery together risks duplicate bridge methods or inconsistent signatures.

Gradual vs atomic

What can be done gradually

  • Add characterization tests.
  • Add pure semantic helpers.
  • Fix superclass method satisfying multiple interfaces.
  • Split source overload-equivalence from ABI collision helpers.
  • Add effective signature type helper.
  • Introduce overload-set builder behind current APIs.
  • Compute override graph without consuming it heavily.
  • Migrate diagnostics and validations one by one to the graph.
  • Clean up obsolete helper paths after replacement.
Gradual vs atomic

What should be done all at once

ChangeWhy it must be atomic
Explicit overload group expansionChecker, synthetic type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree on candidate count and order.
Resolved call target representationChecker and lowering must switch together, otherwise lowering will keep relying on fragile owner-variable assumptions.
Graph-driven bridge generationOld and new bridge discovery running together can create duplicate or missing bridge methods.
Direct overload-set call resolutionMember expressions, call expressions, method references, and explicit overload aliases must share the same candidate source.
Global effective overload-equivalenceFunctions, methods, constructors, and interfaces must follow the same source-language duplicate rule.
Recommended order

Practical implementation sequence

  1. Add tests and fix concrete superclass method implementing multiple interfaces.
  2. Add pure override compatibility and overload-equivalence helpers.
  3. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision logic.
  4. Implement effective signature type and use it for overload-equivalence.
  5. Implement explicit overload group expansion as an atomic patch.
  6. Introduce overload-set builder behind existing synthetic property APIs.
  7. Compute override graph but keep old behavior initially.
  8. Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to override graph.
  9. Migrate overload-set inherited duplicate suppression to override graph.
  10. Switch bridge generation to override graph atomically.
  11. Remove old ad-hoc/synthetic overload paths where no longer needed.
Final architecture

End state: explicit semantic pipeline

Parse declarations→ Bind names/scopes→ Build signatures→ Build override graph→ Build overload sets→ Resolve calls→ Lower aliases/bridges→ Codegen

Correctness

Multiple interface implementation and class hierarchy methods are resolved using one override model.

Traceability

Diagnostics, call resolution, and bridge generation can point to the same semantic facts.

Maintainability

Future spec changes affect central helpers instead of scattered property lookup and lowering code.

Key takeaway

Do not let lookup, checking, and lowering rediscover the same semantics

The source-language truth should be produced once by the checker: which methods override which inherited methods, what ordered candidates each overloaded name has, and what target each call selected. Once these are explicit, class inheritance and multiple interface implementation become much easier to reason about and test.

The first low-risk step is still practical: fix interface conflict checking to account for concrete class/superclass implementations before reporting a collision.

content.text:
Yes, but I would **not** expose a direct plugin-facing API like:

```cpp
RecomputeOverrideGraph(...)
RecomputeOverloadSet(...)
```

at least not as the main interface.

I would expose a higher-level **semantic invalidation / incremental reanalysis API**, and make override/overload graph recomputation an internal consequence of that API.

Reason: override/overload graphs are not independent data. They depend on binding, scopes, type annotations, type aliases, generic constraints, class/interface hierarchy, member order, explicit overload declarations, and call-site resolution. If a plugin directly recomputes only the graph, it can easily leave stale semantic state elsewhere.

---

# Short answer

## Should you provide an interface?

**Yes**, but the interface should be:

```text
“AST changed here; this kind of semantic information is dirty; reanalyze affected region.”
```

not:

```text
“Plugin manually recomputes override graph / overload graph.”
```

## Recommended public shape

Expose something like:

```cpp
enum class SemanticChangeKind {
    BODY_ONLY,
    CALL_SITE,
    LOCAL_DECLARATION,
    FUNCTION_SIGNATURE,
    CLASS_MEMBER_SET,
    CLASS_HERITAGE,
    INTERFACE_HERITAGE,
    EXPLICIT_OVERLOAD_DECLARATION,
    TYPE_ALIAS_OR_GENERIC_BOUND,
    MODULE_IMPORT_EXPORT,
    UNKNOWN,
};

class SemanticUpdateContext {
public:
    void MarkChanged(ir::AstNode *node, SemanticChangeKind kind);
    void Apply();
};
```

Internally, `Apply()` decides whether to:

- rebind a subtree;
- rebuild function/method signatures;
- invalidate object properties;
- recompute override graph;
- recompute overload sets;
- re-resolve affected calls;
- regenerate bridge/helper metadata;
- or fall back to full module/program recheck.

---

# Why direct graph recompute is dangerous

The override/overload graph is only one derived cache.

A plugin AST mutation can invalidate many connected things:

```text
AST
 ↓
Scopes / bindings
 ↓
Variables / declarations
 ↓
Signatures
 ↓
Object properties
 ↓
Override graph
 ↓
Overload sets
 ↓
Resolved call targets
 ↓
Bridge decisions
 ↓
Lowered code
```

If a plugin changes a method signature and only calls:

```cpp
RecomputeOverrideGraph(C)
```

then the frontend may still have stale:

- `Identifier::Variable()`;
- `Variable::TsType()`;
- `MethodDefinition::TsType()`;
- `ScriptFunction::Signature()`;
- object property maps;
- explicit overload alias signatures;
- `CallExpression::Signature()`;
- bridge method requirements;
- type relation caches;
- diagnostics.

So a direct graph recompute API would be too easy to misuse.

---

# Phase-dependent policy

Because plugins can run at different pipeline points, the right invalidation behavior depends heavily on the phase.

## 1. Plugin after parse, before binding/checking

If a plugin modifies AST here, there is usually no need for override/overload recompute because semantic information has not been built yet.

Allowed:

```text
AST structural changes
```

Required after plugin:

```text
normal scope init → binding → checking pipeline
```

No special graph API needed.

---

## 2. Plugin after bind, before check

Now scopes and variables may exist, but checker graphs probably do not yet exist.

If plugin modifies declarations, names, class members, imports, etc., it must invalidate or rebuild binding information.

Useful API:

```cpp
RebindSubtree(node)
RebindDeclarationOwner(node)
```

But still probably no override/overload graph recompute yet, because signatures and override facts are checker products.

---

## 3. Plugin after check

This is where the incremental semantic API matters most.

After checker has run, AST mutations may invalidate:

- signatures;
- override graph;
- overload sets;
- resolved calls;
- bridges;
- lowered helper declarations.

So after-check plugins should not freely mutate checked AST without going through an update context.

Example:

```cpp
auto update = ctx.BeginSemanticUpdate();
plugin.ModifyAst(...);
update.MarkChanged(method, SemanticChangeKind::FUNCTION_SIGNATURE);
update.Apply();
```

This is the main place where an incremental recompute interface can save resources compared with full program recheck.

---

## 4. Plugin after lowering

At this point source-level semantic changes are very risky.

I would strongly restrict plugins here:

- body-local low-level transformations only;
- no externally visible declaration changes;
- no class heritage changes;
- no method signature changes;
- no overload declaration changes.

If a plugin changes declarations after lowering, I would either:

1. reject the mutation; or
2. force full recheck/re-lowering of the affected program.

Incremental graph recompute alone is not enough after lowering, because already-lowered AST may encode previous semantic decisions.

---

# What should be invalidated for each change kind

## Body-only change

Example:

```ts
foo(): number {
    return 1
}
```

changed to:

```ts
foo(): number {
    return 2
}
```

Needed:

- recheck function body;
- re-resolve calls inside that body if callee/args changed;
- no override graph recompute;
- no overload-set recompute.

Change kind:

```cpp
SemanticChangeKind::BODY_ONLY
```

---

## Call-site change

Example:

```ts
x.foo(1)
```

changed to:

```ts
x.foo("a")
```

Needed:

- recheck expression;
- rerun overload resolution for this call;
- no class override graph recompute.

Change kind:

```cpp
SemanticChangeKind::CALL_SITE
```

---

## Function/method signature change

Example:

```ts
foo(x: number): string
```

changed to:

```ts
foo(x: string): string
```

Needed:

- rebuild function signature;
- invalidate containing class/interface property for that method name;
- recompute overload set for that name;
- recompute override graph for containing type;
- recompute override graph for derived classes / implementing classes;
- re-resolve call sites that may target this overload set;
- recompute bridge requirements.

Change kind:

```cpp
SemanticChangeKind::FUNCTION_SIGNATURE
```

This cannot be solved by local method recheck only.

---

## Class member set change

Example:

```ts
class C {
    foo() {}
}
```

plugin adds:

```ts
bar() {}
```

or removes/renames/reorders methods.

Needed:

- update class scope;
- update object properties;
- update overload sets for changed names;
- recompute override graph if methods participate in overriding;
- re-resolve affected call sites.

Change kind:

```cpp
SemanticChangeKind::CLASS_MEMBER_SET
```

---

## Class/interface heritage change

Example:

```ts
class C extends A implements I
```

changed to:

```ts
class C extends B implements I, J
```

Needed:

- rebuild type hierarchy;
- recompute inherited members;
- recompute override graph for `C`;
- recompute override graph for all subclasses of `C`;
- recompute overload sets for many names;
- re-resolve many call sites;
- recompute bridge requirements.

Change kind:

```cpp
SemanticChangeKind::CLASS_HERITAGE
```

This is expensive. In early implementation, I would conservatively escalate to full module/program recheck.

---

## Explicit overload declaration change

Example:

```ts
overload foo { a, b }
```

changed to:

```ts
overload foo { b, a, c }
```

Needed:

- revalidate overload declaration;
- rebuild explicit overload alias candidate list;
- re-resolve calls to alias `foo`;
- maybe recompute inherited explicit overload conflicts;
- no override graph recompute unless listed methods or inheritance changed.

Change kind:

```cpp
SemanticChangeKind::EXPLICIT_OVERLOAD_DECLARATION
```

---

## Type alias or generic bound change

Example:

```ts
type T = string
```

changed to:

```ts
type T = number
```

or:

```ts
class C<T extends A>
```

changed to:

```ts
class C<T extends B>
```

This can affect many signatures indirectly.

Needed:

- invalidate all signatures depending on that type;
- invalidate overload-equivalence results;
- invalidate override compatibility;
- invalidate bridges;
- invalidate call resolution.

Change kind:

```cpp
SemanticChangeKind::TYPE_ALIAS_OR_GENERIC_BOUND
```

This is hard to make precise without dependency tracking. Initially, escalate conservatively.

---

# Recommended API design

## 1. Do not let plugins edit semantic caches directly

Bad public API:

```cpp
ctx.RecomputeOverrideGraph(classType);
ctx.RecomputeOverloadSet(classType, name);
ctx.ReplaceCallTarget(call, target);
```

This exposes internal representation and lets plugins create inconsistent state.

Better public API:

```cpp
class SemanticUpdateContext {
public:
    void MarkChanged(ir::AstNode *node, SemanticChangeKind kind);
    void Apply();
};
```

The frontend remains responsible for correct invalidation.

---

## 2. Provide coarse invalidation first

Start simple and conservative.

Example policy:

```cpp
BODY_ONLY
    -> rebind/recheck containing function body

CALL_SITE
    -> recheck containing expression/function body

FUNCTION_SIGNATURE
    -> recheck containing class/interface + direct dependents

CLASS_MEMBER_SET
    -> recheck containing class/interface + direct dependents

CLASS_HERITAGE / INTERFACE_HERITAGE
    -> full module or full program recheck initially

TYPE_ALIAS_OR_GENERIC_BOUND
    -> full module or full program recheck initially

UNKNOWN
    -> full program recheck
```

This gives correctness first. Later you can optimize.

---

## 3. Add dependency indexes later

To avoid full program rechecks safely, you need dependency indexes.

Useful indexes:

```cpp
base type -> derived classes
interface -> implementing classes
type alias -> signatures that use it
method name + static receiver type -> call sites
explicit overload alias -> call sites
signature -> bridge methods generated from it
```

Then an update can find the affected closure.

Example:

```text
I.foo signature changed
  -> subinterfaces of I
  -> classes implementing I
  -> override graphs of those types
  -> overload sets for name foo
  -> calls whose static receiver type is I or affected subtype
  -> bridges for affected override edges
```

Without these indexes, fine-grained recompute is guesswork.

---

# Suggested internal architecture

## Semantic cache manager

Introduce a manager that owns all derived semantic caches:

```cpp
class SemanticCacheManager {
public:
    void Invalidate(ir::AstNode *node, SemanticChangeKind kind);
    void RecomputeAffected();

private:
    void InvalidateScopes(...);
    void InvalidateSignatures(...);
    void InvalidateObjectProperties(...);
    void InvalidateOverrideGraphs(...);
    void InvalidateOverloadSets(...);
    void InvalidateCallTargets(...);
    void InvalidateBridgeRequirements(...);
};
```

Plugins call only the public invalidation API. The cache manager handles the rest.

---

## Versioning / epochs

Each major semantic object can have a version:

```cpp
struct SemanticEpochs {
    uint64_t scopeEpoch;
    uint64_t signatureEpoch;
    uint64_t hierarchyEpoch;
    uint64_t overrideGraphEpoch;
    uint64_t overloadSetEpoch;
    uint64_t callResolutionEpoch;
};
```

Cached data records the epochs it depends on. If dependency epochs change, cached data is stale.

This is safer than trying to remember every cache manually.

---

# How this interacts with override/overload graph design

The proposed override/overload model actually makes incremental plugin support easier.

Without explicit graphs:

```text
plugin changes AST
  -> property lookup, synthetic vars, signatures, bridges all have hidden dependencies
```

With explicit semantic products:

```text
plugin changes AST
  -> invalidate signatures
  -> invalidate override graph
  -> invalidate overload sets
  -> invalidate affected calls
  -> regenerate bridges
```

The dependency chain is visible.

So I would design the override/overload graph with invalidation in mind from the start.

---

# What I would expose to plugin authors

## Minimal safe public API

```cpp
class PluginSemanticAPI {
public:
    SemanticUpdateContext BeginSemanticUpdate();

    void RebindSubtree(ir::AstNode *node);
    void RecheckSubtree(ir::AstNode *node);

    // Optional convenience:
    void ReplaceNode(ir::AstNode *oldNode,
                     ir::AstNode *newNode,
                     SemanticChangeKind kind);

    void AddClassMember(ir::ClassDefinition *cls,
                        ir::AstNode *member,
                        SemanticChangeKind kind);

    void RemoveClassMember(ir::ClassDefinition *cls,
                           ir::AstNode *member,
                           SemanticChangeKind kind);
};
```

## Not public initially

I would keep these internal:

```cpp
RecomputeOverrideGraph(...)
RecomputeOverloadSet(...)
RecomputeBridgeRequirements(...)
```

They can exist, but they should be implementation details of `SemanticCacheManager`.

---

# Practical recommendation

## Short term

Do **not** provide fine-grained public graph recompute yet.

Provide:

```cpp
MarkChanged(node, kind)
Apply()
```

with conservative fallback.

Initially, for hard changes, use full module/program recheck.

## Medium term

After the override graph and overload-set builder exist, add internal incremental recomputation:

- recompute graph for one class/interface;
- recompute overload set for one type/name;
- re-resolve indexed call sites.

Still keep plugin API invalidation-based.

## Long term

Expose more precise APIs only if plugin authors genuinely need them, and only as high-level semantic operations, not raw graph mutation.

---

# Answer in one sentence

Yes, you should support incremental recomputation for plugin AST mutations, but expose it as a **semantic invalidation/reanalysis interface**, not as direct plugin-controlled override/overload graph recomputation; the frontend should own dependency tracking and decide whether local recompute or full recheck is safe.

Yes: if you prioritize correctness and do **not** want to rely on plugins setting precise invalidation marks, then the safest design is:

> After any plugin phase that may have modified AST, conservatively discard semantic caches and rerun the required semantic pipeline. Recompute override graph and overload sets as normal checker products.

Do **not** expose plugin-controlled “recompute override graph for X” as the main mechanism.

---

# 1. How expensive is override graph computation?

Usually, **not very expensive compared with a full type check**.

Let:

- `T` = number of classes/interfaces;
- `M` = number of methods/accessors/constructors;
- `E` = number of inheritance / implements / extends edges;
- `H` = average inheritance depth;
- `K` = average number of same-name inherited candidates.

A reasonable override graph computation is roughly:

```text
O(M + E + sum(method same-name inherited candidates))
```

or practically:

```text
O(M * H * K)
```

In normal code, `K` is small. Most classes do not have huge overload families of the same name. So override graph computation is generally modest.

The expensive part inside graph construction is not graph traversal itself, but type relation checks:

```cpp
IsOverrideCompatible(baseSig, derivedSig)
```

because that may involve:

- generics;
- substitutions;
- union types;
- effective signature types;
- type parameter constraints;
- return type covariance;
- parameter contravariance.

But these relation checks are still usually cheaper than rechecking all function bodies.

## Pathological case

The worst case can be bad:

```text
deep hierarchy
many methods with the same name
many overloaded signatures per type
generic signatures with complex constraints
```

Then a naive implementation can become close to quadratic.

But with a per-type method-name index:

```cpp
name -> signatures
```

you avoid comparing every method with every inherited method.

## Practical conclusion

Override graph recomputation for the whole program is usually acceptable if you already plan to rerun checker after plugins.

---

# 2. How expensive are overload sets?

Overload sets should usually be computed **lazily**, not globally.

You need an overload set when something asks for it:

- a function call;
- a method call;
- a constructor call;
- a method reference;
- a function reference;
- `typeof` on an overloaded name;
- explicit overload declaration validation;
- explicit overload lowering;
- overload warnings such as “candidate can never be selected”.

For a call expression:

```ts
x.foo(arg1, arg2)
```

the checker needs:

```text
static type of x
method name foo
candidate set for that name
argument types
```

So the cost is roughly:

```text
O(size of overload set * cost of candidate validation)
```

Candidate validation can include:

- arity check;
- optional/rest parameter handling;
- assignability checks;
- generic inference;
- lambda compatibility;
- spread argument handling.

Usually overload sets are small, so this is fine.

## Should you precompute all overload sets?

I would not.

A global precompute of all overload sets for all names and all types can be wasteful:

```text
for every class/interface
  for every possible member name
    build full inherited overload set
```

Many overload sets are never used.

Better:

- build overload sets on demand;
- cache them only for the current checker run;
- clear the cache on full recheck.

Example cache key:

```cpp
struct OverloadSetKey {
    ETSObjectType *receiverType;
    util::StringView name;
    bool isStatic;
    OverloadSetKind kind;
    uint64_t semanticEpoch;
};
```

If you do not want plugin invalidation marks, just clear the entire cache after every plugin mutation barrier.

## Practical conclusion

Overload-set construction is cheap enough to compute lazily and discard aggressively. Do not persist overload-set caches across plugin phases unless you have a reliable semantic epoch.

---

# 3. When do you need the override graph?

You need the override graph after:

1. scopes are initialized;
2. identifiers are bound;
3. class/interface hierarchy is known;
4. method signatures are built;
5. declared members are resolved into object types.

In other words:

```text
parse
  -> scope init
  -> bind identifiers
  -> build class/interface types
  -> build method signatures
  -> compute override graph
```

You need it before:

## A. Override diagnostics

Examples:

```ts
class D extends B {
    override foo() {}
}
```

Need to know whether `foo` actually overrides something.

Also needed for:

- overriding `final` method;
- access weakening;
- bad return type;
- bad parameter type;
- bad type parameter constraint;
- more than one method overriding the same inherited method.

## B. Interface implementation validation

Example:

```ts
class C extends B implements I1, I2 {}
```

Need to know:

- which class/superclass methods implement interface methods;
- which interface requirements remain abstract;
- which default methods conflict;
- which conflicts are resolved by class hierarchy methods.

## C. Overload-set construction

When forming an inherited overload set, overridden inherited methods should not appear twice.

Example:

```ts
class B {
    foo(x: string) {}
}
class D extends B {
    override foo(x: string) {}
}
```

The overload set for `D.foo` should contain the derived method, not both derived and base as separate callable choices.

So overload-set builder benefits from override graph.

## D. Bridge generation

Bridge lowering should know:

```text
D.foo overrides B.foo
```

Then it can ask:

```text
Do these signatures require a bridge?
```

Without the graph, bridge lowering has to rediscover override relationships.

---

# 4. When do you need overload sets?

You need overload sets mostly during checking expressions and declarations.

## A. Call expressions

```ts
foo(1)
obj.foo(1)
new C(1)
```

The checker must build the candidate list and choose the first valid signature.

## B. Explicit overload declarations

```ts
overload foo { fooNumber, fooString }
```

The checker must validate and expand the list.

Important: if a listed name is itself implicitly overloaded, it expands:

```ts
function bar(x: number) {}
function bar(x: string) {}

overload foo { bar }
// foo contains both bar(number) and bar(string)
```

## C. Method/function references

Spec prohibits or restricts references to overloaded names in some contexts:

```ts
let f = foo // may be invalid if foo is overloaded
```

You need to know whether the name denotes an overload set.

## D. `typeof`

The spec also has rules for `typeof` on overloaded functions/methods.

## E. Explicit overload lowering

After checker selected a real target, lowering rewrites alias calls.

So lowering needs the **selected target**, not the whole overload set.

---

# 5. If you do not trust plugins to set invalidation marks

Then do not ask plugins to set invalidation marks.

Use a **plugin barrier policy**.

That means:

```text
run plugin hook
assume AST may have changed
discard semantic caches
rerun the safe semantic pipeline
```

This is simple, safe, and does not rely on plugin cooperation beyond “plugins run at known pipeline points”.

---

# 6. Recommended safe plugin policy

## Plugin after parse

At this point, no binding/checking products exist yet.

Safe behavior:

```text
plugin mutates AST
continue normal pipeline
```

No special recomputation needed.

```text
Parse
  -> plugins-after-parse
  -> scope init
  -> bind
  -> check
```

Cost: no extra cost beyond normal compilation.

---

## Plugin after bind

At this point, scopes and variables may already exist. If plugin mutates AST, binding may be stale.

Conservative safe behavior:

```text
plugins-after-bind
  -> clear scopes/variables/types/signatures
  -> rerun scope init
  -> rerun resolve identifiers
  -> rerun checker
```

This is more expensive, but safe.

Do not try to recompute only override graph. If the plugin changed AST after binding, the graph is not the first stale thing. Bindings and signatures may already be stale.

---

## Plugin after check

This is the dangerous one.

After checker, many semantic products exist:

- `TsType` on nodes;
- `Variable::TsType`;
- `ScriptFunction::Signature`;
- object properties;
- type relation caches;
- call expression signatures;
- maybe metadata emitted by earlier phases;
- explicit overload synthetic types;
- override/overload graph caches if added.

If a plugin mutates AST here and you do not trust invalidation marks, the safe behavior is:

```text
plugins-after-check
  -> clear all semantic state
  -> rerun bind/check
  -> rerun semantic post-check products
```

Important: avoid infinite loops.

Do not rerun the same plugin hook again unless explicitly requested. The control flow should be:

```text
CheckerPhase
plugins-after-check run once
semantic rebuild excluding already-run plugin hook
continue post-check lowering
```

or:

```text
CheckerPhase
plugins-after-check run once
restart from bind/check with plugin hook marked consumed
continue
```

## Plugin after lowering

I would be very strict here.

After lowering, the AST may already encode decisions made by checker:

- overload alias calls rewritten;
- bridge methods inserted;
- optional/default/rest lowering done;
- helper declarations generated;
- casts/boxing/unboxing inserted.

If a plugin changes source-level declarations after lowering, a local recompute of override/overload graphs is not enough.

Safe policy:

```text
After-lowering plugins may only do low-level body-local transformations
that do not change externally visible declarations or call semantics.
```

If they change declarations, method signatures, class heritage, explicit overloads, or call callee/arguments:

```text
restart from an earlier phase
```

or reject the mutation.

---

# 7. Recommended cache policy

Since you prefer safety over performance:

## Make override graph and overload sets ephemeral

Do not treat them as long-lived across plugin barriers.

Use this policy:

```text
At the beginning of a checker run:
    clear override graph cache
    clear overload set cache
    clear explicit overload expansion cache
    clear resolved call target cache

During checker:
    compute override graph for all types
    compute overload sets lazily as needed

After any plugin barrier that may mutate AST:
    discard all semantic state
    rerun checker
```

This avoids fine-grained invalidation entirely.

## Use semantic epochs internally

Even with full clearing, epochs help catch stale use.

```cpp
struct SemanticEpochs {
    uint64_t astEpoch;
    uint64_t bindingEpoch;
    uint64_t signatureEpoch;
    uint64_t hierarchyEpoch;
    uint64_t overrideGraphEpoch;
    uint64_t overloadSetEpoch;
};
```

Every cached item records the epoch it was built under. If code accidentally uses an old overload set or graph, assert in debug builds.

But plugins do not need to set marks.

---

# 8. What exactly should be cleared on conservative recheck?

If a plugin can mutate AST after binding/checking, clear at least:

- node `TsType`;
- identifier `Variable` links if rebinding;
- variable `TsType`;
- function signatures;
- method `TsType`;
- class/interface object property instantiation state;
- construct signatures;
- call expression signatures;
- selected resolved call targets;
- explicit overload synthetic types;
- override graph cache;
- overload set cache;
- bridge requirement cache;
- type relation caches;
- diagnostics from previous run if diagnostics are retained;
- lowered/generated helper nodes if they depend on old semantics.

In practice, if this is whole-program recheck, use existing cleanup/rebind/recheck infrastructure and extend it to include new graph/set caches.

---

# 9. Should override graph be computed eagerly or lazily?

Given your preference, I would compute override graph **eagerly for all classes/interfaces during checker**.

Reason:

- It is needed for many validations anyway.
- It makes diagnostics deterministic.
- It makes interface implementation checks simpler.
- It makes bridge generation straightforward.
- Its cost is acceptable compared with full checking.

Recommended order:

```text
1. Build all object types and hierarchy.
2. Resolve declared members and method signatures.
3. Compute override graph base-first.
4. Validate override graph.
5. Validate abstract/interface implementation.
6. Check method bodies / calls as needed.
```

Some current code checks method bodies interleaved with signature building. The exact order may need adaptation, but conceptually graph should be available before final class/interface validation and before bridge generation.

---

# 10. Should overload sets be computed eagerly or lazily?

I would compute overload sets **lazily**.

Reason:

- Most possible member names are never called.
- A call needs context: static receiver type, static/non-static, explicit type arguments, accessibility context.
- Candidate validation depends on actual arguments.
- Global precomputation can waste memory and time.

But lazy does not mean unsafe. Make the cache short-lived:

```text
one checker run only
clear after plugin barrier
```

If you want maximum simplicity, you can even skip caching initially:

```text
build overload set every time a call needs it
```

That is slower but safest and easiest to validate. Add caching later if needed.

---

# 11. Conservative full-recheck strategy

If you do not want plugin invalidation marks, the simplest robust architecture is:

```text
for each plugin extension point:
    run all plugins at that point
    if this point is before semantic analysis:
        continue normally
    else:
        assume AST changed
        clear semantic state
        rerun semantic analysis from a safe phase
```

More concretely:

| Plugin point | Conservative action |
|---|---|
| after parse | continue normal bind/check |
| after bind | full rebind + full recheck |
| after check | full rebind + full recheck, then continue post-check lowering |
| after lowering | allow only non-semantic changes, otherwise restart earlier pipeline or reject |

This requires no per-plugin invalidation marks.

---

# 12. Do you need an API for plugins at all?

If you do not trust plugins to mark invalidation correctly, the plugin API can be simpler:

```cpp
enum class PluginMutationPolicy {
    READ_ONLY,
    MAY_MUTATE_AST,
};
```

But even that can be optional. If you want maximum safety:

```text
all plugins are treated as MAY_MUTATE_AST
```

Then every plugin barrier triggers the conservative action.

If performance becomes an issue later, you can allow trusted plugins to opt into `READ_ONLY`.

But correctness should not depend on fine-grained marks like:

```cpp
MarkChanged(method, FUNCTION_SIGNATURE)
```

---

# 13. Recommended implementation approach

## Short term

Do this:

1. Treat plugin callbacks as mutation barriers.
2. After post-bind or post-check plugin callbacks, run full semantic cleanup and recheck.
3. Compute override graph eagerly during checker.
4. Compute overload sets lazily during call resolution.
5. Do not cache graphs/sets across recheck.

This is safe and relatively simple.

## Medium term

Add internal semantic epochs and debug assertions to catch stale semantic data.

## Long term

If full recheck becomes too expensive, add internal dependency tracking. But keep it internal. Plugins still should not need to supply precise invalidation marks.

---

# 14. Final recommendation

Given your priorities, I would choose this policy:

```text
Correctness-first plugin mode:

- Plugins may mutate AST only at defined extension points.
- After any plugin point at or after binding, the frontend assumes mutation happened.
- The frontend clears all semantic products.
- The frontend reruns binding/checking as needed.
- Override graph is recomputed eagerly.
- Overload sets are recomputed lazily and cached only within the current checker run.
- Plugins are not asked to mark invalidation.
```

This is less performant than fine-grained incremental recomputation, but it is much safer and much easier to reason about.

The cost of recomputing override graphs and overload sets is not the main concern. The expensive operation is full recheck, but if plugins can arbitrarily mutate AST and correctness is the priority, full recheck at plugin barriers is the right tradeoff.
