content.text:
---

## What can be done gradually

Safe gradual changes:

1. Add characterization tests.
2. Add pure helper functions.
3. Fix superclass method satisfying multiple interfaces.
4. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision.
5. Add effective signature type helper.
6. Introduce overload-set builder behind existing API.
7. Build override graph without consuming it.
8. Migrate diagnostics one by one to the graph.
9. Remove duplicate predicates after graph consumers are stable.

---

## What should be done all at once

Some changes must be atomic because partial migration would create inconsistent semantics.

| Change | Why it should be atomic |
| --- | --- |
| Explicit overload expansion | Validation, synthetic type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree about candidate count/order. |
| Resolved call target representation | Checker and lowering must switch together from owner-variable assumptions to explicit target metadata. |
| Graph-driven bridge generation | Running old rediscovery and new graph-driven generation together risks duplicate or missing bridges. |
| Direct overload-set call resolution | `MemberExpression`, `CallExpression`, method references, explicit overloads, and lowering must agree. |
| Effective overload-equivalence across declaration kinds | Functions, methods, interfaces, and constructors must use the same language rule. |

---

## Recommended implementation order

1. Add tests and a local fix for concrete superclass method implementing multiple interfaces.
2. Add pure override compatibility and overload-equivalence helpers.
3. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision checks.
4. Implement effective signature type and use it for overload-equivalence.
5. Implement explicit overload expansion as an atomic patch.
6. Introduce `OverloadSetBuilder` behind existing APIs.
7. Compute override graph but initially keep old behavior.
8. Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to override graph.
9. Migrate overload-set duplicate suppression to override graph.
10. Switch bridge generation to override graph atomically.
11. Remove obsolete synthetic/ad-hoc overload paths.

---

## Minimum test coverage matrix

| Area | Required tests |
| --- | --- |
| Multiple interfaces | Superclass method implements two interfaces; conflicting defaults without class method; diamond inheritance. |
| Override compatibility | Contravariant parameters; covariant returns; access weakening; final method; duplicate override of same base method. |
| Overload-equivalence | Same parameters with different return type; generic erasure collisions; constructor overload-equivalence. |
| Overload order | Textual order; explicit list order; own before superclass before interfaces; `implements`/`extends` order. |
| Explicit overloads | Listed implicit overload group expansion; inherited explicit overload from multiple interfaces; alias same as method name. |
| Runtime dispatch | Calls through superclass reference; calls through interface reference; one method overriding several inherited signatures; bridge dispatch. |

---

## Final target architecture

The frontend should move from this implicit flow:

```text
property lookup
  -> synthetic overload variables
  -> local signature vectors
  -> local override checks
  -> bridge phases rediscover overrides
```

to this explicit flow:

```text
declarations
  -> signatures
  -> override graph
  -> overload sets
  -> resolved call targets
  -> lowering / bridge generation
  -> codegen
```

Benefits:

- spec order is explicit and testable;
- multiple interface implementation is handled consistently;
- class/superclass methods correctly satisfy interface requirements before conflicts are reported;
- explicit overload aliases behave according to the spec;
- bridge generation uses the same override facts as diagnostics;
- lowering and codegen become consumers of checker decisions, not semantic rediscovery layers.

This makes bridge generation a mechanical consequence of checker semantics. The bridge phase no longer needs to ask “does this method override that method?” It only asks “does this already-known override edge need an ABI/runtime adapter?”

  • Deduplicate bridges by effective or assembly descriptor.
  • Mark generated methods as synthetic/bridge.
  • Exclude bridge methods from source overload sets.
  • Preserve existing bridge body generation machinery where it is correct.
Migration plan

Principle: do not rewrite everything at once

The current code is intertwined with many other frontend phases. A total rewrite would be risky. The safe strategy is to introduce better semantic primitives while keeping existing APIs alive, then migrate consumers one by one.

Good gradual changes

Add tests, helper predicates, local bug fixes, a builder behind old APIs, and an override graph initially used for validation/debug.

Atomic changes

Some changes must update checker + lowering together, especially explicit overload expansion and resolved call target representation.

Migration phase 0

Add characterization tests first

Before refactoring, write tests that describe both current failures and intended behavior. These tests become the safety net for each later phase.

Multiple interfacesSuperclass method satisfies two interface methods; class method dominates interface defaults if specified; conflicting defaults without class method.
Override compatibilityContravariant params, covariant returns, access weakening, final method override, duplicate override of same base.
Overload-equivalenceSame parameters with different returns; generic/effective type collisions; constructors.
Explicit overloadsListed implicit overload group expansion; alias same as method; inherited aliases from multiple interfaces.
Runtime dispatchCalls through superclass and interface references; bridge dispatch; one method overrides several inherited methods.

Local fix for class method satisfying multiple interfaces

This is the first practical patch because it addresses a concrete deficiency without forcing the whole redesign.

Before reporting a collision between two interface methods inherited by a class, check whether a concrete method in the class or its superclass chain implements both.

edits.newText:
## Phase 9: cleanup

After migration:

- reduce overload-specific property lookup flags;
- remove or shrink synthetic overload variable construction in `GetProperty`;
- remove duplicated override predicates;
- remove casual `CallSignatures().front()` in overload paths;
- make call resolution consume overload sets directly.

## Plugin and LSP note

Plugins can modify AST at several pipeline points, so override/overload data must not be treated as permanent across plugin mutation barriers.

Short-term correctness-first policy:

- If a plugin runs after parse, continue with the normal bind/check pipeline.
- If a plugin runs after binding but before checking, a checker `Recheck` is not needed because no check has happened yet. If the plugin modified AST in a way that invalidates binding, rerun the relevant scope initialization/binding and then proceed to the first checker run.
- If a plugin runs after checking and may modify AST, use the existing safe `Recheck` path. During that `Recheck`, method signatures, override graph data, overload-set caches, and resolved call targets should be rebuilt from the updated AST.
- Do not rely on plugins to set precise invalidation marks in the short term; prefer conservative recomputation.

Long-term optimization:

- Introduce an internal or public semantic invalidation API that lets trusted callers mark what changed, such as body-only change, method signature change, class member set change, heritage change, or explicit overload declaration change.
- Use that information to recompute override graphs and overload sets incrementally where safe.
- This incremental recomputation is not only useful for plugins; it can also be beneficial for LSP support, where small edits should ideally avoid a full program recheck.

Plugin and LSP note

Short-term safe recompute, long-term incremental API

Plugins may modify AST at defined points in the pipeline. Override graphs and overload-set caches should therefore be treated as derived semantic data that can be discarded and rebuilt when a plugin mutation barrier is crossed.

Short-term policy

  • After parse: continue normal scope init, binding, and checking.
  • After bind but before check: no checker Recheck is needed, because no check has happened yet. If binding is invalidated, rerun binding and then proceed to the first check.
  • After check: use the safe Recheck path. During that recheck, signatures, override graph data, overload-set caches, and resolved call targets are rebuilt.

Long-term optimization

  • Introduce an API to mark what changed: body, call site, method signature, class member set, heritage, explicit overload declaration, etc.
  • Use those marks to recompute override graphs and overload sets incrementally where safe.
  • This is useful not only for plugins, but also for LSP support where small edits should avoid full program recheck.

Short-term correctness should not depend on plugins providing precise invalidation marks. Conservative recomputation is safer.

Migration phase 0

Add characterization tests first

**Analyzing pointer identity**

I'm considering using pointer identity within a checker run. However, I'm aware that substituted signatures can differ from query to query. If I build substituted signatures on an ad hoc basis, the pointer keys might not be stable. So it looks like I need to canonicalize or keep track of the original signature along with the substitution context to ensure everything remains consistent and reliable. Let's figure out the best approach!

content.text:
Works for many simple cases

Simple same-name methods, ordinary class overrides, and many direct method calls are already handled.

Fragile for hard cases

Multiple interfaces, inherited explicit overload aliases, erasure collisions, and bridge requirements are handled by separate mechanisms that can disagree.

Needed end state

The checker should compute override edges and overload sets once. Lowering should consume those facts, not rediscover them.

Key idea: the frontend needs explicit semantic products: an override graph, spec-ordered overload sets, and resolved call targets.

Terminology

Glossary for the rest of the deck

[830 more lines in file. Use offset=325 to continue.]
TermMeaning in this discussion
SignatureType parameters, parameter types, return type, flags, owner method/function.
Override-compatibleSpec relation that allows a subtype method to override a supertype method.
Overload-equivalentSpec relation used to reject duplicate implicit overload declarations. It ignores return type.

• Bridge generation becomes mechanical.
    • Target design

    Three explicit semantic products

    1. Override graph

    Edges from derived signatures to base/interface signatures they override or implement.

    2. Overload sets

    Ordered vectors of call candidates built from declarations, explicit overload aliases, and inheritance.

    3. Resolved call target

    The concrete selected function/method/constructor target attached to every call expression.

    Declarations→ Signatures→ Override graph→ Overload sets→ Resolved calls→ Lowering / bridges
    Target design

    Override graph in detail

    struct OverrideEdge {
    Signature *derived;
    Signature *base;
    OverrideKind kind;      // class override, interface override, implementation
    bool requiresBridge;
};

    The graph is computed once the type's own members and supertypes are known. It should be built by pure compatibility checks followed by explicit marking.

    • Diagnostics use the graph to report bad override, final override, access weakening, return mismatch, and type parameter issues.
    • Interface implementation validation uses the graph to know which requirements are satisfied.
    • Overload-set construction uses the graph to avoid adding overridden inherited methods twice.
    • Bridge generation uses the graph to know exactly which base descriptors must be supported.
    Target design

    Overload candidate representation

    struct OverloadCandidate {
    Signature *signature;
    varbinder::LocalVariable *variable;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    CandidateOrigin origin; // own, explicit, superclass, interface
    size_t sourceOrder;
};

    A candidate is more than a signature. Lowering needs to know which declaration was selected. Diagnostics may need the origin. Ordering must be stable and spec-derived.

    This also avoids guessing selected targets later from Signature::OwnerVar(), which is fragile with synthetic/helper/imported signatures.

    Target design

    Resolved call target

    After overload resolution, the call expression should store both the selected signature and the selected semantic target.

    struct ResolvedCallTarget {
    Signature *signature;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    varbinder::Variable *variable;
    CallTargetKind kind; // function, instance method, static method, constructor
};

callExpr->SetSignature(target.signature);
callExpr->SetResolvedCallTarget(target);

    Checker responsibility

    Resolve overloads and choose a target using source-language semantics.

    Lowering responsibility

    Rewrite syntax according to the already selected target. Do not redo overload resolution.

    Target design

    Graph-driven bridge generation

    for (OverrideEdge edge : classType->OverrideGraph()) {
    if (NeedsBridge(edge.base, edge.derived)) {
        GenerateBridge(edge.base, edge.derived);
    }
}

    This makes bridge generation a mechanical consequence of checker semantics. The bridge phase no longer needs to ask “does this method override that method?” It only asks “does this already-known override edge need an ABI/runtime adapter?”

    • Deduplicate bridges by effective or assembly descriptor.
    • Mark generated methods as synthetic/bridge.
    • Exclude bridge methods from source overload sets.
    • Preserve existing bridge body generation machinery where it is correct.
    Migration plan
    [320 more lines in file. Use offset=835 to continue.]

Principle: do not rewrite everything at once

The current code is intertwined with many other frontend phases. A total rewrite would be risky. The safe strategy is to introduce better semantic primitives while keeping existing APIs alive, then migrate consumers one by one.

Good gradual changes

Add tests, helper predicates, local bug fixes, a builder behind old APIs, and an override graph initially used for validation/debug.

Atomic changes

Some changes must update checker + lowering together, especially explicit overload expansion and resolved call target representation.

Plugin and LSP note

Short-term safe recompute, long-term incremental API

Plugins may modify AST at defined points in the pipeline. Override graphs and overload-set caches should therefore be treated as derived semantic data that can be discarded and rebuilt when a plugin mutation barrier is crossed.

Short-term policy

  • After parse: continue normal scope init, binding, and checking.
  • After bind but before check: no checker Recheck is needed, because no check has happened yet. If binding is invalidated, rerun binding and then proceed to the first check.
  • After check: use the safe Recheck path. During that recheck, signatures, override graph data, overload-set caches, and resolved call targets are rebuilt.

Long-term optimization

  • Introduce an API to mark what changed: body, call site, method signature, class member set, heritage, explicit overload declaration, etc.
  • Use those marks to recompute override graphs and overload sets incrementally where safe.
  • This is useful not only for plugins, but also for LSP support where small edits should avoid full program recheck.

Short-term correctness should not depend on plugins providing precise invalidation marks. Conservative recomputation is safer.

Migration phase 0

Add characterization tests first

Before refactoring, write tests that describe both current failures and intended behavior. These tests become the safety net for each later phase.

AreaTests
Multiple interfacesSuperclass method satisfies two interface methods; class method dominates interface defaults if specified; conflicting defaults without class method.
Override compatibilityContravariant params, covariant returns, access weakening, final method override, duplicate override of same base.
Overload-equivalenceSame parameters with different returns; generic/effective type collisions; constructors.
Explicit overloadsListed implicit overload group expansion; alias same as method; inherited aliases from multiple interfaces.
Runtime dispatchCalls through superclass and interface references; bridge dispatch; one method overrides several inherited methods.
Migration phase 1

Local fix for class method satisfying multiple interfaces

This is the first practical patch because it addresses a concrete deficiency without forcing the whole redesign.

bool HasConcreteClassImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                    Signature *interfaceSig);

bool HasCommonConcreteClassImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                          Signature *a,
                                          Signature *b);

Before reporting a collision between two interface methods inherited by a class, check whether a concrete method in the class or its superclass chain implements both.

if (HasCommonConcreteClassImplementation(classType, sigA, sigB)) {
    return; // conflict resolved by class hierarchy
}
Migration phase 2

Extract pure semantic helpers

The next step is to make semantic relations explicit and side-effect-free. A predicate should not mutate the AST or mark a method as overriding while answering a yes/no question.

bool IsOverrideCompatible(Signature *base, Signature *derived);
bool AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature *a, Signature *b);
bool IsConcreteImplementationOf(Signature *impl, Signature *requirement);

Before

Compatibility checks can call SetOverride() as a side effect.

After

First compute compatibility. Then a separate analyzer records or marks the override relation.

Migration phase 3

Separate overload-equivalence from ABI collision

This is a cleanup with behavior impact. It prevents source-language diagnostics from depending on backend descriptor behavior.

// Source-language rule
bool AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature *a, Signature *b);

// Backend/helper/bridge rule
bool HaveSameAssemblySignature(Signature *a, Signature *b, bool includeReturn);

// Ambient/helper-specific rule
bool NeedHelperOverload(...);

Apply the language-level helper consistently to functions, methods, interfaces, and constructors.

Migration phase 4

Implement effective signature type

Start by implementing the helper without replacing every use immediately. Then migrate one consumer at a time.

  1. Implement EffectiveType and EffectiveSignatureType.
  2. Use it in AreOverloadEquivalent.
  3. Add erasure-collision override diagnostics.
  4. Use it in bridge necessity checks after override graph is available.

Do not confuse effective signature type with the assembler descriptor. They are related but serve different semantic layers.

Migration phase 5

Atomic explicit overload expansion patch

This change should be done all at once because validation, type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree about how many candidates an explicit overload alias has.

  • Allow listed names that resolve to implicit overload groups.
  • Expand all signatures of a listed group in source order.
  • Remove front()-only behavior from explicit overload construction.
  • Store selected target after resolution.
  • Update overload mapping lowering to consume the selected target.

A partial implementation is dangerous: the checker could resolve to a candidate that lowering cannot correctly rewrite.

Migration phase 6

Introduce overload-set builder behind existing APIs

Do not immediately delete synthetic property lookup behavior. Instead, make it delegate to the new builder first.

ETSObjectType::CreateSyntheticVarFromEverySignature(...) {
    auto set = OverloadSetBuilder(checker).BuildInstanceMethodSet(...);
    return CreateSyntheticFunctionTypeFrom(set);
}

This lets existing call sites keep working while overload set formation becomes centralized and testable.

Migration phase 7

Compute override graph, then migrate consumers

The override graph can be introduced before it is used for all decisions. Initially, compute it and compare it with old behavior in assertions/debug logs or focused tests.

  1. Build graph per class/interface.
  2. Use it for override keyword diagnostics.
  3. Use it for final/access/return diagnostics.
  4. Use it for duplicate override-of-same-base detection.
  5. Use it for interface implementation and conflict validation.
  6. Use it for inherited overload candidate suppression.
Migration phase 8

Atomic switch to graph-driven bridge generation

Once override graph consumers are stable, bridge generation should stop rediscovering overrides and consume graph edges instead.

  • Disable old bridge discovery in the same patch.
  • Generate bridges from override edges.
  • Deduplicate by effective/assembly descriptor.
  • Reuse bridge body builders where possible.
  • Add runtime dispatch tests for generated bridges.

Running old and new bridge discovery together risks duplicate bridge methods or inconsistent signatures.

Gradual vs atomic

What can be done gradually

  • Add characterization tests.
  • Add pure semantic helpers.
  • Fix superclass method satisfying multiple interfaces.
  • Split source overload-equivalence from ABI collision helpers.
  • Add effective signature type helper.
  • Introduce overload-set builder behind current APIs.
  • Compute override graph without consuming it heavily.
  • Migrate diagnostics and validations one by one to the graph.
  • Clean up obsolete helper paths after replacement.
Gradual vs atomic

What should be done all at once

ChangeWhy it must be atomic
Explicit overload group expansionChecker, synthetic type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree on candidate count and order.
Resolved call target representationChecker and lowering must switch together, otherwise lowering will keep relying on fragile owner-variable assumptions.
Graph-driven bridge generationOld and new bridge discovery running together can create duplicate or missing bridge methods.
Direct overload-set call resolutionMember expressions, call expressions, method references, and explicit overload aliases must share the same candidate source.
Global effective overload-equivalenceFunctions, methods, constructors, and interfaces must follow the same source-language duplicate rule.
Recommended order

Practical implementation sequence

  1. Add tests and fix concrete superclass method implementing multiple interfaces.
  2. Add pure override compatibility and overload-equivalence helpers.
  3. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision logic.
  4. Implement effective signature type and use it for overload-equivalence.
  5. Implement explicit overload group expansion as an atomic patch.
  6. Introduce overload-set builder behind existing synthetic property APIs.
  7. Compute override graph but keep old behavior initially.
  8. Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to override graph.
  9. Migrate overload-set inherited duplicate suppression to override graph.
  10. Switch bridge generation to override graph atomically.
  11. Remove old ad-hoc/synthetic overload paths where no longer needed.
Final architecture

End state: explicit semantic pipeline

Parse declarations→ Bind names/scopes→ Build signatures→ Build override graph→ Build overload sets→ Resolve calls→ Lower aliases/bridges→ Codegen

Correctness

Multiple interface implementation and class hierarchy methods are resolved using one override model.

Traceability

Diagnostics, call resolution, and bridge generation can point to the same semantic facts.

Maintainability

Future spec changes affect central helpers instead of scattered property lookup and lowering code.

edits.newText:
Updated target design

Stateless, lazy semantic relation services

The updated approach does not store a permanent override graph on AST nodes or object types. Instead, the checker owns short-lived relation services that recompute facts lazily and cache them for the current semantic epoch.

1. OverrideOracle

Answers questions such as “does this method override that one?” and “which inherited targets does this method override?”

2. OverloadSetOracle

Builds ordered overload candidate sets on demand, including explicit overload expansion and inherited candidate suppression.

3. Resolved call target

Stores the selected function/method/constructor target on each call so lowering does not redo semantic discovery.

The “override graph” remains a useful conceptual model, but the first implementation can expose it as lazy cached queries rather than a stored graph.

Updated target design

SemanticRelationCache

class SemanticRelationCache {
public:
    void Clear();
    void BumpEpochAndClear();

    OverrideOracle &Overrides();
    OverloadSetOracle &Overloads();

private:
    uint64_t epoch_ {};
    OverrideOracle overrideOracle_;
    OverloadSetOracle overloadOracle_;
};
  • Owned by ETSChecker.
  • Cache keys include the current semantic epoch.
  • Caches are cleared during safe Recheck and after plugin mutation barriers.
  • This is similar in spirit to TypeRelation: relation answers are cached, but not permanently stored on every AST/type node.
Updated target design

OverrideOracle in detail

class OverrideOracle {
public:
    OverrideDecision CheckOverride(Signature *base,
                                   Signature *derived,
                                   OverrideContext ctx);

    ArenaVector<OverrideTarget> GetOverriddenTargets(ETSObjectType *owner,
                                                     Signature *derived);

    bool HasConcreteImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                   Signature *interfaceSig);

    bool HasCommonConcreteImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                         Signature *a,
                                         Signature *b);
};

Class/interface validation still asks all necessary questions, so diagnostics are complete. The difference is that answers are computed lazily and cached, not stored as a permanent graph.

edits.oldText:
Migration phase 6

Introduce overload-set builder behind existing APIs

Do not immediately delete synthetic property lookup behavior. Instead, make it delegate to the new builder first.

ETSObjectType::CreateSyntheticVarFromEverySignature(...) {
    auto set = OverloadSetBuilder(checker).BuildInstanceMethodSet(...);
    return CreateSyntheticFunctionTypeFrom(set);
}

This lets existing call sites keep working while overload set formation becomes centralized and testable.

Migration phase 7

Compute override graph, then migrate consumers

The override graph can be introduced before it is used for all decisions. Initially, compute it and compare it with old behavior in assertions/debug logs or focused tests.

  1. Build graph per class/interface.
  2. Use it for override keyword diagnostics.
  3. Use it for final/access/return diagnostics.
  4. Use it for duplicate override-of-same-base detection.
  5. Use it for interface implementation and conflict validation.
  6. Use it for inherited overload candidate suppression.
Migration phase 8

Atomic switch to graph-driven bridge generation

Once override graph consumers are stable, bridge generation should stop rediscovering overrides and consume graph edges instead.

  • Disable old bridge discovery in the same patch.
  • Generate bridges from override edges.
  • Deduplicate by effective/assembly descriptor.
  • Reuse bridge body builders where possible.
  • Add runtime dispatch tests for generated bridges.

Running old and new bridge discovery together risks duplicate bridge methods or inconsistent signatures.
edits.newText:
Migration phase 6

Introduce SemanticRelationCache and lazy oracles

Add checker-owned relation services before removing old code. Initially, they can delegate internally to existing helpers while adding a common API, cache clearing, semantic epoch checks, and debug tracing.

checker->SemanticRelations().Overrides();
checker->SemanticRelations().Overloads();
  • OverrideOracle answers override and implementation questions.
  • OverloadSetOracle builds overload sets on demand.
  • Both caches are valid only for the current semantic epoch.
Migration phase 7

Move overload-set construction into OverloadSetOracle

Do not immediately delete synthetic property lookup behavior. Instead, make it delegate to the oracle first.

ETSObjectType::CreateSyntheticVarFromEverySignature(...) {
    auto set = checker->SemanticRelations().Overloads().GetOverloadSet(...);
    return CreateSyntheticFunctionTypeFrom(set);
}

This lets existing call sites keep working while overload set formation becomes centralized, cached, and testable.

Migration phase 8

Migrate override consumers to OverrideOracle

No permanent graph is required. Each validation pass asks the oracle the exhaustive questions it needs; the oracle caches answers.

  1. Use it for override keyword diagnostics.
  2. Use it for final/access/return diagnostics.
  3. Use it for duplicate override-of-same-base detection.
  4. Use it for interface implementation and conflict validation.
  5. Use it for inherited overload candidate suppression.
Migration phase 9

Atomic switch to oracle-driven bridge generation

Once OverrideOracle consumers are stable, bridge generation should stop rediscovering overrides and query GetOverriddenTargets instead.

  • Disable old bridge discovery in the same patch.
  • Generate bridges from oracle targets.
  • Deduplicate by effective/assembly descriptor.
  • Reuse bridge body builders where possible.
  • Add runtime dispatch tests for generated bridges.

Running old and new bridge discovery together risks duplicate bridge methods or inconsistent signatures.

content.text:
Oracle-driven bridge generationOld rediscovery and new oracle-driven generation running together can create duplicate or missing bridge methods. Direct overload-set call resolutionMember expressions, call expressions, method references, and explicit overload aliases must share the same candidate source. Global effective overload-equivalenceFunctions, methods, constructors, and interfaces must follow the same source-language duplicate rule.
Recommended order

Practical implementation sequence

  1. Add tests and fix concrete superclass method implementing multiple interfaces.
  2. Add pure override compatibility and overload-equivalence helpers.
  3. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision logic.
  4. Implement effective signature type and use it for overload-equivalence.
  5. Add checker-owned SemanticRelationCache, OverrideOracle, and OverloadSetOracle.
  6. Implement explicit overload group expansion as an atomic patch.
  7. Move overload-set construction into OverloadSetOracle behind existing APIs.
  8. Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to OverrideOracle.
  9. Migrate overload-set inherited duplicate suppression to OverrideOracle queries.
  10. Switch bridge generation to OverrideOracle atomically.
  11. Remove old ad-hoc/synthetic overload paths where no longer needed.
Final architecture

End state: explicit but stateless semantic pipeline

Parse declarations→ Bind names/scopes→ Build signatures→ SemanticRelationCache→ OverrideOracle queries→ OverloadSetOracle queries→ Resolved calls→ Lower aliases/bridges→ Codegen

Correctness

Multiple interface implementation and class hierarchy methods are resolved through one override relation service.

Cache safety

No permanent override graph is stored on AST/type nodes; plugin barriers and Recheck clear relation caches.

Incremental future

The oracle design can later support precise invalidation for plugins and LSP without changing source semantics.

Key takeaway

Do not let lookup, checking, and lowering rediscover the same semantics

The source-language truth should be produced once by the checker: which methods override which inherited methods, what ordered candidates each overloaded name has, and what target each call selected. Once these are explicit, class inheritance and multiple interface implementation become much easier to reason about and test.

The first low-risk step is still practical: fix interface conflict checking to account for concrete class/superclass implementations before reporting a collision.

- `ets-overriding-overloading-frontend-findings.md`
- `ets-overriding-overloading-frontend-design.html`

Main changes added:

- Do not store a permanent override graph on AST/type nodes initially.
- Introduce checker-owned:
  - `SemanticRelationCache`
  - `OverrideOracle`
  - `OverloadSetOracle`
- Cache override/overload answers per semantic epoch, inspired by `TypeRelation`.
- Clear caches after plugin mutation barriers / during safe `Recheck`.
- Compute overload sets lazily.
- Query override relations lazily but ensure validation passes ask exhaustive questions needed for diagnostics.
- Bridge generation becomes oracle-driven, not stored-graph-driven.
- Long-term incremental invalidation/change-kind API can benefit plugins and LSP.

Do we need store resolved call targets? does it affect statelessness?

Yes, I would still store **resolved call targets on call expressions**, and no, that does **not** meaningfully violate the stateless approach — as long as you treat them as **ordinary checker metadata**, not as long-lived semantic truth across plugin/recheck boundaries.

There is an important distinction:

```text
Long-lived global semantic relation state:
    override graph / overload graph stored on types/classes
    => avoid

Per-node checker result:
    this call resolved to this signature/target during this checker run
    => OK
```

`CallExpression::Signature()` already exists today. A resolved call target is just a more explicit and safer version of the same kind of metadata.

---

# Why store resolved call target?

Because lowering and codegen need to know exactly what the checker selected.

Example:

```ts
function fNumber(x: number) {}
function fString(x: string) {}

overload f { fNumber, fString }

f(1)
```

Checker resolves:

```text
f(1) -> fNumber(number)
```

Lowering must rewrite or encode the call accordingly. If lowering recomputes overload resolution, you risk:

- different result because AST changed;
- different checker context;
- changed visibility status;
- caches cleared;
- different generic inference state;
- different overload ordering bug;
- repeated diagnostics;
- performance overhead.

So the checker should leave an explicit result:

```cpp
callExpr->SetSignature(selected.signature);
callExpr->SetResolvedCallTarget(selected.target);
```

---

# Does storing it break statelessness?

Not if we define statelessness correctly.

The stateless approach means:

> Do not store global/layer-crossing override/overload relation structures that must be incrementally maintained across AST mutations.

It does **not** mean:

> Checker cannot annotate AST nodes with their checked type/signature/variable.

The frontend already stores checker metadata:

- `node->TsType()`;
- `identifier->Variable()`;
- `ScriptFunction::Signature()`;
- `CallExpression::Signature()`;
- `MethodDefinition::TsType()`;
- `Variable::TsType()`.

A resolved call target is comparable to these.

It is valid only for the current checked AST and current semantic epoch.

---

# Recommended representation

Use a small target object or struct:

```cpp
enum class ResolvedCallTargetKind {
    FUNCTION,
    INSTANCE_METHOD,
    STATIC_METHOD,
    CONSTRUCTOR,
    EXPLICIT_OVERLOAD_ALIAS,
    EXTENSION_FUNCTION,
    UNKNOWN,
};

struct ResolvedCallTarget {
    ResolvedCallTargetKind kind;
    checker::Signature *signature;
    varbinder::Variable *variable;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
};
```

Then:

```cpp
class CallExpression {
public:
    void SetSignature(checker::Signature *sig);
    checker::Signature *Signature() const;

    void SetResolvedCallTarget(ResolvedCallTarget target);
    std::optional<ResolvedCallTarget> const &ResolvedCallTarget() const;

    void ClearCheckInformation();
};
```

If optional storage is inconvenient with arena allocation, store pointer/null:

```cpp
ResolvedCallTarget *resolvedCallTarget_ {nullptr};
```

allocated in checker arena.

---

# What should be stored?

Store only what lowering/codegen needs.

Minimum:

```cpp
Signature *signature;
ir::AstNode *declaration;
varbinder::Variable *variable;
ResolvedCallTargetKind kind;
```

Possibly also:

```cpp
bool selectedThroughExplicitOverloadAlias;
ir::OverloadDeclaration *aliasDecl;
```

This helps `OverloadMappingLowering`.

But do **not** store the full overload set on the call unless needed for diagnostics or LSP. The selected target is enough for compilation.

---

# What about overload sets?

Do not store overload sets on every call expression by default.

Bad:

```cpp
callExpr->SetAllCandidates(overloadSet);
```

This increases memory and makes invalidation harder.

Better:

```cpp
callExpr->SetResolvedCallTarget(selected);
```

If LSP needs candidates for signature help, it can ask `OverloadSetOracle` again under the current semantic epoch.

---

# Invalidation rule

Resolved call target should be cleared whenever normal check metadata is cleared.

For example:

```cpp
void CallExpression::CleanCheckInformation()
{
    SetTsType(nullptr);
    SetSignature(nullptr);
    resolvedCallTarget_ = nullptr;
    // clear other checker metadata
}
```

On safe `Recheck`:

```text
clear call signatures
clear resolved call targets
clear overload-set oracle cache
clear override oracle cache
rerun checker
```

After post-check plugins that may mutate AST, resolved targets from the previous check are invalid.

---

# How it interacts with lazy OverloadSetOracle

The flow should be:

```text
CallExpression::Check
    -> ask OverloadSetOracle for candidates
    -> run first-match overload resolution
    -> selected candidate
    -> store Signature
    -> store ResolvedCallTarget
```

Then later:

```text
OverloadMappingLowering
    -> read ResolvedCallTarget
    -> rewrite explicit overload alias to selected declaration
```

No need to ask `OverloadSetOracle` again in lowering.

---

# Why Signature alone is not enough

Current code often tries to infer the target from:

```cpp
callExpr->Signature()->OwnerVar()
```

This is fragile.

Reasons:

1. The signature can be substituted.
2. The owner variable can be synthetic.
3. Explicit overload aliases can wrap methods/functions with different names.
4. Helper overloads and bridge methods may modify signature ownership.
5. Imported declarations can obscure direct AST declaration.
6. Constructor overloads and named constructors need special handling.
7. Extension functions and function-with-receiver cases differ from methods.

A selected overload candidate already knows the real target. Store it directly.

---

# Does this duplicate data?

Slightly, but usefully.

`Signature` answers:

```text
what callable type was selected?
```

`ResolvedCallTarget` answers:

```text
what source/semantic declaration should be invoked or lowered to?
```

Those are related but not identical.

For example, an explicit overload alias has its own name, but the selected target is a different function/method name.

---

# Should identifiers also store resolved target?

Usually no.

For calls, store on `CallExpression`.

For method/function references, you may need equivalent metadata on the reference expression if it is resolved to a single callable target.

Examples:

```ts
let f = obj.foo
let g = foo
```

If allowed and resolved, the expression may need:

```cpp
ResolvedReferenceTarget
```

But do not overload `Identifier::Variable()` for every semantic case if it becomes ambiguous.

---

# Is this compatible with LSP?

Yes.

For LSP, this is useful:

- go to definition from a call;
- hover shows selected overload;
- signature help can use `OverloadSetOracle`;
- find references can distinguish alias from selected target.

But for LSP, stale metadata must be epoch-checked or cleared between edits.

Long-term, resolved call target could carry the semantic epoch:

```cpp
struct ResolvedCallTarget {
    uint64_t epoch;
    Signature *signature;
    varbinder::Variable *variable;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    ResolvedCallTargetKind kind;
};
```

Then LSP can detect stale targets.

---

# Recommended rule

Use this rule:

```text
Oracle caches are stateless derived services.
Resolved call targets are per-node checker results.
Both are invalidated on Recheck/plugin mutation.
```

That keeps the design clean.

---

# When not to store resolved call target

You could avoid storing it only if lowering immediately follows checking and reuses a transient side table:

```cpp
ArenaMap<ir::CallExpression *, ResolvedCallTarget> resolvedCalls;
```

But that is not really more stateless. It just moves the metadata from the node to a side table.

Side table pros:

- easier to clear all at once;
- no AST class changes;
- can be epoch-owned.

Side table cons:

- every consumer needs access to checker side table;
- AST dumps/debugging less direct;
- harder across phases if checker object lifetime differs.

Given current frontend already stores `CallExpression::Signature`, storing `ResolvedCallTarget` on the node is natural.

---

# Final recommendation

Yes: store resolved call targets.

But define them as:

- ephemeral checker metadata;
- cleared by `CleanCheckInformation` / `Recheck`;
- guarded by semantic epoch if needed;
- selected by checker from `OverloadSetOracle`;
- consumed by lowering/codegen;
- not a persistent override/overload relation cache.

This preserves the stateless/lazy oracle design while avoiding semantic rediscovery in lowering.

Updated target design

Oracle-driven bridge generation

for (auto *methodSig : OwnConcreteMethodSignatures(classType)) {
    for (auto target : overrides.GetOverriddenTargets(classType, methodSig)) {
        if (NeedsBridge(target.base, methodSig)) {
            GenerateBridge(target.base, methodSig);
        }
    }
}

This makes bridge generation a mechanical consequence of the same override relation service used by diagnostics. The bridge phase no longer independently rediscovers override semantics.

  • Deduplicate bridges by effective or assembly descriptor.
  • Mark generated methods as synthetic/bridge.
  • Exclude bridge methods from source overload sets.
  • Preserve existing bridge body generation machinery where it is correct.
  • No permanent stored override relation table is required.
Migration plan

Principle: do not rewrite everything at once

The current code is intertwined with many other frontend phases. A total rewrite would be risky. The safe strategy is to introduce better semantic primitives while keeping existing APIs alive, then migrate consumers one by one.

Good gradual changes

Add tests, helper predicates, local bug fixes, checker-owned lazy oracles behind old APIs, and semantic-epoch cache clearing.

Atomic changes

Some changes must update checker + lowering together, especially explicit overload expansion and resolved call target representation.

Plugin and LSP note

Short-term safe recompute, long-term incremental API

Plugins may modify AST at defined points in the pipeline. Override-oracle and overload-set caches should therefore be treated as derived semantic data that can be discarded and rebuilt lazily when a plugin mutation barrier is crossed.

Short-term policy

  • After parse: continue normal scope init, binding, and checking.
  • After bind but before check: no checker Recheck is needed, because no check has happened yet. If binding is invalidated, rerun binding and then proceed to the first check.
  • After check: use the safe Recheck path. During that recheck, signatures, override-oracle caches, overload-set caches, and resolved call targets are cleared and rebuilt lazily.

Long-term optimization

    [309 more lines in file. Use offset=925 to continue.]

• Introduce an API to mark what changed: body, call site, method signature, class member set, heritage, explicit overload declaration, etc.
  • Use those marks to recompute override queries and overload sets incrementally where safe.
  • This is useful not only for plugins, but also for LSP support where small edits should avoid full program recheck.

    • Short-term correctness should not depend on plugins providing precise invalidation marks. Conservative recomputation is safer.

content.text:
Cache safety

No permanent override relation table is stored on AST/type nodes; plugin barriers and Recheck clear relation caches.

Incremental future

The oracle design can later support precise invalidation for plugins and LSP without changing source semantics.

Key takeaway

Do not let lookup, checking, and lowering rediscover the same semantics

The source-language truth should be owned by the checker through lazy relation services: override queries, ordered overload-set queries, and resolved call targets. Once these are centralized, class inheritance and multiple interface implementation become much easier to reason about and test, without storing permanent override state on AST/type nodes.

The first low-risk step is still practical: fix interface conflict checking to account for concrete class/superclass implementations before reporting a collision.

561:
  • Diagnostics and bridge generation can disagree.
    • 614:

    Current logic around duplicate overloads mixes several concepts: signature identity, return type, assembly descriptor collision, and helper overload generation. This is dangerous because the spec has a simpler source-level rule.

    704:

    Bridge generation rediscovers checker semantics

    705:

    Generic and override bridge phases currently scan the class hierarchy again. That means bridge generation performs its own override analysis instead of using the checker's result.

    720:
  • Bridge generation becomes mechanical.
    • 768:
  • No epoch is required for the short-term design if cache lifetime is strictly tied to checker runs and explicit clearing.
    • 769:
  • An epoch/generation counter can be added later as a debug guard or for fine-grained LSP/plugin incremental invalidation.
    • 875:

    Oracle-driven bridge generation

    883:

    This makes bridge generation a mechanical consequence of the same override relation service used by diagnostics. The bridge phase no longer independently rediscovers override semantics.

    888:
  • Preserve existing bridge body generation machinery where it is correct.
    • 1043:

    Add checker-owned relation services before removing old code. Initially, they can delegate internally to existing helpers while adding a common API, cache clearing, and debug tracing. Epoch/generation checks are optional and can be added later.

    1085:

    Atomic switch to oracle-driven bridge generation

    1086:

    Once OverrideOracle consumers are stable, bridge generation should stop rediscovering overrides and query GetOverriddenTargets instead.

    1124: Oracle-driven bridge generationOld rediscovery and new oracle-driven generation running together can create duplicate or missing bridge methods. 1145:
  • Switch bridge generation to OverrideOracle atomically.

• Reuse bridge body builders where possible.
  • Add runtime dispatch tests for generated bridges.

    • Running old and new bridge discovery together risks duplicate bridge methods or inconsistent signatures.

    Gradual vs atomic

    What can be done gradually

    • Add characterization tests.
    • Add pure semantic helpers.
    • Fix superclass method satisfying multiple interfaces.
    • Split source overload-equivalence from ABI collision helpers.
    • Add effective signature type helper.
    • Introduce SemanticRelationCache with lazy oracle APIs.
    • Move overload-set construction behind OverloadSetOracle.
    • Migrate diagnostics and validations one by one to OverrideOracle.
    • Clean up obsolete helper paths after replacement.
    Gradual vs atomic

    What should be done all at once

    ChangeWhy it must be atomic
    Explicit overload group expansionChecker, synthetic type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree on candidate count and order.
    Resolved call target representationChecker and lowering must switch together, otherwise lowering will keep relying on fragile owner-variable assumptions.
    Oracle-driven bridge generationOld rediscovery and new oracle-driven generation running together can create duplicate or missing bridge methods.
    Direct overload-set call resolutionMember expressions, call expressions, method references, and explicit overload aliases must share the same candidate source.
    Global effective overload-equivalenceFunctions, methods, constructors, and interfaces must follow the same source-language duplicate rule.
    Recommended order

    Practical implementation sequence

      [133 more lines in file. Use offset=1170 to continue.]

• Add tests and fix concrete superclass method implementing multiple interfaces.
  • Add pure override compatibility and overload-equivalence helpers.
  • Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision logic.
  • Implement effective signature type and use it for overload-equivalence.
  • Add checker-owned SemanticRelationCache, OverrideOracle, and OverloadSetOracle.
  • Implement explicit overload group expansion as an atomic patch.
  • Move overload-set construction into OverloadSetOracle behind existing APIs.
  • Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to OverrideOracle.
  • Migrate overload-set inherited duplicate suppression to OverrideOracle queries.
  • Switch bridge generation to OverrideOracle atomically.
  • Remove old ad-hoc/synthetic overload paths where no longer needed.
    • Final architecture

    End state: explicit but stateless semantic pipeline

    Parse declarations→ Bind names/scopes→ Build signatures→ SemanticRelationCache→ OverrideOracle queries→ OverloadSetOracle queries→ Resolved calls→ Lower aliases/bridges→ Codegen

    Correctness

    Multiple interface implementation and class hierarchy methods are resolved through one override relation service.

    Cache safety

    No permanent override relation table is stored on AST/type nodes; plugin barriers and Recheck clear relation caches.

    Incremental future

    The oracle design can later support precise invalidation for plugins and LSP without changing source semantics.

    Key takeaway

    Do not let lookup, checking, and lowering rediscover the same semantics

    The source-language truth should be owned by the checker through lazy relation services: override queries, ordered overload-set queries, and resolved call targets. Once these are centralized, class inheritance and multiple interface implementation become much easier to reason about and test, without storing permanent override state on AST/type nodes.

Estimation model requested for planning:


Important assumptions:

- The estimate below is based on **added C++ production code**, not total churn. Refactoring may also delete or move code.
- Tests, diagnostics text, documentation, CI debugging, review iterations, and flaky investigation are listed separately where relevant because they are not well represented by added C++ lines.

| Work item | Estimated added C++ LOC | Man-months by model | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |

| Pure semantic helpers + overload-equivalence split + first effective-signature helpers | 600-900 | 1.2-1.8 | Introduces side-effect-free override compatibility, overload-equivalence, and effective signature type utilities. |
| `SemanticRelationCache` + base `OverrideOracle` caches | 600-900 | 1.2-1.8 | Includes query API, cache clearing, inherited method candidate cache, override pair cache, and common-implementation query. |
| `OverloadSetOracle` base + spec ordering + explicit overload expansion | 900-1400 | 1.8-2.8 | Largest early chunk. Expands implicit overload groups in explicit overload lists and centralizes overload-set order. |

| Oracle-driven bridge generation | 450-800 | 0.9-1.6 | Replaces bridge rediscovery with `GetOverriddenTargets` queries; includes deduplication and runtime tests. |
| Cleanup, compatibility shims removal, Recheck/cache integration | 300-600 | 0.6-1.2 | Removes old ad-hoc paths, casual `front()` usage, and ensures Recheck clears all new metadata/caches. |
| **Subtotal production C++** | **4050-6650** | **8.1-13.3** | Based strictly on the 500 added C++ LOC = 1 man-month model. |

Additional non-C++ / process effort:

| Work item | Estimated effort | Notes |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Test suite expansion | 0.8-1.8 MM | Positive/negative checker tests, runtime dispatch tests, bridge tests, plugin/Recheck cache-safety tests. |

Planning totals:

- **Immediate local bug fix only:** roughly **0.5-1.0 MM** including tests/review.
- **Useful MVP** (helpers, local fix, base oracles, overload-set centralization for common calls, explicit overload expansion): roughly **4.5-7.5 MM** plus tests/review buffer.
- **Full migration** to the proposed oracle-based design: roughly **9.5-16.5 MM** including tests/review/CI buffer.

## Minimum test coverage matrix

| Area | Required tests |
| --- | --- |
| Multiple interfaces | Superclass method implements two interfaces; conflicting defaults without class method; diamond inheritance. |
| Override compatibility | Contravariant parameters; covariant returns; access weakening; final method; duplicate override of same base method. |
| Overload-equivalence | Same parameters with different return type; generic erasure collisions; constructor overload-equivalence. |
| Overload order | Textual order; explicit list order; own before superclass before interfaces; `implements`/`extends` order. |
| Explicit overloads | Listed implicit overload group expansion; inherited explicit overload from multiple interfaces; alias same as method name. |
| Runtime dispatch | Calls through superclass reference; calls through interface reference; one method overriding several inherited signatures; bridge dispatch. |
| Plugin/LSP cache safety | Recheck after post-check plugin mutation clears relation caches; post-bind plugin mutation does not call checker `Recheck`; optional epoch/generation checks can later catch stale cache reuse. |

---

## Final target architecture

The frontend should move from this implicit flow:

```text
property lookup
  -> synthetic overload variables
  -> local signature vectors
  -> local override checks
  -> bridge phases rediscover overrides
```

to this explicit but stateless/lazy flow:

```text
declarations
  -> signatures
  -> checker-owned SemanticRelationCache
       -> OverrideOracle queries
       -> OverloadSetOracle queries
  -> resolved call targets
  -> lowering / bridge generation using oracle answers
  -> codegen
```

+ 781 ## Generics-specific obligations
+ 782 
+ 783 Generics must be a first-class part of the oracle design. Override and overload answers for generic supertypes are often **viewpoint-dependent**: the same declaration signature can look different when inherited through a particular subclass or interface instantiation.
+ 784 
+ 785 Example:
+ 786 
+ 787 ```ts
+ 788 class B<T extends Object> {
+ 789     foo(p: T): T { return p }
+ 790 }
+ 791 
+ 792 class D extends B<string> {
+ 793     override foo(p: string): string { return p }
+ 794 }
+ 795 ```
+ 796 
+ 797 The implementation must distinguish:
+ 798 
+ 799 ```text
+ 800 original declaration signature:  B.foo(T): T
+ 801 signature as seen from D:        B.foo(string): string
+ 802 erased/runtime descriptor:       descriptor based on effective/erased types
+ 803 ```
+ 804 
+ 805 Design consequences:
+ 806 
+ 807 - `OverrideOracle` must compare a derived method against the inherited method **view signature**, not blindly against the original generic declaration signature.
+ 808 - `OverloadSetOracle` must add inherited generic methods as candidates using the correct substituted view from the receiver type.
+ 809 - `NeedsBridge(baseViewSignature, derivedSignature)` must consider generic erasure and substituted inherited signatures.
+ 810 - Explicit overload expansion must preserve generic candidates rather than eagerly instantiate or drop them.
+ 811 - Call resolution over generic overload candidates must still perform explicit type-argument filtering, optional/default type-parameter handling, and implicit type inference per candidate.
+ 812 
+ 813 A useful helper layer is:
+ 814 
+ 815 ```cpp
+ 816 class GenericViewResolver {
+ 817 public:
+ 818     Signature *ViewSignatureFrom(ETSObjectType *derivedType,
+ 819                                  ETSObjectType *declaringType,
+ 820                                  Signature *signature);
+ 821 
+ 822     ETSObjectType *ViewTypeFrom(ETSObjectType *derivedType,
+ 823                                 ETSObjectType *declaringType);
+ 824 };
+ 825 ```
+ 826 
+ 827 The checker should also cache substituted signature views to avoid repeated allocation and substitution:
+ 828

edits.newText:
Generics-specific design

Inherited generic signatures are viewpoint-dependent

Generics are not a corner case for this feature. Override and overload answers for inherited generic methods depend on how a generic supertype is instantiated by the current derived type.

class B<T extends Object> {
    foo(p: T): T { return p }
}

class D extends B<string> {
    override foo(p: string): string { return p }
}

Original

B.foo(T): T

View from D

B.foo(string): string

Runtime/erased

Descriptor based on effective or erased types; may require a bridge.

Generics-specific design

GenericViewResolver

class GenericViewResolver {
public:
    Signature *ViewSignatureFrom(ETSObjectType *derivedType,
                                 ETSObjectType *declaringType,
                                 Signature *signature);

    ETSObjectType *ViewTypeFrom(ETSObjectType *derivedType,
                                ETSObjectType *declaringType);
};
  • OverrideOracle compares derived methods against inherited view signatures, not always original declaration signatures.
  • OverloadSetOracle adds inherited generic candidates using the correct receiver-type view.
  • Bridge generation uses the same view signature to decide whether a runtime adapter is needed.
  • Substituted signature views should be cached until Recheck or plugin cache clear.
  • Generic type-parameter constraint variance needs a consistent rule; clarify spec wording if needed.
Target design

Overload candidate representation

The current implementation is not empty or naive. It already parses explicit overload declarations, groups same-name methods, resolves calls by scanning signatures, validates many override cases, and creates bridge methods. The problem is that these pieces are not coordinated by one semantic representation.

ets-overriding-overloading-frontend-design.html:339:

Multiple interfaces, inherited explicit overload aliases, erasure collisions, and bridge requirements are handled by separate mechanisms that can disagree.

The checker should implement this as one pure relation helper. It should not be duplicated in interface validation, method checking, and bridge lowering.

ets-overriding-overloading-frontend-design.html:519:

The frontend must preserve both facts: the selected compile-time signature and the override relation used for runtime dispatch/bridges.

ets-overriding-overloading-frontend-design.html:526:

Effective types and bridge methods

ets-overriding-overloading-frontend-design.html:527:

Effective signature types are needed when source types erase to broader runtime representations. If a derived method overrides a base method but the runtime descriptor differs, a synthetic bridge method may be required.

A caller through B<string> may dispatch by the erased/base descriptor, so the derived class must contain a matching bridge.

summary:
## Goal
User is designing a correct frontend implementation strategy for ETS **overriding**, **overloading**, and **overload resolution**, especially with class inheritance, multiple interface implementation, plugins that mutate AST, and possible LSP/incremental support. User also wants durable documentation of the findings as both HTML slide deck and Markdown.

## Constraints & Preferences
- Spec-first; do not assume behavior not in spec.
- Ask questions when in doubt.
- Prefer correctness/safety over performance.
- Do not rely on plugins to provide precise invalidation marks in the short term.
- User wants a **stateless/lazy cached** approach instead of storing a permanent override graph.
- Clean docs from “override graph” artifacts; use `OverrideOracle` / `OverloadSetOracle` terminology.
- Epoch/generation counters are **not required** short term if caches are cleared on `Recheck` / plugin barriers; may be optional later for debug/LSP.
- Post-bind plugin note: checker `Recheck` is not needed after binder because checking has not happened yet.

## Progress
### Done
- [x] Read relevant spec areas:
  - `15_semantics.rst`: Overriding, Overloading, Overload Resolution, Type Erasure.
  - `20_implementation.rst`: bridge methods for overriding.
  - `17_experimental.rst`: explicit overload declarations.

  - long-term: optional change-kind invalidation API for incremental recomputation and LSP.

### In Progress

### Blocked
- No blockers. Potential spec clarification remains around interface default conflict resolution/class method dominance, but docs note the issue.

## Key Decisions
- **Use stateless/lazy semantic relation services**: Do not store permanent override relation data on AST nodes or `ETSObjectType`; use checker-owned lazy caches.
- **Introduce `SemanticRelationCache`**: Owns `OverrideOracle` and `OverloadSetOracle`; cleared on `Recheck` and plugin mutation barriers.
- **Use `OverrideOracle`**: Answers override/implementation questions lazily, e.g. `CheckOverride`, `GetOverriddenTargets`, `HasConcreteImplementation`, `HasCommonConcreteImplementation`.
- **Use `OverloadSetOracle`**: Builds ordered overload sets lazily for functions, methods, constructors, explicit aliases; uses `OverrideOracle` to skip inherited candidates represented by overrides.
- **Store resolved call targets**: Storing selected call target on `CallExpression` is acceptable as ephemeral checker metadata, similar to `CallExpression::Signature()`, and must be cleared on `Recheck`.
- **No mandatory epoch short term**: If caches are strictly cleared on `Recheck`/plugin barriers, cache epoch/generation is optional; useful later for debug/incremental LSP.
- **Plugin policy**: After parse continue normally; after bind but before check rerun binding only if invalidated, then first check; after check use safe `Recheck`.
- **Bridge generation should query oracle**: Bridge lowering should use `OverrideOracle::GetOverriddenTargets` rather than rediscovering override semantics independently.
- **Explicit overload aliases must expand implicit overload groups**: Avoid `CallSignatures().front()` in overload-related code unless exactly-one is guaranteed.

• If no local overload declaration exists, the checker must still detect conflicting inherited aliases.
    • Finding #8

    Bridge generation rediscovers checker semantics

    Generic and override bridge phases currently scan the class hierarchy again. That means bridge generation performs its own override analysis instead of using the checker's result.

    Problem

    • Bridge phase may miss an override the checker accepted.
    • Bridge phase may generate a bridge for a relation the checker would reject.
    • Deduplication is harder.

    Better

    • Checker records override edges.
    • Lowering asks each edge whether a bridge is needed.
    • Bridge generation becomes mechanical.
    Updated target design

    Stateless, lazy semantic relation services

    The updated approach does not store permanent override relation data on AST nodes or object types. Instead, the checker owns short-lived relation services that recompute facts lazily and are explicitly cleared on Recheck and plugin mutation barriers.

    1. OverrideOracle

    Answers questions such as “does this method override that one?” and “which inherited targets does this method override?”

    2. OverloadSetOracle

    Builds ordered overload candidate sets on demand, including explicit overload expansion and inherited candidate suppression.

edits.newText:
`OverloadMappingLowering` rewrites calls to explicit overload aliases to the selected real method name.

Current bridge generation is split into two physical lowering phases:

- `GenericBridgesPhase` / `CreateGenericBridges` in `genericBridgesLowering.cpp`;
- `OverrideBridgesPhase` / `CreateOverrideBridges` in `overrideBridgesLowering.cpp`.

Both phases can reason about inherited methods and generated bridge descriptors. This is a correctness risk because generic substitution bridges and override-conversion bridges are not independent semantic domains; they are two reasons why the same source-level override relation may need a runtime adapter.

Target direction: keep at most one semantic **bridge planning** path. Existing bridge-body builders may be reused internally, but hierarchy traversal, override discovery, deduplication, and `NeedsBridge` decisions should be centralized and oracle-driven.

edits.oldText:
Finding #8

Bridge generation rediscovers checker semantics

Generic and override bridge phases currently scan the class hierarchy again. That means bridge generation performs its own override analysis instead of using the checker's result.

Problem

  • Bridge phase may miss an override the checker accepted.
  • Bridge phase may generate a bridge for a relation the checker would reject.
  • Deduplication is harder.

Better

  • Checker records override edges.
  • Lowering asks each edge whether a bridge is needed.
  • Bridge generation becomes mechanical.
edits.newText:
Finding #8

Two bridge lowerings rediscover checker semantics

Current code has two physical bridge phases: CreateGenericBridges and CreateOverrideBridges. Both can scan class hierarchy information again instead of consuming the checker’s override decision.

Problem

  • The checker and lowering may disagree.
  • The two bridge lowerings may disagree with each other.
  • Generic-substitution and override-conversion bridge reasons can overlap.
  • Deduplication by descriptor is harder.

Target

  • One oracle-driven bridge planning path.
  • Lowering queries GetOverriddenTargets.
  • NeedsBridge decides descriptor/adaptation needs.
  • Existing body builders can be reused mechanically.

• Move overload-set construction behind OverloadSetOracle.
  • Migrate diagnostics and validations one by one to OverrideOracle.
  • Clean up obsolete helper paths after replacement.
    • Gradual vs atomic

    What should be done all at once

    ChangeWhy it must be atomic
    Explicit overload group expansionChecker, synthetic type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree on candidate count and order.
    Resolved call target representationChecker and lowering must switch together, otherwise lowering will keep relying on fragile owner-variable assumptions.
    Oracle-driven bridge generationOld rediscovery and new oracle-driven generation running together can create duplicate or missing bridge methods.
    Direct overload-set call resolutionMember expressions, call expressions, method references, and explicit overload aliases must share the same candidate source.
    Global effective overload-equivalenceFunctions, methods, constructors, and interfaces must follow the same source-language duplicate rule.
    Recommended order

    Practical implementation sequence

    1. Add tests and fix concrete superclass method implementing multiple interfaces.
    2. Add pure override compatibility and overload-equivalence helpers.
    3. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision logic.
    4. Implement effective signature type and use it for overload-equivalence.
    5. Add checker-owned SemanticRelationCache, OverrideOracle, and OverloadSetOracle.
    6. Add generic view/substitution support for inherited signatures used by both oracles.
    7. Implement explicit overload group expansion as an atomic patch.
    8. Move overload-set construction into OverloadSetOracle behind existing APIs.
    9. Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to OverrideOracle.
    10. Migrate overload-set inherited duplicate suppression to OverrideOracle queries.
    11. Switch bridge generation to OverrideOracle atomically.
    12. Remove old ad-hoc/synthetic overload paths where no longer needed.

Spec overview

Overload-equivalence is not signature identity

Implicit overloads cannot contain two overload-equivalent signatures. The important subtlety is that the return type is irrelevant for overload-equivalence.

function foo(x: number): string { return "" }
function foo(x: number): number { return 1 }
// Should be compile-time error.
// Return type cannot distinguish overloads.

What to compare

  • same number of parameters;
  • effective signature type of each parameter.

What not to compare

  • return type;
  • method body;
  • source parameter names.

This deserves a dedicated helper, not reuse of ordinary signature identity.

Spec overview

Explicit overload declarations can expand implicit groups

An explicit overload declaration lists names, not necessarily single signatures. If a listed name denotes an implicit overload group, the group expands at that position.

function foo(x: number) {}
function foo(x: string) {}
function bar(x: boolean) {}

overload baz { foo, bar }

// baz's overload set should be:
// 1. foo(number)
// 2. foo(string)
// 3. bar(boolean)

This is one of the places where using CallSignatures().front() is incorrect. The implementation must preserve all signatures in order.

Spec overview

Class method overload-set order

For an instance method call, the static receiver type determines the overload set. The set is not just “all methods with that name”. It is ordered by specificity and source order.

  1. Add explicit/implicit methods declared in the current class.
  2. Append the direct superclass overload set.
  3. Append each direct superinterface overload set in implements order.
  4. Skip methods already represented by an earlier overriding candidate.
class D extends C implements I1, I2 {
    foo(x: boolean) {}
}
// overload set for D.foo:
// own D.foo candidates,
// then C.foo set,

[926 more lines in file. Use offset=495 to continue.]

When a class implements several interfaces, an apparent conflict between interface methods may already be resolved by a concrete method in the class or superclass chain. The checker must account for the class hierarchy before reporting an interface conflict.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string }
interface I2 { foo(): string }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}

Correct interpretation

C1.foo implements both I1.foo and I2.foo. C2 inherits that implementation.

What goes wrong if rejected

The checker treats I1.foo and I2.foo as conflicting interface members before checking the class hierarchy implementation.

Even if a specific build accepts the abstract-interface variant, the same deficiency appears in related default-method cases if class methods should dominate interface defaults.

Finding #2 explained

Correct algorithm for class + multiple interfaces

  1. Collect concrete instance methods declared in the class.
  2. Collect concrete instance methods inherited from the superclass chain.
  3. Collect abstract/default methods from direct and indirect interfaces.
  4. For each interface method, check whether a concrete class/superclass method implements it.
  5. Remove satisfied interface requirements from the conflict set.
  6. Only report conflicts among unresolved interface defaults/requirements.
// For C2:
C1.foo -> I1.foo
C1.foo -> I2.foo

// Both requirements satisfied; no conflict remains.

This is naturally represented by centralized override/implementation relation queries.

Finding #3

Overload-equivalence is not cleanly implemented

Current logic around duplicate overloads mixes several concepts: signature identity, return type, assembly descriptor collision, and helper overload generation. This is dangerous because the spec has a simpler source-level rule.

Language-level question

Are these two declarations illegally overload-equivalent in source?

same parameter count
same effective parameter types
ignore return type

ABI-level question

Will these two methods collide in generated descriptors or require helper/bridge methods?

assembly type descriptors
possibly include return
backend/runtime constraints

These questions should not be answered by the same helper.

Finding #4

Effective signature type is not explicit

The spec gives effective type mapping rules. The implementation needs an actual helper that represents this mapping, otherwise the checker will keep using approximations such as ordinary subtyping or assembler type strings.

Type *EffectiveType(Type *type);
Type *EffectiveSignatureType(Type *type);
EffectiveSignature EffectiveSignatureOf(Signature *sig);
  • Use this helper for overload-equivalence.
  • Use it for “not override-compatible but erasure-compatible” diagnostics.
  • Use it later for bridge necessity decisions.

This reduces the risk that different subsystems implement slightly different erasure semantics.

Finding #5

Explicit overload declarations mishandle groups

Migration phase 0

Add characterization tests first

Before refactoring, write tests that describe both current failures and intended behavior. These tests become the safety net for each later phase.

AreaTests
Multiple interfacesSuperclass method satisfies two interface methods; class method dominates interface defaults if specified; conflicting defaults without class method.
Override compatibilityContravariant params, covariant returns, access weakening, final method override, duplicate override of same base.
Overload-equivalenceSame parameters with different returns; generic/effective type collisions; constructors.
Explicit overloadsListed implicit overload group expansion; alias same as method; inherited aliases from multiple interfaces.
GenericsGeneric class/interface override views; substituted inherited signatures; generic overload candidates; generic bridge dispatch; type-parameter constraint compatibility.
Runtime dispatchCalls through superclass and interface references; bridge dispatch; one method overrides several inherited methods.
Migration phase 1

Local fix for class method satisfying multiple interfaces

This is the first practical patch because it addresses a concrete deficiency without forcing the whole redesign.

bool HasConcreteClassImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                    Signature *interfaceSig);

bool HasCommonConcreteClassImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                          Signature *a,
                                          Signature *b);

Before reporting a collision between two interface methods inherited by a class, check whether a concrete method in the class or its superclass chain implements both.

if (HasCommonConcreteClassImplementation(classType, sigA, sigB)) {
    return; // conflict resolved by class hierarchy
}
Migration phase 2

Extract pure semantic helpers

The next step is to make semantic relations explicit and side-effect-free. A predicate should not mutate the AST or mark a method as overriding while answering a yes/no question.

bool IsOverrideCompatible(Signature *base, Signature *derived);
bool AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature *a, Signature *b);
bool IsConcreteImplementationOf(Signature *impl, Signature *requirement);

Before

Compatibility checks can call SetOverride() as a side effect.

After

First compute compatibility. Then a separate analyzer records or marks the override relation.

content.text:
The checker should compute override edges once and make every consumer use them.

Finding #2

Multiple interface conflicts can be checked too early

When a class implements several interfaces, an apparent conflict between interface methods may already be resolved by a concrete method in the class or superclass chain. The checker must account for the class hierarchy before reporting an interface conflict.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string }
interface I2 { foo(): string }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}

Correct interpretation

C1.foo implements both I1.foo and I2.foo. C2 inherits that implementation.

What goes wrong if rejected

The checker treats I1.foo and I2.foo as conflicting interface members before checking the class hierarchy implementation.

Even if a specific build accepts the abstract-interface variant, the same deficiency appears in related default-method cases if class methods should dominate interface defaults.

Finding #2 explained

Correct algorithm for class + multiple interfaces

  1. Collect concrete instance methods declared in the class.
  2. Collect concrete instance methods inherited from the superclass chain.
  3. Collect abstract/default methods from direct and indirect interfaces.
  4. For each interface method, check whether a concrete class/superclass method implements it.
  5. Remove satisfied interface requirements from the conflict set.
  6. Only report conflicts among unresolved interface defaults/requirements.
// For C2:
C1.foo -> I1.foo
C1.foo -> I2.foo

// Both requirements satisfied; no conflict remains.

This is naturally represented by centralized override/implementation relation queries.

Finding #3

Overload-equivalence is not cleanly implemented

Current logic around duplicate overloads mixes several concepts: signature identity, return type, assembly descriptor collision, and helper overload generation. This is dangerous because the spec has a simpler source-level rule.

Language-level question

Are these two declarations illegally overload-equivalent in source?

same parameter count
same effective parameter types
