class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}

Expected interpretation

C1.foo implements both I1.foo and I2.foo. C2 inherits that implementation.

Planning consequence

Do not count a local false-rejection fix for this abstract-interface case in the workload estimate.

Keep the example in tests: it protects multiple-interface behavior while the implementation moves toward centralized oracle queries.

Finding #2 follow-up

Default interface methods still need a spec decision

A related variant with two interface defaults was rejected locally. Whether this is wrong depends on whether the spec says a class/superclass method dominates conflicting interface defaults.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string { return "1" } }
interface I2 { foo(): string { return "2" } }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}
  1. If class methods dominate interface defaults, suppress the conflict when one concrete class/superclass method implements both defaults.
  2. If they do not dominate, the current rejection may be correct.
  3. Either way, the oracle should expose HasCommonConcreteImplementation so validation code has one semantic query.

Count this area as tests/spec clarification unless the default-method rule is confirmed to require a production fix.

Yes — we should **keep Finding #2 in the docs**, but **not count it as an active production-code bug/fix**.

I updated the docs accordingly.

Changed interpretation:

- The abstract-interface case:

  ```ts
  class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
  interface I1 { foo(): string }
  interface I2 { foo(): string }
  class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}
  ```

  is now documented as **accepted in current smoke testing**, so it is a **regression guard / oracle-design motivator**, not an active deficiency.

- The default-method variant remains documented as an **open spec question**:

  ```ts
  class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
  interface I1 { foo(): string { return "1" } }
  interface I2 { foo(): string { return "2" } }
  class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}
  ```

  If the spec says class/superclass methods dominate interface defaults, then this may still require a small fix. Otherwise, current rejection may be correct.

.. _Default Interface Method Declarations:

Default Interface Method Declarations
*************************************

.. meta:
    frontend_status: Done

The syntax of *interface default method* is presented below:

.. code-block:: abnf

    interfaceDefaultMethodDeclaration:
        'private'? identifier signature block

A default method can be explicitly declared ``private`` in an interface body.

A block of code that represents the body of a default method in an interface
provides a default implementation for any class if such a class does not
override the method that implements the interface.

Finding #2 status

Superclass method + two abstract interfaces appears accepted

The baseline multiple-interface case is important, but a local smoke check accepted it. So it should be documented as a regression guard and oracle-design motivator, not as an active production-code bug.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string }
interface I2 { foo(): string }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}

Expected interpretation

C1.foo implements both I1.foo and I2.foo. C2 inherits that implementation.

Planning consequence

Do not count a local false-rejection fix for this abstract-interface case in the workload estimate.

Keep the example in tests: it protects multiple-interface behavior while the implementation moves toward centralized oracle queries.

Finding #2 follow-up

Default interface methods still need a spec decision

A related variant with two interface defaults was rejected locally. Whether this is wrong depends on whether the spec says a class/superclass method dominates conflicting interface defaults.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string { return "1" } }
interface I2 { foo(): string { return "2" } }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}
  1. If class methods dominate interface defaults, suppress the conflict when one concrete class/superclass method implements both defaults.
  2. If they do not dominate, the current rejection may be correct.
  3. Either way, the oracle should expose HasCommonConcreteImplementation so validation code has one semantic query.

Count this area as tests/spec clarification unless the default-method rule is confirmed to require a production fix.
edits.newText:
Finding #2 status

Abstract interfaces pass; default interfaces expose the bug

The baseline multiple-interface case is accepted locally and should remain a regression guard. The active finding is the related default-interface case, where the checker reports a conflict even though the class hierarchy has a concrete implementation.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string }
interface I2 { foo(): string }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}

Accepted baseline

C1.foo implements both abstract interface requirements. Keep this as a regression test.

Design consequence

The same relation query should be used when interface methods have default bodies.

Finding #2

Concrete class method should dominate interface defaults

Spec reading: an interface default provides an implementation only if the class does not override the method. No separate CTE was found for two defaults when a concrete class/superclass method already implements both.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string { return "1" } }
interface I2 { foo(): string { return "2" } }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}
  1. C2 inherits C1.foo.
  2. C1.foo implements both interface methods.
  3. The two defaults are not needed as implementations.
  4. No interface-default conflict should remain.

Current local behavior rejects this with an interface collision diagnostic; count it as a compiler deficiency.

content.text:
The checker should compute override edges once and make every consumer use them.

Finding #2 status

Abstract interfaces pass; default interfaces expose the bug

The baseline multiple-interface case is accepted locally and should remain a regression guard. The active finding is the related default-interface case, where the checker reports a conflict even though the class hierarchy has a concrete implementation.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string }
interface I2 { foo(): string }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}

Accepted baseline

C1.foo implements both abstract interface requirements. Keep this as a regression test.

Design consequence

The same relation query should be used when interface methods have default bodies.

Finding #2

Concrete class method should dominate interface defaults

Spec reading: an interface default provides an implementation only if the class does not override the method. No separate CTE was found for two defaults when a concrete class/superclass method already implements both.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string { return "1" } }
interface I2 { foo(): string { return "2" } }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}
  1. C2 inherits C1.foo.
  2. C1.foo implements both interface methods.
  3. The two defaults are not needed as implementations.
  4. No interface-default conflict should remain.

Current local behavior rejects this with an interface collision diagnostic; count it as a compiler deficiency.

Finding #3

Overload-equivalence is not cleanly implemented

Current logic around duplicate overloads mixes several concepts: signature identity, return type, assembly descriptor collision, and helper overload generation. This is dangerous because the spec has a simpler source-level rule.

Language-level question

Are these two declarations illegally overload-equivalent in source?

Finding #2 status

Default-interface conflict should respect concrete class implementation

Status: active compiler deficiency. A concrete class/superclass method that implements an interface method should suppress conflicts between inherited defaults for that same method.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string { return "1" } }
interface I2 { foo(): string { return "2" } }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}

Expected

C2 inherits C1.foo; that method implements both interface methods, so no default conflict remains.

Fix direction

Before reporting a default-method conflict, query HasCommonConcreteImplementation(classType, sigA, sigB).

Keep the abstract-interface variant as regression coverage, but it is not the active Finding #2 issue.

## 3. Недостатки текущей реализации

### 3.1 Попарная проверка вместо групповой

Текущий алгоритм проверяет коллизии **попарно**. Для каждой пары сигнатур ищется конкретная реализация, совместимая с **обеими** сигнатурами. Это недостаточно для случаев, где одна реализация должна быть совместима со всеми сигнатурами одновременно.

**Пример проблемы:** Пусть есть три интерфейса:
- `I1.foo(): string`
- `I2.foo(): number`  
- `I3.foo(): string | number`

Суперкласс содержит `C1.foo(): string | number`. Проверка пар:
- `(I1, I2)` → `C1.foo` совместим? `string|number` супертип `string` и `number`? Да, union супертип каждого элемента.
- `(I1, I3)` → `C1.foo` совместим (`string|number` супертип `string`).
- `(I2, I3)` → `C1.foo` совместим (`string|number` супертип `number`).

Все пары проходят, но `C1.foo(): string|number` **не является подтипом** `I1.foo(): string` для возвращаемого типа (ковариантность): `string|number` не подтип `string`. Значит, на самом деле коллизия не разрешима. Попарная проверка дала **ложноположительный результат**.

**Корень проблемы:** Проверка пар `(I1, I2)`, `(I1, I3)`, `(I2, I3)` не гарантирует, что существует тип, являющийся подтипом **всех трёх** интерфейсов одновременно. Нужна групповая проверка.

### 3.2 Отсутствие учёта generic параметров

Интерфейсы могут быть generic, а их методы иметь параметры типов. В текущей реализации `AreOverrideCompatible` не выполняет подстановку типа (type substitution) для generic параметров. В других частях кода (например, `ValidateAbstractSignature`) используется `AdjustForTypeParameters` для адаптации сигнатур.

**Пример:**
```ets
interface I1<T> { foo(t: T): T }
interface I2<T> { foo(t: T): T }
class C1 { foo(t: any): any { return t; } }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1<string>, I2<number> {}
```

После инстанцирования:
- `I1<string>.foo(t: string): string`
- `I2<number>.foo(t: number): number`

Реализация `C1.foo(t: any): any` **не совместима**:
- Для параметров: `any` супертип `string` и `number` (контравариантность) — OK.
- Для возвращаемого типа: `any` **не является подтипом** `string` или `number` (ковариантность) — FAIL.

Для корректной проверки необходимо:
1. Инстанцировать generic сигнатуры с фактическими типами-параметрами.
2. Применить подстановку через `AdjustForTypeParameters`.
3. Проверить совместимость с учётом variance.

### 3.3 Edge cases не покрыты

Текущая реализация не обрабатывает ряд краевых случаев:
- Разное количество параметров (optional, rest)
- Типы `never`, `unknown` в позициях ковариантности/контравариантности
- Несколько перегрузок метода в суперклассе (выбор совместимой)
- Сочетание union/intersection типов в сигнатурах

### 3.4 Ограничение на поиск только в суперклассах

Функция ищет реализацию только в иерархии суперклассов. В ETS нет default-методов интерфейсов, но это ограничение стоит отметить.

derived types, including generic types (See :ref:`Generics`), member
signatures of generic types (type of parameters, return type),

.. _Overriding:

Overriding
**********

*Method overriding* is the language feature closely connected with inheritance.
It allows a subclass or a subinterface to offer a specific
implementation of a method already defined in its supertype optionally
with modified signature.

The actual method to be called is determined at runtime based on object type.
Thus, overriding is related to *runtime polymorphism*.

.. note::
   *Overriding* does not apply to constructors.

|LANG| uses the *override-compatibility* rule to check the correctness of
overriding. The *overriding* is correct if method signature in a subtype
(subclass or subinterface) is *override-compatible* with the method defined
in a supertype (see :ref:`Override-Compatible Signatures`).

An implementation is forced to :ref:`Make a Bridge Method for Overriding Method`
in some cases of *method overriding*.

Overriding in Classes
=====================

.. meta:
    frontend_status: Partly

.. note::
   Only accessible (see :ref:`Accessible`) methods are subjected to overriding.
   The same rule applies to accessors in case of overriding.

An overriding method can retain access modifier of a method from a superclass
or a superinterface, or change `protected` for `public`
(see :ref:`Access Modifiers`).
Otherwise, a :index:`compile-time error` occurs.

.. code-block:: typescript

   class Base {
      public public_member() {}
      protected protected_member() {}
      private private_member() {}
   }

   interface Interface {
      public_member()             // All members are public in interfaces
      private private_member() {} // Except private methods with default implementation
   }

   class Derived extends Base implements Interface {
      public override public_member() {}
         // Public member can be overridden and/or implemented by the public one
      public override protected_member() {}
         // Protected member can be overridden by the protected or public one
      override private_member() {}
         // A compile-time error occurs as private methods of a superclass or
         // a superinterface are not accessible in the derived class, and such
         // a declaration attempt has nothing to override. 
      private_member() {}
         // Will be a correct method declaration which is not related to 
         // private methods with the same name and signature from a supoer class
         // or superinterfaces

If an *instance method* is defined or inherited by a subclass with the same name as the
*instance method* in a superclass or superinterface, then the following semantic rules are
applied:

- If signatures are not *override-compatible* (see
  :ref:`Override-Compatible Signatures`), and
  if signatures formed by using *effective
  signature types* of original signatures
  are *override-compatible* after type erasure,
  then a :index:`compile-time error` occurs.

- If signatures are *override-compatible* (see
  :ref:`Override-Compatible Signatures`), then the method of subinterface overrides
  the method of superinterface *in* the subinterface.

- Otherwise, :ref:`Implicit Method Overloading` is used.

Overriding methods from a superclass is represented in the example below:

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

   class Base {
      method_1() {}
      method_2(p: number) {}
   }
   class Derived extends Base {
      override method_1() {} // overriding
      override method_2(p: string) {} // Compile-time error, not override-compatible
   }

Overriding a method from a superinterface by a method from a superclass is represented in the example below:

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

   interface I {
      m(): void
   }

   class Base {
      m() { }
   }
   class Derived extends Base implements I {
      // method 'm' inherited from 'Base' overrides 'm' defined in 'I'
   }

A single method in a subclass can override several methods of a superclass:

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

    class B {}
    class C {
        foo(a: A) {}
        foo(b: B) {}
    }
    class D extends C {
        foo(o: Object) { console.log("foo in D")}
    }

    let c: C = new D()
    c.foo(new A()) // output: foo in D
    c.foo(new B()) // output: foo in D


If more than one method of the subclass overrides the same method of the
superclass a :index:`compile-time error` occurs:

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

     class I{
        foo (p: C) {}
     }
     class C extends I { // More than one method of class C overrides the same method
        foo (p: C) {}
        foo (p: I) {}
     }

.. _Overriding in Interfaces:

Overriding in Interfaces
========================

.. meta:
    frontend_status: Done

If a method is defined in a subinterface with the same name as an accessible
method in the superinterface, then the following semantic rules apply:

- If signatures are not *override-compatible* (see
  :ref:`Override-Compatible Signatures`), and
  if signatures formed by using *effective
  signature types* of original signatures
  are *override-compatible* after type erasure,
  then a :index:`compile-time error` occurs.

- If signatures are *override-compatible* (see
  :ref:`Override-Compatible Signatures`), then the method of subinterface overrides
  the method of superinterface *in* the subinterface.

- Otherwise, :ref:`Implicit Method Overloading` is used.

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

   interface Base {
      m(p: string): void
      m(p: number): void
   }
   interface Derived extends Base {
      m(p: object): void  // m overrides both Base.m(string) and Base.m(number)
   }

.. note::
   Several methods of superinterface can be overridden by a single method in
   a subinterface.

.. _Override-Compatible Signatures:

Override-Compatible Signatures
==============================

.. meta:
    frontend_status: Partly

Let's consider classes ``Derived`` and ``Base`` for which:

- ``Derived`` is a subclass of ``Base``
- both classes declare method ``foo``
- in ``Base``, ``foo()`` has a signature ``S``:sub:`1`
  <``V``:sub:`1` ``, ... V``:sub:`k`>
  (``U``:sub:`1` ``, ..., U``:sub:`n`) ``:U``:sub:`n+1`,
- in ``Derived``, ``foo()`` has a signature ``S``:sub:`2`
  <``W``:sub:`1` ``, ... W``:sub:`j`>
  (``T``:sub:`1` ``, ..., T``:sub:`m`) ``:T``:sub:`m+1`

as in the example below:

.. index::
   override-compatible signature
   override-compatibility
   class
   base class
   derived class
   signature

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

    class Base {
       foo <V1, ... Vk> (p1: U1, ... pn: Un): Un+1
    }
    class Derived extends Base {
       override foo <W1, ... Wj> (p1: T1, ... pm: Tm): Tm+1
    }

The signature ``S``:sub:`2` is override-compatible with ``S``:sub:`1`
only if **all** of the following conditions are met:

1. Number of parameters of both methods is the same, i.e., ``n = m``.
2. Each parameter type ``T``:sub:`i` is a supertype of ``U``:sub:`i`
   for ``i`` in ``1..n`` (contravariance).
3. If return type ``T``:sub:`m+1` is ``this``, then ``U``:sub:`n+1` is ``this``,
   or any of superinterfaces or superclass of the current type.
4. If return type ``T``:sub:`m+1` is not ``this``, then it must be a subtype
   of ``U``:sub:`n+1` (covariance).
5. Number of type parameters of either method is the same, i.e., ``k = j``.
6. Constraints of ``W``:sub:`1`, ... ``W``:sub:`j` are to be contravariant
   (see :ref:`Invariance, Covariance and Contravariance`) to the appropriate
   constraints of ``V``:sub:`1`, ... ``V``:sub:`k`.

.. _Subtyping for Tuple Types:

Subtyping for Tuple Types
=========================

.. meta:
    frontend_status: None

Any tuple type is a subtype of type ``Tuple`` (see :ref:`Type Tuple`).

Tuple type ``T`` (``P``:sub:`1` ``, ... , P``:sub:`n`) is a subtype of
type ``S`` (``P``:sub:`1` ``, ... , P``:sub:`m`), where ``n`` :math:`\geq` ``m``.
I.e., a tuple type is a subtype of a tuple type with fewer identical
constituent types  (:ref:`Type Identity`).

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

    function foo(t1: [number], t2: [string, number]) {
        let a: [] = t1       // OK
        let b: [string] = t2 // OK

        t1 = t2 // Compile-time error
        t2 = t1 // Compile-time error

        let d: [string, number, boolean] = ["a", 1, true]
        let t2 = d // OK
        let d = t2 // Compile-time error
    }

|

.. _Subtyping for Union Types:

Subtyping for Union Types
=========================

.. meta:
    frontend_status: Done

A union type ``U`` participates in a subtyping relationship
(see :ref:`Subtyping`) in the following cases:

1. Union type ``U`` (``U``:sub:`1` ``| ... | U``:sub:`n`) is a subtype of
type ``T`` if each ``U``:sub:`i` is a subtype of ``T``.

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

    let s1: "1" | "2" = "1"
    let s2: string = s1 // OK

    let a: string | number | boolean = "abc"
    let b: string | number = 42
    a = b // OK
    b = a // Compile-time error, boolean is absent is 'b'

    class Base {}
    class Derived1 extends Base {}
    class Derived2 extends Base {}

    let x: Base = ...
    let y: Derived1 | Derived2 = ...

    x = y // OK, both Derived1 and Derived2 are subtypes of Base
    y = x // Compile-time error

    let x: Base | string = ...
    let y: Derived1 | string ...
    x = y // OK, Derived1 is subtype of Base
    y = x // Compile-time error

2. Type ``T`` is a subtype of union type ``U``
(``U``:sub:`1` ``| ... | U``:sub:`n`) if for some ``i``
``T`` is a subtype of ``U``:sub:`i`.

.. code-block:: typescript
   :linenos:

    let u: number | string = 1 // OK
    u = "aa" // OK
    u = 1.0  // OK, 1.0 is of type 'number' (double)

I read Chapter 3 of `/tmp/panda_claude/.plans/detailed_override_collision_analysis.md`.

Short verdict: **not all Chapter 3 findings are spec-aligned as written. Your doubt about 3.1 is justified.**

## Chapter 3 verdict

| Finding | Spec-aligned? | Verdict |
|---|---:|---|
| **3.1 Pairwise check instead of group check** | ❌ Mostly no | The example is wrong under the spec’s return covariance rule. Pairwise-vs-group may be an implementation concern, but the given reasoning does not follow from the spec. |
| **3.2 Missing generic parameter handling** | ✅ Yes | Correct direction. Override checks must compare instantiated/substituted signatures as seen from the implementing class/interface. |
| **3.3 Edge cases not covered** | ⚠️ Partly | Some listed cases are real spec areas, but this is too broad and should be converted into concrete test requirements, not treated as one proven finding. |
| **3.4 Search only in superclasses** | ⚠️ As written, no | The statement “ETS has no default interface methods” contradicts the current spec. But superclass-only search is OK for the specific query “does the class hierarchy already provide a concrete implementation?” |

---

# 3.1 Pairwise check instead of group check

I agree with your doubt: **3.1 is not correct as written.**

The document’s example:

```ts
interface I1 { foo(): string }
interface I2 { foo(): number }
interface I3 { foo(): string | number }

class C1 {
    foo(): string | number { ... }
}
```

The document claims pairwise checks may incorrectly pass because `string | number` is a supertype of both `string` and `number`.

But for overriding, return types are **covariant**.

From the spec section **Override-Compatible Signatures**:

> If the derived return type is not `this`, then it must be a subtype of the base return type.

So for `C1.foo()` to implement `I1.foo(): string`, this must hold:

```text
string | number <: string
```

But under the spec’s union subtyping rule, this is false. A union type `U1 | ... | Un` is a subtype of `T` only if **each** constituent is a subtype of `T`.

```text
string <: string       yes
number <: string       no
--------------------------
string | number <: string   false
```

Therefore:

```text
C1.foo(): string | number
```

does **not** override:

```text
I1.foo(): string
```

The pair `(I1, I3)` should already fail. The supposed false positive should not exist if override compatibility is implemented according to the spec.

## Correct conclusion for 3.1

The claim:

> pairwise checking is insufficient because a common implementation must be compatible with the whole group

is **not established by the spec**.

The spec defines override compatibility as a **binary relation between two signatures**. It explicitly has examples where one method overrides several inherited methods, but that still means:

```text
derived method overrides base method A
derived method overrides base method B
derived method overrides base method C
```

i.e. several pairwise override edges.

A “group” algorithm may still be useful for diagnostics or deduplication, but 3.1’s example and reasoning should not be used as a spec-based finding.

Better wording would be:

> Interface conflict validation should remove every interface default that is overridden by a concrete class/superclass method. This can be implemented through pairwise `OverrideOracle` queries. A grouping layer may be useful for diagnostics and deduplication, but it is not a separate source-language rule.

---

# 3.2 Missing generic parameter handling

This one **does correspond to the spec**.

For generic interfaces/classes, the inherited method signature must be viewed after substitution.

Example:

```ts
interface I1<T> {
    foo(t: T): T
}

class C implements I1<string> {
    foo(t: string): string { return t }
}
```

The checker must compare:

```text
I1<string>.foo(string): string
```

not raw:

```text
I1<T>.foo(T): T
```

So the document’s direction is right:

- instantiate generic supertypes;
- substitute type parameters;
- compare the effective inherited signature as seen from the implementing class;
- then apply override compatibility.

This matches our earlier `GenericViewResolver` / substituted inherited signature view design.

One caveat: the example in that document uses `any`:

```ts
class C1 { foo(t: any): any { return t; } }
```

I would avoid using `any` as the main spec example unless we confirm its exact ArkTS-Sta semantics. The finding itself is valid, but the example should probably use `Object`, explicit constraints, or ordinary class types.

---

# 3.3 Edge cases not covered

This is **partly spec-aligned but too vague**.

The listed cases:

```text
- different parameter counts / optional / rest
- never / unknown
- several overloads in superclass
- union / intersection combinations
```

Some are definitely relevant:

- parameter count matters;
- rest/optional parameters need exact spec handling;
- overloaded superclass methods matter;
- union/intersection subtyping matters;
- `never` matters if it appears in valid method signatures.

But as a “finding”, 3.3 is not precise enough. It does not prove that current implementation violates the spec in each case.

I would rewrite 3.3 as:

> Add regression coverage for override compatibility involving parameter count, optional/rest parameters, overload sets, union/intersection types, and bottom/top-like types supported by the spec. Promote individual cases to implementation findings only after a concrete mismatch is demonstrated.

Also, `unknown` should be checked against the current ETS spec. I saw `never` in the spec, but `unknown` may not be a language-level type here.

---

# 3.4 Search only in superclasses

As written, this is **not spec-correct**.

The document says:

> In ETS there are no default methods in interfaces.

That contradicts `17_experimental.rst`, section **Default Interface Method Declarations**:

> A block of code that represents the body of a default method in an interface provides a default implementation for any class if such a class does not override the method that implements the interface.

So this statement should be removed.

However, there are two different questions:

## Question A: Does the class hierarchy already provide a concrete implementation?

For this query, searching only the class/superclass chain is reasonable:

```cpp
HasCommonConcreteImplementation(classType, sigA, sigB)
```

This is exactly what we need for Finding #2:

```ts
class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }

interface I1 { foo(): string { return "1" } }
interface I2 { foo(): string { return "2" } }

class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}
```

Here the relevant concrete implementation is `C1.foo`.

## Question B: Which default interface implementation is active if no class method exists?

That is broader. Then the implementation may need to consider:

- interface default methods;
- superinterface/subinterface overriding;
- multiple inherited defaults;
- conflicts between unresolved defaults.

So 3.4 should not say “ETS has no default methods”. It should instead say:

> For class-method dominance, superclass search is intentional. For complete default-interface resolution, interface default methods and interface overriding relationships must also be modeled.

---

# Recommended action on Chapter 3

I would revise Chapter 3 like this:

## Keep / promote

### 3.2 Generics

Keep as a real finding.

### Default interface conflict with concrete superclass implementation

Keep as a real finding:

```ts
class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string { return "1" } }
interface I2 { foo(): string { return "2" } }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}
```

Expected: no conflict, because `C1.foo` implements both interface methods.

## Rewrite

### 3.1

Do **not** claim group checking is required based on the `string | number` example.

Better:

> Conflict resolution should be based on override edges from concrete class/superclass methods to inherited interface defaults. Pairwise override compatibility is the spec rule; grouping is only a diagnostic/deduplication convenience.

### 3.3

Convert to test matrix, not one finding.

### 3.4

Remove “ETS has no default methods”. Replace with:

> Superclass-only search is sufficient only for detecting class hierarchy dominance. Full interface-default conflict resolution must also understand default methods and interface overriding.

---

# Bottom line

Your doubt about **3.1** is correct.

The chapter’s 3.1 example contradicts the spec because it treats return types in the wrong direction. `string | number` is **not** a valid covariant return for `string`.

So I would not carry 3.1 into our docs as a spec-based finding. I would keep the real issue as:

> Interface default conflict validation must first ask whether a concrete class/superclass method overrides both defaults. If yes, no default conflict remains.

*Interface members* include:

-  Members declared explicitly in the interface declaration;
-  Members inherited from a direct superinterface (see
   :ref:`Superinterfaces and Subinterfaces`).

A :index:`compile-time error` occurs if the method explicitly declared by the
interface has the same name as the ``Object``'s ``public`` method.

A class *implements* all its superinterfaces.

A :index:`compile-time error` occurs if:

- Class implements two interface types
  that represent different instantiations of the same
  generic interface (see :ref:`Generics`);

- Class field and a method inherited from one of
  its superinterfaces have the same name, except
  where either is static and the other is not.

.. index::
   class type
   direct superinterface
   superinterface

If a class is not *abstract*, then the following conditions must be met:

- Methods of a superinterface have implementation bodies
  that can be defined either in the class itself, or in its superclass
  or superinterface (see :ref:`Overriding in Classes` for detail);

- Required properties of superinterfaces are implemented
  (see :ref:`Implementing Required Interface Properties`).

- Otherwise, a :index:`compile-time error` occurs.

An optional property from a superinterface can be implemented or implicitly
defined (see :ref:`Implementing Optional Interface Properties`).

.. _Implementing Required Interface Properties:

Implementing Required Interface Properties
==========================================


[2877 more lines in file. Use offset=530 to continue.]

==================================

.. meta:
    frontend_status: Done

The actual method to be invoked during the :ref:`Method Call Expression` evaluation is
determined in the runtime with respect to the method statically resolved
during the compile time (see :ref:`Overload Set at Method Call`) and the actual
*type* of the ``objectReference``.

The resolution depends on the form of the call expression:

- For *static method calls*, overriding is not used and the statically
  determined method is the one to be invoked

- For *super calls*, overriding is not used and the statically resolved
  method of superclass is the one to be invoked

- For *instance method calls*, the actual type of the ``objectReference``
  referred to as *T* is used to determine the method to be invoked.

For the statically resolved method *M* defined in the type *D*, let the type *C* be

- *D* if the method *M* is found in the type *D* during the execution.

- The *closest* superclass of *C* that defines the method of the signature of *M*.

- The *closest* superinterface of *C* that defines the method of the signature of *M*.

Note: For the set of programs compiled without source code updates *C* is always *D*

Type *T* (which is always a class) and the statically
determined method *M* defined in the type *C* (where *T* is necessarily a subtype of
*C*) are used to perform the resolution, which is defined as follows:

- If *T* is *C*, the result of the resolution is *M*.

- If *T* has a superclass and the resolution of the method *M*
  for the superclass of *T* succeeds and the resolved method is defined in
  class, let *Ms* be the result of the resolution:

  - If the type *T* defines several method declarations that override the method *Ms*
    in *T*:

    - If the set of such methods contains exactly one method, this method is the
      result of the resolution.

    - Otherwise, the method resolution fails for type *T*.

  - Otherwise, *Ms* is the result of the resolution.

- Otherwise, the set of the *superinterfaces* of *T* is searched for a matching method:

  - Each considered method should be declared in the superinterface of *T*
    and should override the method *M* in *C*.

  - For each considered method *Mi*, there should be no other method *Mio*
    satisfying the previous criterion that overrides *Mi* in the interface
    that defines *Mio*.

  Note: That means, all considered method belong to subinterfaces of
  the declaring interface of *M*.

  If the set contains exactly one default method, this method is the result of
  the resolution. Otherwise, the set either

  - has multiple default methods

  - has no default methods

  In these cases, the resolution fails for type *T*.

If the method resolution fails, then a :index:`runtime error` occurs.

Note: For the set of programs compiled without source code updates
the resolution always results in method resolved and does never throw.

*Type erasure* is the concept that refers to a special handling of some language
*types*, primarily :ref:`Generics`, as members of a smaller subset of the language
*type system* when considering certain parts of the language semantics.

• Owned by ETSChecker.
  • Caches are cleared during safe Recheck and after plugin mutation barriers.
  • No epoch is required for the short-term design if cache lifetime is strictly tied to checker runs and explicit clearing.
  • An epoch/generation counter can be added later as a debug guard or for fine-grained LSP/plugin incremental invalidation.
  • This is similar in spirit to TypeRelation: relation answers are cached, but not permanently stored on every AST/type node.
Updated target design

OverrideOracle in detail

class OverrideOracle {
public:
    OverrideDecision CheckOverride(Signature *base,
                                   Signature *derived,
                                   OverrideContext ctx);

    ArenaVector<OverrideTarget> GetOverriddenTargets(ETSObjectType *owner,
                                                     Signature *derived);

    bool HasConcreteImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                   Signature *interfaceSig);

    bool HasCommonConcreteImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                         Signature *a,
                                         Signature *b);
};

Class/interface validation still asks all necessary questions, so diagnostics are complete. The difference is that answers are computed lazily and cached, not stored as permanent override state.

Updated target design

OverloadSetOracle in detail

enum class OverloadSetKind {
    FUNCTION,
    INSTANCE_METHOD,
    STATIC_METHOD,
    INTERFACE_METHOD,
    CONSTRUCTOR,
    EXPLICIT_ALIAS,
};

struct OverloadSetKey {
    ETSObjectType *receiverType;  // null for free functions
    varbinder::Scope *scope;      // for functions / namespaces
    util::StringView name;
    OverloadSetKind kind;
};

class OverloadSetOracle {
public:
    const OverloadSet &GetOverloadSet(const OverloadSetKey &key);
    const OverloadSet &ExpandExplicitOverload(ir::OverloadDeclaration *decl);
    void Clear();
};
  • Builds sets lazily for calls, references, explicit overload validation, and constructor calls.
  • Preserves spec order: own methods, direct superclass, direct interfaces in source order.
  • Expands explicit overload entries that denote implicit overload groups.
  • Uses OverrideOracle to skip inherited candidates already represented by overriding methods.
  • Caches results only until the next Recheck or plugin cache clear.
Generics-specific design

Inherited generic signatures are viewpoint-dependent

Generics are not a corner case for this feature. Override and overload answers for inherited generic methods depend on how a generic supertype is instantiated by the current derived type.

class B<T extends Object> {
    foo(p: T): T { return p }
}

class D extends B<string> {
    override foo(p: string): string { return p }
}

Original

B.foo(T): T

View from D

B.foo(string): string

Runtime/erased

Descriptor based on effective or erased types; may require a bridge.

Generics-specific design

GenericViewResolver

class GenericViewResolver {
public:
    Signature *ViewSignatureFrom(ETSObjectType *derivedType,
                                 ETSObjectType *declaringType,
                                 Signature *signature);

    ETSObjectType *ViewTypeFrom(ETSObjectType *derivedType,
                                ETSObjectType *declaringType);
};
  • OverrideOracle compares derived methods against inherited view signatures, not always original declaration signatures.
  • OverloadSetOracle adds inherited generic candidates using the correct receiver-type view.
  • Bridge generation uses the same view signature to decide whether a runtime adapter is needed.
  • Substituted signature views should be cached until Recheck or plugin cache clear.
  • Generic type-parameter constraint variance needs a consistent rule; clarify spec wording if needed.
Target design

Overload candidate representation

struct OverloadCandidate {
    Signature *signature;
    varbinder::LocalVariable *variable;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    CandidateOrigin origin; // own, explicit, superclass, interface
    size_t sourceOrder;
};

A candidate is more than a signature. Lowering needs to know which declaration was selected. Diagnostics may need the origin. Ordering must be stable and spec-derived.

This also avoids guessing selected targets later from Signature::OwnerVar(), which is fragile with synthetic/helper/imported signatures.

Target design

Resolved call target

After overload resolution, the call expression should store both the selected signature and the selected semantic target.

struct ResolvedCallTarget {
    Signature *signature;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    varbinder::Variable *variable;
    CallTargetKind kind; // function, instance method, static method, constructor
};

callExpr->SetSignature(target.signature);
callExpr->SetResolvedCallTarget(target);

Checker responsibility

Resolve overloads and choose a target using source-language semantics.

Lowering responsibility

Rewrite syntax according to the already selected target. Do not redo overload resolution.

Updated target design

Single oracle-driven bridge planning

for (auto *methodSig : OwnConcreteMethodSignatures(classType)) {
    for (auto target : overrides.GetOverriddenTargets(classType, methodSig)) {
        if (NeedsBridge(target.base, methodSig)) {
            GenerateBridge(target.base, methodSig);
        }
    }
}

This makes bridge planning a mechanical consequence of the same override relation service used by diagnostics. The final implementation should have one semantic discovery/planning path; existing generic/override bridge body builders may remain as mechanical helpers.

  • Deduplicate bridges by effective or assembly descriptor.
  • Treat generic-substitution and override-conversion bridges as reasons attached to the same override target.
  • Mark generated methods as synthetic/bridge.
  • Exclude bridge methods from source overload sets.
  • No permanent stored override relation table is required.
Migration plan

Principle: do not rewrite everything at once

The current code is intertwined with many other frontend phases. A total rewrite would be risky. The safe strategy is to introduce better semantic primitives while keeping existing APIs alive, then migrate consumers one by one.

Good gradual changes

Add tests, helper predicates, local bug fixes, checker-owned lazy oracles behind old APIs, and conservative cache clearing on Recheck/plugins.

Atomic changes

Some changes must update checker + lowering together, especially explicit overload expansion and resolved call target representation.

Plugin and LSP note

Short-term safe recompute, long-term incremental API

Plugins may modify AST at defined points in the pipeline. Override-oracle and overload-set caches should therefore be treated as derived semantic data that can be discarded and rebuilt lazily when a plugin mutation barrier is crossed.

Short-term policy

  • After parse: continue normal scope init, binding, and checking.
  • After bind but before check: no checker Recheck is needed, because no check has happened yet. If binding is invalidated, rerun binding and then proceed to the first check.
  • After check: use the safe Recheck path. During that recheck, signatures, override-oracle caches, overload-set caches, and resolved call targets are cleared and rebuilt lazily.

Long-term optimization

  • Introduce an API to mark what changed: body, call site, method signature, class member set, heritage, explicit overload declaration, etc.
  • Use those marks to recompute override queries and overload sets incrementally where safe.
  • This is useful not only for plugins, but also for LSP support where small edits should avoid full program recheck.

Recheck cleanup must include

  • node check metadata: TsType, checked flags, and diagnostics tied to the previous run;
  • rebuilt binding/type metadata as needed: identifier variables, Variable::TsType, function signatures, method types, object properties, construct signatures;
  • call metadata: CallExpression::Signature, resolved call targets, explicit overload alias selections;
  • derived caches: explicit-overload expansion, SemanticRelationCache, OverrideOracle, OverloadSetOracle, relevant TypeRelation caches, and bridge/helper requirement caches.

Short-term correctness should not depend on plugins providing precise invalidation marks. Conservative recomputation is safer.

Migration phase 0

Add characterization tests first

Before refactoring, write tests that describe both current failures and intended behavior. These tests become the safety net for each later phase.

Migration phase 1

Local fix for default-interface conflict

Keep the abstract-interface case as a regression test, and fix the default-interface collision when the class/superclass chain already provides one concrete implementation for both defaults.

bool HasConcreteClassImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                    Signature *interfaceSig);

bool HasCommonConcreteClassImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                          Signature *a,
                                          Signature *b);

Before reporting a collision between two inherited interface defaults:

if (HasCommonConcreteClassImplementation(classType, sigA, sigB)) {
    return; // conflict resolved by class hierarchy
}
Migration phase 2

Extract pure semantic helpers

The next step is to make semantic relations explicit and side-effect-free. A predicate should not mutate the AST or mark a method as overriding while answering a yes/no question.

bool IsOverrideCompatible(Signature *base, Signature *derived);
bool AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature *a, Signature *b);
bool IsConcreteImplementationOf(Signature *impl, Signature *requirement);

Before

Compatibility checks can call SetOverride() as a side effect.

After

First compute compatibility. Then a separate analyzer records or marks the override relation.

Migration phase 3

Separate overload-equivalence from ABI collision

This is a cleanup with behavior impact. It prevents source-language diagnostics from depending on backend descriptor behavior.

// Source-language rule
bool AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature *a, Signature *b);

// Backend/helper/bridge rule
bool HaveSameAssemblySignature(Signature *a, Signature *b, bool includeReturn);

// Ambient/helper-specific rule
bool NeedHelperOverload(...);

Apply the language-level helper consistently to functions, methods, interfaces, and constructors.

Migration phase 4

Implement effective signature type

Start by implementing the helper without replacing every use immediately. Then migrate one consumer at a time.

  1. Implement EffectiveType and EffectiveSignatureType.
  2. Use it in AreOverloadEquivalent.
  3. Add erasure-collision override diagnostics.
  4. Use it in bridge necessity checks through the OverrideOracle.

Do not confuse effective signature type with the assembler descriptor. They are related but serve different semantic layers.

Migration phase 5

Atomic explicit overload expansion patch

This change should be done all at once because validation, type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree about how many candidates an explicit overload alias has.

  • Allow listed names that resolve to implicit overload groups.
  • Expand all signatures of a listed group in source order.
  • Remove front()-only behavior from explicit overload construction.
  • Store selected target after resolution.
  • Update overload mapping lowering to consume the selected target.

A partial implementation is dangerous: the checker could resolve to a candidate that lowering cannot correctly rewrite.

Migration phase 6

Introduce SemanticRelationCache and lazy oracles

Add checker-owned relation services before removing old code. Initially, they can delegate internally to existing helpers while adding a common API, cache clearing, and debug tracing. Epoch/generation checks are optional and can be added later.

checker->SemanticRelations().Overrides();
checker->SemanticRelations().Overloads();
  • OverrideOracle answers override and implementation questions.
  • OverloadSetOracle builds overload sets on demand.
  • Both caches are valid only until the next explicit cache clear.
Migration phase 7

Move overload-set construction into OverloadSetOracle

Do not immediately delete synthetic property lookup behavior. Instead, make it delegate to the oracle first.

ETSObjectType::CreateSyntheticVarFromEverySignature(...) {
    auto set = checker->SemanticRelations().Overloads().GetOverloadSet(...);
    return CreateSyntheticFunctionTypeFrom(set);
}

This lets existing call sites keep working while overload set formation becomes centralized, cached, and testable.

Migration phase 8

Migrate override consumers to OverrideOracle

No permanent override state is required. Each validation pass asks the oracle the exhaustive questions it needs; the oracle caches answers.

  1. Use it for override keyword diagnostics.
  2. Use it for final/access/return diagnostics.
  3. Use it for duplicate override-of-same-base detection.
  4. Use it for interface implementation and conflict validation.
  5. Use it for inherited overload candidate suppression.
Migration phase 9

Atomic switch to single bridge planning

Once OverrideOracle consumers are stable, bridge planning should stop rediscovering overrides in both current bridge phases and query GetOverriddenTargets instead.

  • Disable semantic bridge rediscovery in CreateGenericBridges and CreateOverrideBridges in the same patch.
  • Generate bridge plans from oracle targets.
  • Treat generic-substitution and override-conversion needs as reasons on the same target.
  • Deduplicate by effective/assembly descriptor.
  • Reuse bridge body builders where possible.
  • Add runtime dispatch tests for generated bridges.

Running old generic/override rediscovery and new bridge planning together risks duplicate bridge methods or inconsistent signatures.

Gradual vs atomic

What can be done gradually

  • Add characterization tests.
  • Add pure semantic helpers.
  • Fix default-interface conflict handling when a concrete superclass method implements both defaults.
  • Split source overload-equivalence from ABI collision helpers.
  • Add effective signature type helper.
  • Introduce SemanticRelationCache with lazy oracle APIs.
  • Move overload-set construction behind OverloadSetOracle.
  • Migrate diagnostics and validations one by one to OverrideOracle.
  • Clean up obsolete helper paths after replacement.
Gradual vs atomic

What should be done all at once

ChangeWhy it must be atomic
Explicit overload group expansionChecker, synthetic type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree on candidate count and order.
Resolved call target representationChecker and lowering must switch together, otherwise lowering will keep relying on fragile owner-variable assumptions.
Single oracle-driven bridge planningOld generic/override rediscovery and new oracle-driven planning running together can create duplicate or missing bridge methods.
Direct overload-set call resolutionMember expressions, call expressions, method references, and explicit overload aliases must share the same candidate source.
Global effective overload-equivalenceFunctions, methods, constructors, and interfaces must follow the same source-language duplicate rule.
Recommended order

Practical implementation sequence

  1. Add tests and a local fix for concrete superclass method dominating multiple interface defaults.
  2. Add pure override compatibility and overload-equivalence helpers.
  3. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision logic.
  4. Implement effective signature type and use it for overload-equivalence.
  5. Add checker-owned SemanticRelationCache, OverrideOracle, and OverloadSetOracle.
  6. Add generic view/substitution support for inherited signatures used by both oracles.
  7. Implement explicit overload group expansion as an atomic patch.
  8. Move overload-set construction into OverloadSetOracle behind existing APIs.
  9. Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to OverrideOracle.
  10. Migrate overload-set inherited duplicate suppression to OverrideOracle queries.
  11. Switch to single oracle-driven bridge planning atomically.
  12. Remove old ad-hoc/synthetic overload paths where no longer needed.
Workload estimation

Planning model and caveats

For planning, use the requested model: 500 added C++ production lines ≈ 1 man-month.

What the model captures

  • new checker/oracle/lowering C++ code;
  • new helper types and cache APIs;
  • integration code for Recheck/cache clearing.

What it undercounts

  • tests and diagnostics text;
  • review iterations and CI debugging;
  • large refactors with low net added lines;
  • flaky/runtime bridge investigation.

Ranges below are broad. The implementation touches checker, object type lookup, explicit overload validation, lowering, bridge generation, and Recheck cleanup.

# ETS Frontend Findings: Overriding, Overloading, and Overload Resolution

## Scope

This document summarizes findings from reading the ETS specification chapters for:

- **Overriding**
- **Overloading**
- **Overload Resolution**
- linked **Type Erasure** semantics
- linked **Bridge Method for Overriding Method** implementation guidance

It also summarizes the current `ets2panda` frontend implementation shape, observed flaws, proposed design, and a gradual migration plan.

Primary frontend areas inspected:

- `parser/ETSparser*.cpp`
- `ir/base/overloadDeclaration.h`
- `compiler/lowering/scopesInit/scopesInitPhase.cpp`
- `varbinder/ETSBinder.cpp`
- `checker/ets/function.cpp`
- `checker/ets/object.cpp`
- `checker/ets/typeCheckingHelpers.cpp`
- `checker/types/ets/etsObjectType.cpp`
- `compiler/lowering/ets/overloadMappingLowering.cpp`
- `compiler/lowering/ets/genericBridgesLowering.cpp`
- `compiler/lowering/ets/overrideBridgesLowering.cpp`

## Main conclusion

The current frontend already has many pieces of the feature:

- syntax and AST support for `overload` declarations;
- parser support for `override` and overload syntax;
- method grouping through `MethodDefinition::Overloads()`;
- checker-side first-match call resolution;
- interface/class validation logic;
- explicit overload validation logic;
- explicit overload lowering;
- generic and override bridge lowering phases.

However, the design is **fragmented**. Several subsystems rediscover or partially model the same semantic facts:

- member/property lookup constructs synthetic function types;
- override checks are performed locally per method;
- interface conflict checks independently compare interface methods;
- explicit overload declaration logic builds synthetic signatures in another way;
- bridge lowering scans supertypes again instead of consuming one checker-owned semantic relation service.

The updated recommended design is **stateless from the AST/type-system perspective**:

1. do **not** permanently store override relation data on AST nodes or `ETSObjectType` initially;
2. introduce a lazy, cached **OverrideOracle** / override relation service owned by the checker;
3. introduce a lazy, cached **OverloadSetOracle** / overload-set service owned by the checker;
4. cache results only for the current checker run / until the next explicit cache clear;
5. clear these caches after plugin mutation barriers or during `Recheck`;
6. later introduce finer-grained invalidation for trusted plugin/LSP incremental support.

The first implementation should expose override information as **queries over a lazy relation cache**, not as long-lived materialized state.

---

## Spec-derived semantic requirements

## Overriding

A method in a subtype overrides a method in a supertype if their signatures are override-compatible.

Relevant requirements:

- Constructors do **not** participate in overriding.
- Only accessible methods/accessors are override candidates.
- Static methods do not participate in instance override dispatch.
- Private methods are not inherited override candidates.
- Parameter types are contravariant: the overriding method parameter type must be a **supertype** of the overridden method parameter type.
- Return types are covariant: the overriding method return type must be a **subtype** of the overridden method return type.
- Access cannot be weakened:
  - `public` must stay `public`;
  - `protected` may stay `protected` or become `public`;
  - `private` is not an override candidate.

content.text:
- reduce overload-specific property lookup flags;
- remove or shrink synthetic overload variable construction in `GetProperty`;
- remove duplicated override predicates;
- remove casual `CallSignatures().front()` in overload paths;
- make call resolution consume overload sets directly from the oracle.

---

## What can be done gradually

Safe gradual changes:

1. Add characterization tests.
2. Add pure helper functions.
3. Fix default-interface conflict handling when a concrete superclass method implements both defaults.
4. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision.
5. Add effective signature type helper.
6. Introduce `SemanticRelationCache` with empty or delegated oracle implementations.
7. Move overload-set construction behind `OverloadSetOracle`.
8. Move override diagnostics and interface validation behind `OverrideOracle`.
9. Remove duplicate predicates after oracle consumers are stable.

---

## What should be done all at once

Some changes must be atomic because partial migration would create inconsistent semantics.

| Change | Why it should be atomic |
| --- | --- |
| Explicit overload expansion | Validation, synthetic type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree about candidate count/order. |
| Resolved call target representation | Checker and lowering must switch together from owner-variable assumptions to explicit target metadata. |
| Single oracle-driven bridge planning | Running old generic/override rediscovery and new oracle-driven planning together risks duplicate or missing bridges. |
| Direct overload-set call resolution | `MemberExpression`, `CallExpression`, method references, explicit overloads, and lowering must agree. |
| Effective overload-equivalence across declaration kinds | Functions, methods, interfaces, and constructors must use the same language rule. |

---

## Recommended implementation order

1. Add tests and a local fix for concrete superclass method dominating multiple interface defaults.
2. Add pure override compatibility and overload-equivalence helpers.
3. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision checks.
4. Implement effective signature type and use it for overload-equivalence.
5. Add checker-owned `SemanticRelationCache`, `OverrideOracle`, and `OverloadSetOracle` with coarse cache clearing.
6. Add generic view/substitution support for inherited signatures used by both oracles.
7. Implement explicit overload expansion as an atomic patch.
8. Move overload-set construction into `OverloadSetOracle` behind existing APIs.
9. Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to `OverrideOracle`.
10. Migrate overload-set duplicate suppression to `OverrideOracle` queries.
11. Switch to single oracle-driven bridge planning atomically.
12. Remove obsolete synthetic/ad-hoc overload paths.

---

## Workload estimation

Estimation model requested for planning:

```text
500 added C++ production lines ~= 1 man-month
```

Important assumptions:

- The estimate below is based on **added C++ production code**, not total churn. Refactoring may also delete or move code.
- Tests, diagnostics text, documentation, CI debugging, review iterations, and flaky investigation are listed separately where relevant because they are not well represented by added C++ lines.
- Ranges are intentionally broad because the current implementation is intertwined with checker, object type lookup, lowering, and bridge generation.
- The safest plan is still incremental: land small correctness-preserving steps instead of one large rewrite.

| Work item | Estimated added C++ LOC | Man-months by model | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Default-interface conflict fix + regression tests | 150-300 | 0.3-0.6 | Fix default-interface conflict handling so a concrete class/superclass method suppresses conflicts between defaults it implements; keep abstract-interface coverage as regression tests. |
| Pure semantic helpers + overload-equivalence split + first effective-signature helpers | 600-900 | 1.2-1.8 | Introduces side-effect-free override compatibility, overload-equivalence, and effective signature type utilities. |
| `SemanticRelationCache` + base `OverrideOracle` caches | 600-900 | 1.2-1.8 | Includes query API, cache clearing, inherited method candidate cache, override pair cache, and common-implementation query. |
| `OverloadSetOracle` base + spec ordering + explicit overload expansion | 900-1400 | 1.8-2.8 | Largest early chunk. Expands implicit overload groups in explicit overload lists and centralizes overload-set order. |
| Generic view/substitution support for oracles | 500-900 | 1.0-1.8 | Adds substituted inherited signature views, generic candidate handling, and bridge/override support for generic supertypes. |
| Resolved call target metadata + lowering consumption | 350-650 | 0.7-1.3 | Adds selected target metadata and updates explicit-overload lowering to consume it instead of rediscovering owners. |
| Migrate class/interface validation to `OverrideOracle` | 700-1100 | 1.4-2.2 | Moves override diagnostics, interface implementation, default conflict checks, and duplicate override checks to oracle queries. |
| Single oracle-driven bridge planning | 450-800 | 0.9-1.6 | Replaces both bridge rediscovery paths with `GetOverriddenTargets` queries; includes descriptor deduplication and runtime tests. |
| Cleanup, compatibility shims removal, Recheck/cache integration | 300-600 | 0.6-1.2 | Removes old ad-hoc paths, casual `front()` usage, and ensures Recheck clears all new metadata/caches. |
| **Subtotal production C++** | **4550-7550** | **9.1-15.1** | Based strictly on the 500 added C++ LOC = 1 man-month model. |

Additional non-C++ / process effort:

| Work item | Estimated effort | Notes |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Test suite expansion | 1.2-2.7 MM | Positive/negative checker tests, runtime dispatch tests, bridge tests, plugin/Recheck cache-safety tests, and generic substitution/viewpoint tests. |
| Diagnostics polish and review iterations | 0.4-0.8 MM | Especially around overload-equivalence, inherited explicit overloads, and interface conflicts. |
| CI/flaky/debugging buffer | 0.3-0.7 MM | Needed because changes touch checker ordering, lowering, and bridges. |

Planning totals:

| Override compatibility | Contravariant parameters; covariant returns; access weakening; final method; duplicate override of same base method. |
| Overload-equivalence | Same parameters with different return type; generic erasure collisions; constructor overload-equivalence. |
| Overload order | Textual order; explicit list order; own before superclass before interfaces; `implements`/`extends` order. |
| Explicit overloads | Listed implicit overload group expansion; inherited explicit overload from multiple interfaces; alias same as method name. |
| Generics | Generic class/interface override views; substituted inherited signatures; generic overload candidates; generic bridge dispatch; type-parameter constraint compatibility. |
| Runtime dispatch | Calls through superclass reference; calls through interface reference; selected default interface dispatch; one method overriding several inherited signatures; bridge dispatch. |
| Plugin/LSP cache safety | Recheck after post-check plugin mutation clears relation caches; post-bind plugin mutation does not call checker `Recheck`; optional epoch/generation checks can later catch stale cache reuse. |

---

## Final target architecture

The frontend should move from this implicit flow:

```text
property lookup
  -> synthetic overload variables
  -> local signature vectors
  -> local override checks
  -> generic/override bridge phases rediscover overrides separately
```

to this explicit but stateless/lazy flow:

```text
declarations
  -> signatures
  -> checker-owned SemanticRelationCache
       -> OverrideOracle queries
       -> OverloadSetOracle queries
  -> resolved call targets
  -> lowering / single bridge planning using oracle answers
  -> codegen
```

Benefits:

- no permanent override relation table to invalidate on AST/type nodes;
- spec order is explicit and testable;
- multiple interface implementation is handled consistently;
- class/superclass methods correctly satisfy interface requirements before conflicts are reported;
- explicit overload aliases behave according to the spec;
- bridge planning uses the same override relation service as diagnostics;
- lowering and codegen become consumers of checker decisions, not semantic rediscovery layers;
- coarse cache clearing is safe for plugins;
- later incremental invalidation can benefit both plugins and LSP.

Updated target design

Stateless, lazy semantic relation services

The updated approach does not store permanent override relation data on AST nodes or object types. Instead, the checker owns short-lived relation services that recompute facts lazily and are explicitly cleared on Recheck and plugin mutation barriers.

1. OverrideOracle

Answers questions such as “does this method override that one?” and “which inherited targets does this method override?”

2. OverloadSetOracle

Builds ordered overload candidate sets on demand, including explicit overload expansion and inherited candidate suppression.

3. Resolved call target

Stores the selected function/method/constructor target on each call so lowering does not redo semantic discovery.

Override information is exposed as lazy cached relation queries, not as a stored data structure on AST/type nodes.

Updated target design

SemanticRelationCache

class SemanticRelationCache {
public:
    void Clear();

    OverrideOracle &Overrides();
    OverloadSetOracle &Overloads();

private:
    OverrideOracle overrideOracle_;
    OverloadSetOracle overloadOracle_;
};
  • Owned by ETSChecker.
  • Caches are cleared during safe Recheck and after plugin mutation barriers.
  • No epoch is required for the short-term design if cache lifetime is strictly tied to checker runs and explicit clearing.
  • An epoch/generation counter can be added later as a debug guard or for fine-grained LSP/plugin incremental invalidation.
  • This is similar in spirit to TypeRelation: relation answers are cached, but not permanently stored on every AST/type node.
Updated target design

OverrideOracle in detail

class OverrideOracle {
public:
    OverrideDecision CheckOverride(Signature *base,
                                   Signature *derived,
                                   OverrideContext ctx);

    ArenaVector<OverrideTarget> GetOverriddenTargets(ETSObjectType *owner,
                                                     Signature *derived);

    bool HasConcreteImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                   Signature *interfaceSig);

    bool HasCommonConcreteImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                         Signature *a,
                                         Signature *b);
};

Class/interface validation still asks all necessary questions, so diagnostics are complete. The difference is that answers are computed lazily and cached, not stored as permanent override state.

Updated target design

OverloadSetOracle in detail

enum class OverloadSetKind {
    FUNCTION,
    INSTANCE_METHOD,
    STATIC_METHOD,
    INTERFACE_METHOD,
    CONSTRUCTOR,
    EXPLICIT_ALIAS,
};

struct OverloadSetKey {
    ETSObjectType *receiverType;  // null for free functions
    varbinder::Scope *scope;      // for functions / namespaces
    util::StringView name;
    OverloadSetKind kind;
};

class OverloadSetOracle {
public:
    const OverloadSet &GetOverloadSet(const OverloadSetKey &key);
    const OverloadSet &ExpandExplicitOverload(ir::OverloadDeclaration *decl);
    void Clear();
};
  • Builds sets lazily for calls, references, explicit overload validation, and constructor calls.
  • Preserves spec order: own methods, direct superclass, direct interfaces in source order.
  • Expands explicit overload entries that denote implicit overload groups.
  • Uses OverrideOracle to skip inherited candidates already represented by overriding methods.
  • Caches results only until the next Recheck or plugin cache clear.

Updated target design

DefaultImplementationResolver

enum class ImplementationKind {
    CLASS_METHOD,
    SUPERCLASS_METHOD,
    INTERFACE_DEFAULT,
};

struct ImplementationTarget {
    ImplementationKind kind;
    Signature *signature;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    ETSObjectType *declaringType;
};

class DefaultImplementationResolver {
public:
    ImplementationResolution ResolveImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                                   Signature *requirement);
    bool HasCommonImplementation(ETSObjectType *classType,
                                 Signature *a,
                                 Signature *b);
};

Default methods need one semantic resolution path, otherwise checker diagnostics and verifier/linker-visible emitted defaults can disagree.

Updated target design

Default implementation rules

  • Prefer concrete class/superclass methods when they override the interface requirement.
  • Collect applicable interface defaults only when no class implementation exists.
  • Remove defaults overridden by more specific subinterface defaults.
  • Preserve a superclass-selected default as inherited implementation when appropriate.
  • Use substituted generic interface views for parameterized defaults.
  • Feed the selected implementation to lowering/emission so the verifier does not see multiple unresolved defaults.

This service consumes OverrideOracle; it must not rediscover override semantics independently.

content.text:
• Add effective signature type helper.
  • Introduce SemanticRelationCache with lazy oracle APIs.
  • Move overload-set construction behind OverloadSetOracle.
  • Migrate diagnostics and validations one by one to OverrideOracle.
  • Add default implementation resolution behind the same relation services.
  • Clean up obsolete helper paths after replacement.
    • Gradual vs atomic

    What should be done all at once

    ChangeWhy it must be atomic
    Explicit overload group expansionChecker, synthetic type construction, call resolution, and lowering must agree on candidate count and order.
    Resolved call target representationChecker and lowering must switch together, otherwise lowering will keep relying on fragile owner-variable assumptions.
    Single oracle-driven bridge planningOld generic/override rediscovery and new oracle-driven planning running together can create duplicate or missing bridge methods.
    Default-method emission switchChecker default-resolution results and emitted/default-forwarding representation must agree, otherwise verifier/linker can still see multiple defaults.
    Direct overload-set call resolutionMember expressions, call expressions, method references, and explicit overload aliases must share the same candidate source.
    Global effective overload-equivalenceFunctions, methods, constructors, and interfaces must follow the same source-language duplicate rule.
    Recommended order

    Practical implementation sequence

    1. Add tests and a local fix for concrete superclass method dominating multiple interface defaults.
    2. Add pure override compatibility and overload-equivalence helpers.
    3. Split overload-equivalence from ABI collision logic.
    4. Implement effective signature type and use it for overload-equivalence.
    5. Add checker-owned SemanticRelationCache, OverrideOracle, OverloadSetOracle, and default implementation resolver.
    6. Add generic view/substitution support for inherited signatures used by all relation services.
    7. Implement explicit overload group expansion as an atomic patch.
    8. Move overload-set construction into OverloadSetOracle behind existing APIs.
    9. Migrate interface implementation/conflict checks to OverrideOracle.
    10. Add default implementation resolution for selected interface defaults and verifier-safe emission.
    11. Migrate overload-set inherited duplicate suppression to OverrideOracle queries.
    12. Switch to single oracle-driven bridge planning atomically.
    13. Remove old ad-hoc/synthetic overload paths where no longer needed.

content.text:
The checker should compute override edges once and make every consumer use them.

Finding #2 status

Default-interface conflict should respect concrete class implementation

Status: active compiler deficiency. A concrete class/superclass method that implements an interface method should suppress conflicts between inherited defaults for that same method.

class C1 { foo(): string { return "" } }
interface I1 { foo(): string { return "1" } }
interface I2 { foo(): string { return "2" } }
class C2 extends C1 implements I1, I2 {}

Expected

C2 inherits C1.foo; that method implements both interface methods, so no default conflict remains.

Fix direction

Before reporting a default-method conflict, query HasCommonConcreteImplementation(classType, sigA, sigB).

Keep the abstract-interface variant as regression coverage, but it is not the active Finding #2 issue.

Finding #3

Overload-equivalence is not cleanly implemented

Current logic around duplicate overloads mixes several concepts: signature identity, return type, assembly descriptor collision, and helper overload generation. This is dangerous because the spec has a simpler source-level rule.

Language-level question

Are these two declarations illegally overload-equivalent in source?

same parameter count
same effective parameter types
ignore return type
