# Component Design: IR And AST Model
Component ID: ir_ast
Decision: detailed

## Summary
IR/AST participates by preserving stable overload and override syntax facts, source order, and opaque lookup identities. It must not own overload-set semantics, override targets, candidate vectors, or resolved-call results.

## Top-Level Alignment
The approved architecture moves semantics to binder/checker side records and lowering adapters. This component supplies syntax identities and declaration shape only, mainly through `ir/base/overloadDeclaration*` and `ir/base/methodDefinition*`.

## Tasks

### Task 1: OverloadDeclaration Preserve Syntax
Request Tasks: Task 2, Task 3
Description: `OverloadDeclaration` represents explicit `overload name { ... }` syntax and overload-list elements. Its local role is to preserve source shape, declaration order, modifiers, names, signatures, constructors, and accessor syntax for binder/checker grouping.
Dependancies: none
Detailed Design: Add explicit AST/IR accessors for syntax-only overload-list facts: overload-list name, element ordinals, modifier tokens, signature shape, staticness, constructor/accessor category, and source ranges. Change any semantic-looking overload storage on `OverloadDeclaration` into syntax roles only. Remove AST-owned candidate grouping, selected implementation, override-target, or resolution-state fields if present. Binder consumes these syntax facts to create checker-visible side records keyed by declaration identity.
Acceptance Criteria: `OverloadDeclaration` can round-trip AST dump/source-order information for explicit overload lists without exposing `OverloadSet`, selected callable, override target, or candidate-resolution data.
Workload: 1.0 MM

### Task 2: MethodDefinition Expose Syntax Key
Request Tasks: Task 3, Task 4, Task 7
Description: `MethodDefinition` represents real callable declarations that may become implicit overload entities. It must expose a stable syntax identity and lookup key facts while leaving semantic identity to binder/checker side records.
Dependancies: none
Detailed Design: Add or standardize an opaque `MethodDefinition` syntax key plus syntax-only accessors for owner context, declared name, kind, staticness, constructor/accessor category, type parameters, parameter shape, and source ordinal. Change checker/lowering-facing consumers to use the opaque key when requesting semantic facts from side records. Remove any AST-owned overload-group membership, implementation-signature compatibility state, override-validity state, or resolved-call state. `MethodDefinition` hands syntax keys and shape facts to binder; checker and lowering adapter own the semantic records keyed by those identities.
Acceptance Criteria: A `MethodDefinition` can identify a callable declaration deterministically for binder/checker lookup, but inspecting the node cannot reveal overload-set membership, override target, selected candidate, or resolved-call metadata.
Workload: 1.0 MM

### Task 3: SyntaxIdentity Boundary Lock
Request Tasks: Task 3, Task 7, Task 10
Description: The component needs a clear identity boundary so side records can attach semantics without mutating AST meaning. AST/IR may own only opaque declaration or call identities, source ordinals, and existing node links.
Dependancies: OverloadDeclaration Preserve Syntax, MethodDefinition Expose Syntax Key
Detailed Design: Add a component-local `SyntaxIdentity` convention for overload declarations, method definitions, and call-like nodes that lowering may reference through an adapter. Change all IR/AST APIs that currently expose semantic handles to expose only opaque ids or syntax keys. Remove ambiguous “metadata slot” patterns where checker could store `OverloadSet`, override mapping, candidate vectors, selected callable, inferred type arguments, or diagnostics directly on AST nodes. The resulting design works by parser/IR creating stable identities, binder/checker filling side records keyed by identities, and lowering adapter resolving checked facts by key.
Acceptance Criteria: Code review can verify that AST/IR owns only opaque keys and syntax facts; checker-owned `OverloadSet`, override target, selected callable, and `ResolvedOverloadCall` data are stored outside AST/IR.
Workload: 0.8 MM

### Task 4: AST Dump Preserve Overload Order
Request Tasks: Task 2, Task 11
Description: AST dump and clone behavior must keep overload declaration order visible for tests and diagnostics. This component owns the source-order preservation needed by binder/checker to form deterministic overload sets.
Dependancies: OverloadDeclaration Preserve Syntax
Detailed Design: Change AST dumping, cloning, traversal, and child iteration for `OverloadDeclaration` and overload-related `MethodDefinition` nodes so explicit-list order and per-element source ordinals are stable. Remove dump behavior that implies semantic resolution or implementation selection. The parser/IR traversal exposes ordered syntax elements; binder/checker later interpret that order according to spec.
Acceptance Criteria: AST-focused tests can assert explicit overload-list order, constructors/accessors, modifiers, and method declarations without depending on checker semantic metadata.
Workload: 0.6 MM

### Task 5: Lowering Adapter Keys
Request Tasks: Task 7, Task 10
Description: Existing overload lowerings may still need to locate codegen-facing overload facts during migration. IR/AST should provide stable keys for adapter lookup, not semantic data.
Dependancies: SyntaxIdentity Boundary Lock
Detailed Design: Add the minimal AST/IR key access needed by overload-related lowerings to ask a checker/lowering adapter for group id, implementation method, helper need, async/interface facts, or selected call target. Change direct lowering reads of AST-owned overload semantics into adapter queries by syntax key. Remove IR fields whose only purpose is to cache lowering semantic decisions. `OverloadDeclaration`, `MethodDefinition`, and call-like nodes hand off opaque identities; the adapter owns checked metadata.
Acceptance Criteria: Lowering code can reach checked overload facts through adapter lookup by AST/IR key, while AST/IR nodes remain syntax-only and contain no selected-call or override-target payload.
Workload: 0.8 MM

## Cross-Cutting Constraints
- AST/IR owns syntax identity only — semantic overload sets, override mappings, and resolved-call data belong to checker/lowering-adapter side records (source: ref:kotlin-fir-descriptor-override-overload)
- Preserve explicit source order — ETS first-valid overload resolution depends on deterministic candidate ordering formed later from syntax order (source: spec §15.11)
- No AST shape mutation for semantics — checker may attach metadata externally but must not rewrite declaration structure (source: assumption §3)

## Data And Control Flow
- Parser creates `OverloadDeclaration` and `MethodDefinition` syntax nodes — IR/AST — identities and source ordinals are fixed before binding (source: assumption §3)
- Binder reads syntax facts and keys — binder/checker side records — overload groups are formed outside AST/IR (source: ref:typescript)
- Checker resolves override and call semantics — checker side records — selected callable and failure buckets are keyed by syntax identity, not stored on nodes (source: ref:kotlin-fir-descriptor-override-overload)
- Lowering asks adapter by key — lowering adapter and IR/AST — codegen-facing facts are consumed without reinterpreting AST syntax (source: external:index.md)

## Component Interactions
- [id: i1] `ir::OverloadDeclaration` -> `varbinder::ETSBinder` — exposes syntax-only overload-list facts and element order for group creation (source: spec §15.11)
- [id: i2] `ir::MethodDefinition` -> `checker::ETSchecker` — exposes callable syntax key and declaration shape for signature side-record construction (source: ref:typescript)
- [id: i3] `ir_ast SyntaxIdentity` -> `lowering adapter` — supplies opaque lookup keys for checked metadata retrieval (source: external:index.md)

## Rationale
This component is affected because overload declarations and real callable declarations are the source identities for the new semantic model. The clean boundary is essential: Kotlin and TypeScript both support semantic side records/caches, while AST nodes remain declaration carriers.

## Skip Rationale
Not skipped.

# Component Design: Variable Binding And Scopes
Component ID: varbinder
Decision: detailed

## Summary
`varbinder` is materially affected because overload and override syntax must become deterministic scope facts before checker semantics run. The component owns structural grouping, lookup identity, import/export provenance, and scopes-init publication, but not final ETS overload-set construction or semantic ordering.

## Top-Level Alignment
The approved architecture requires `ETSBinder` and scopes initialization to register `ExplicitOverloadList` and `ImplicitOverloadEntity` facts by same scope, owner, name, kind, staticness, and accessor/constructor category. Checker then builds semantic `OverloadSet` records, validates override rules, resolves first-valid calls, and supplies lowering metadata.

## Tasks

### Task 1: ETSBinder Inventory Marks Boundaries
Request Tasks: Task 2, Task 10
Description: Inventory existing overload and override handling inside `ETSBinder`, scope insertion, import/export binding, and scopes initialization. Classify each behavior as syntax capture, structural binding, lookup publication, semantic validation, or lowering compatibility support.
Dependancies: none
Detailed Design: Add a component-local inventory note or design artifact for `ETSBinder` and scope entities. Change the migration baseline by marking binder-owned facts separately from checker-owned overload construction and lowering-owned structural transforms. Remove undocumented assumptions that binder finalization proves overload equivalence, override validity, or call applicability. The resulting inventory drives later `varbinder` work without prescribing checker implementation.
Acceptance Criteria: The inventory names every `varbinder` overload/override entrypoint and records whether it currently mutates AST, inserts scope symbols, links imports, or feeds scopes-init. It explicitly marks inherited candidates, first-valid ordering, overload-equivalence, type compatibility, duplicate candidate skipping, and semantic diagnostics as outside binder ownership.
Workload: 0.5 MM

### Task 2: Overload Roles Capture Source Facts
Request Tasks: Task 3, Task 4
Description: `ETSBinder` must capture overload declaration roles as immutable structural facts. Explicit overload-list declarations and real callable declarations with the same local owner/name become separate role records, not a final semantic overload set.
Dependancies: ETSBinder Inventory Marks Boundaries
Detailed Design: Add binder-side role records for explicit overload-list entries, implicit callable entities, source ordinals, declaration identity, owner identity, and declared name. Change existing binding so `_overload_` declarations and callable declarations are registered through the same structural collection path. Remove binder logic that treats an implementation method as a hidden TypeScript-style signature list member. `ETSBinder` hands role records to scope-owned group storage while checker later interprets them as ETS semantic candidates.
Acceptance Criteria: Same-scope explicit overload declarations and same-name callable declarations are visible as distinct role records with stable source order. Binder output contains no selected overload target, no override target, and no final candidate applicability state.
Workload: 1.5 MM

### Task 3: Scope Group Keys Use Full Dimensions
Request Tasks: Task 3, Task 4, Task 8
Description: Scope grouping must be keyed by the complete structural identity required by the architecture. This prevents methods, constructors, accessors, static members, and instance members from merging accidentally before checker validation.
Dependancies: Overload Roles Capture Source Facts
Detailed Design: Add a scope-local overload group key containing owner, logical name, callable kind, staticness, and accessor/constructor category. Change scope insertion to create or find a frozen group identity only for matching full keys. Remove name-only or method-only grouping paths for overload-related declarations. `ETSBinder` inserts role records into the matching scope group and preserves the full key for checker lookup.
Acceptance Criteria: Scope lookup can distinguish static and instance members with the same name, method and accessor members with the same name, and constructor groups from method groups. Wrong-key lookups return absent or unrelated groups instead of merged declaration vectors.
Workload: 1.5 MM

### Task 4: Same-Scope Groups Freeze Structurally
Request Tasks: Task 4, Task 8
Description: Binder finalization freezes only same-scope structural membership. It establishes group identity, declaration identities, role vectors, and source ordinals, while leaving inherited candidates and spec semantic ordering to checker.
Dependancies: Scope Group Keys Use Full Dimensions
Detailed Design: Add a finalization step for scope-local overload groups that seals role vectors and records duplicate structural owner/name/key conflicts. Change mutable insertion containers into read-only views after scope construction. Remove any finalization behavior that expands supertypes, filters semantic duplicates, performs type-relation checks, or reorders inherited/interface candidates. Frozen groups become stable inputs for checker and for transitional lowering adapters.
Acceptance Criteria: After finalization, same-scope group membership cannot be appended or reordered through normal lookup APIs. The frozen view contains only local structural records and imported structural references, with no inherited candidate expansion or selected overload metadata.
Workload: 1.0 MM

### Task 5: Import Groups Preserve Provenance
Request Tasks: Task 4, Task 9
Description: Import and export binding must preserve overload group provenance without copying mutable local group state. Qualified overload-list names, aliases, and local/import collisions need deterministic structural outcomes for later diagnostics.
Dependancies: Same-Scope Groups Freeze Structurally
Detailed Design: Add imported group references that carry source module identity, exported name, local alias, qualified-name path, original group key, and diagnostic provenance. Change import binding so aliases create local references to immutable imported groups instead of cloning declaration vectors. Remove mutation paths that append local declarations into imported group storage. Local scopes record alias conflicts and qualified-name resolution facts for checker diagnostics.
Acceptance Criteria: Imported overload groups remain immutable through local binding. Alias collisions, local-name collisions, and qualified overload-list name linkage can be verified from scope facts without reconstructing checker candidates.
Workload: 1.0 MM

### Task 6: Lookup Returns Frozen Group Views
Request Tasks: Task 4, Task 6, Task 8
Description: Name lookup must expose structural overload group views efficiently and predictably. The lookup result is a binder/scopes fact, not an authoritative final ETS `OverloadSet`.
Dependancies: Import Groups Preserve Provenance
Detailed Design: Add lookup APIs that accept the full group key dimensions and return frozen local/import group views plus provenance. Change existing overload-related lookup callers to use keyed lookup instead of collecting declarations by name and filtering later inside binder. Remove lookup paths that imply final inherited ordering, first-valid selection, overload-equivalence, or semantic duplicate skipping. Checker consumes these views to build semantic overload sets and resolved-call metadata.
Acceptance Criteria: Lookup is O(1) or indexed by owner/name/key for present and absent names. Returned views include role, source order, declaration identity, key, and provenance, and exclude semantic resolution state.
Workload: 1.0 MM

### Task 7: Binder Diagnostics Report Shape Facts
Request Tasks: Task 4, Task 9
Description: Binder diagnostics should cover only structural name and scope formation problems. Semantic override validity, overload compatibility, accessibility filtering, and call failure diagnostics remain checker-owned.
Dependancies: Lookup Returns Frozen Group Views
Detailed Design: Add diagnostic categories or mapping entries for duplicate structural group keys, multiple same-scope declarations that violate binder-visible syntax/name rules, unresolved qualified overload-list names, alias collisions, and illegal import/export group linkage. Change current binder diagnostics that depend on type compatibility or inherited members to emit only structural facts or defer them. Remove binder emission of semantic overload resolution and override-target diagnostics. Each diagnostic includes declaration provenance for later golden tests.
Acceptance Criteria: Binder can report structural duplicate and import/alias failures without type checking. No binder diagnostic requires inherited-member traversal, type relation, overload-equivalence comparison, or call argument analysis.
Workload: 0.8 MM

### Task 8: ScopesInit Publishes One-Way Facts
Request Tasks: Task 4, Task 7, Task 10
Description: Scopes initialization must publish frozen structural group facts to downstream phases without becoming a semantic overload constructor. Lowering may receive only compatibility data regenerated from frozen facts or checker-approved metadata.
Dependancies: Binder Diagnostics Report Shape Facts
Detailed Design: Add a one-way scopes-init publication record containing frozen group ids, scope-local keys, declaration identities, source order, role, and import provenance. Change scopes-init consumers so checker receives authoritative structural facts first, and lowering receives an adapter view only after checker metadata exists or as a legacy structural compatibility surface. Remove scopes-init logic that selects overload implementations, resolves override targets, or expands inherited overload sets. Ownership flows from `ETSBinder` to frozen scopes, then to checker, then to lowering adapter.
Acceptance Criteria: Scopes-init output can be inspected to show structural group ids and declaration facts only. Lowering-facing data is either checker-derived or explicitly marked as structural compatibility data and cannot claim final semantic membership.
Workload: 1.0 MM

### Task 9: Varbinder Tests Cover Group Facts
Request Tasks: Task 4, Task 9, Task 11, Task 12
Description: Add focused tests for `varbinder` structural behavior around overload groups, imports, aliases, and lookup keys. These tests verify binder/scopes ownership without relying on checker overload resolution.
Dependancies: ScopesInit Publishes One-Way Facts
Detailed Design: Add component-level test cases or existing test-suite fixtures that inspect compile diagnostics and scope-visible behavior for local groups, static/instance separation, method/accessor separation, constructors, qualified imports, aliases, provenance, and immutability. Change legacy tests that assume binder owns semantic overload ordering to assert only structural facts at this layer. Remove no tests; classify obsolete expectations as checker or spec-divergence follow-up. The test data supports later checker and lowering tests without duplicating their responsibilities.
Acceptance Criteria: Tests fail if lookup merges wrong key dimensions, mutates imported groups, loses provenance, or publishes semantic selection from binder/scopes-init. Tests do not require final overload-call success or override compatibility to pass.
Workload: 0.8 MM

## Cross-Cutting Constraints
- Binder freezes structural same-scope facts only — final inherited overload-set construction, first-valid ordering, overload-equivalence, type compatibility, duplicate candidate skipping, and semantic diagnostics belong to checker (source: spec §15.9-15.11)
- Group keys include owner, logical name, callable kind, staticness, and accessor/constructor category — this preserves the architecture’s deterministic grouping and avoids accidental cross-kind merges (source: ref:kotlin-fir-descriptor-override-overload)
- Imported group references are immutable and provenance-carrying — diagnostics and checker lookup need aliases, qualified names, and source module identity without local mutation (source: ref:microsoft/TypeScript)

## Data And Control Flow
- Parser IR declarations enter `ETSBinder` — `ETSBinder` records explicit overload-list roles and implicit callable roles with source ordinals — no semantic ordering is computed (source: spec §15.10-15.11)
- `ETSBinder` inserts role records into keyed scope groups — scopes freeze same-scope structural membership — checker consumes frozen views to build semantic overload sets (source: ref:kotlin-fir-descriptor-override-overload)
- Import binding creates immutable imported group references — local scopes store aliases and provenance — checker uses these facts for accessibility and semantic candidate construction (source: ref:microsoft/TypeScript)
- Scopes-init publishes frozen group ids and declarations — checker produces resolved metadata — lowering receives checker metadata or a structural compatibility adapter (source: assumption §lowering-contract)

## Component Interactions
- [id: i1] `ETSBinder` -> `Scope group storage` — inserts role records under full structural group keys and receives frozen group identities (source: spec §15.11.1)
- [id: i2] `Scope group storage` -> `ETSchecker` — exposes immutable local/import group views, source order, role, declaration identity, key, and provenance (source: ref:kotlin-fir-descriptor-override-overload)
- [id: i3] `Import binder` -> `Scope group storage` — publishes immutable imported group references with alias and qualified-name provenance (source: ref:microsoft/TypeScript)
- [id: i4] `ScopesInit` -> `Lowering adapter` — forwards only structural compatibility data until checker-owned overload/override metadata is available (source: assumption §lowering-contract)

## Rationale
`varbinder` is affected because the architecture depends on deterministic overload facts before checker work begins. The component must make same-scope grouping, imports, aliases, lookup keys, and scopes-init publication precise enough for checker performance and diagnostics, while keeping semantic overload and override decisions out of binder.

## Skip Rationale
Not skipped.

# Component Design: Compiler Core And Bytecode Emission
Component ID: compiler_core
Decision: detailed

## Summary
Compiler core is affected only at the final emission boundary. It must consume checker/lowering-selected overload and override facts and emit the chosen implementation without rebuilding overload sets or validating overrides.

## Top-Level Alignment
The approved architecture places overload-set formation and call selection in binder/checker, with lowering as the structural adapter. Compiler core participates by treating resolved signatures, implementation targets, helper roles, and argument layouts as already-decided inputs for `ETSCompiler`, `ETSGen`, `ETSFunctionEmitter`, and `ETSEmitter`.

## Tasks

### Task 1: ETSCompiler emits resolved calls
Request Tasks: Task 6, Task 7
Description: `ETSCompiler` is the component-local owner of ETS call-expression bytecode emission. Its call path must emit the checker-selected callable for normal calls, `super` calls, static calls, constructor calls, and union-member calls without consulting overload declaration order or overload candidates.
Dependancies: none
Detailed Design: Add a local emission accessor that reads the selected call signature and implementation target from checked call metadata, with a legacy adapter to `CallExpression::Signature()` and constructor signatures during migration. Change `ETSCompiler` call and object-construction emission to pass that selected target into `ETSGen` call helpers. Remove any compiler-core fallback that treats overload declarations, overload lists, or implementation signatures as alternative candidates. The resulting design has `ETSCompiler` own only receiver evaluation and call opcode choice, while checker/lowering owns target selection.
Acceptance Criteria: Every ETS call emission path receives exactly one selected signature or fails an internal invariant before bytecode emission. `ETSCompiler` does not iterate overload declarations or inherited candidates, and emitted static, virtual, exact, `super`, and constructor calls use the selected implementation target.
Workload: 1.0 MM

### Task 2: ETSCompiler uses argument layout
Request Tasks: Task 6, Task 7
Description: `ETSCompiler` currently performs call-argument shaping for rest parameters during emission. In the target architecture, checker selects the overload and lowering prepares any structural argument shape needed for bytecode.
Dependancies: ETSCompiler emits resolved calls
Detailed Design: Add a component-local `EmittedArgumentList` view or equivalent adapter over the lowering-prepared argument layout and selected signature. Change call and constructor emission to compile arguments from that view rather than mutating AST argument vectors during bytecode generation. Remove compiler-core AST rewriting for overload/rest argument conversion, keeping only verifier-safe assertions that the emitted argument layout matches the selected signature. `ETSCompiler` hands the final argument span to `ETSGen`, and `ETSGen` remains responsible only for instruction selection.
Acceptance Criteria: Call and constructor emission no longer changes AST argument containers. Rest, spread, optional, and constructor arguments are emitted from a stable layout associated with the selected signature, and compiler-core assertions catch missing or stale lowering metadata.
Workload: 1.2 MM

### Task 3: ETSFunctionEmitter filters overload stubs
Request Tasks: Task 7, Task 10
Description: `ETSFunctionEmitter` and `ETSEmitter` decide which script functions become Panda functions. Explicit overload signatures and checked helper/bridge functions need a deterministic emission role so bytecode output contains implementation artifacts only when required.
Dependancies: none
Detailed Design: Add a local emission-role query consumed by `ETSFunctionEmitter::IsEmissionRequired` and `ETSEmitter::GenFunction`, backed by checker/lowering metadata with a compatibility adapter for existing script-function flags. Change function emission to distinguish implementation body, overload declaration stub, generated helper, interface bridge, async wrapper, external declaration, and declare-only function. Remove emission decisions based on overload declaration shape alone. The resulting handoff lets lowering request helper or bridge emission explicitly while compiler core filters non-emittable overload signatures.
Acceptance Criteria: Explicit overload declarations without bodies are never emitted as standalone Panda functions. Implementation methods, required helpers, async wrappers, and bridge functions are emitted once with stable internal names, and external/declare overload surfaces remain filtered by the emission-role query.
Workload: 1.0 MM

### Task 4: ETSEmitter records selected dependencies
Request Tasks: Task 7, Task 12
Description: `ETSEmitter` tracks emitted records and function dependencies for full and simultaneous incremental output. Overload rework must make dependencies point to selected implementation functions and required helper artifacts, not to overload-surface declarations.
Dependancies: ETSCompiler emits resolved calls, ETSFunctionEmitter filters overload stubs
Detailed Design: Change dependency recording in ETS emission to consume the selected implementation internal name and helper emission role produced by checker/lowering metadata. Keep class/type dependency recording unchanged, but remove any need to scan overload groups or declaration lists during bytecode dependency discovery. `ETSCompiler` emits calls through `ETSGen`, `ETSGen` exposes the selected target name to `ETSEmitter`, and `ETSEmitter` records only bytecode-visible functions.
Acceptance Criteria: Incremental and normal emission produce dependency sets containing implementation and helper function names only. Overload declaration stubs do not appear in function tables or dependency deltas, and repeated overload calls do not cause duplicate function-table entries.
Workload: 0.8 MM

## Cross-Cutting Constraints
- Compiler core must not form overload sets or validate overrides — those are checker responsibilities under the approved semantic split (source: spec §15.9-15.11)
- Bytecode emission must consume one selected target per call — ETS overload resolution is first-valid over a spec-ordered set before lowering/codegen (source: ref:typescript)
- Emission roles must remain metadata-driven — helper and bridge generation are structural lowering outputs, not compiler-core semantic decisions (source: ref:kotlin)

## Data And Control Flow
- Checked call metadata is produced before lowering — `ETSCompiler` reads the selected signature and implementation target only after structural lowering is complete (source: spec §15.11)
- Lowering prepares argument layout — `ETSCompiler` compiles the layout and `ETSGen` emits call instructions without mutating AST shape (source: assumption §3)
- Function emission role is assigned before bytecode output — `ETSFunctionEmitter` filters stubs and emits only bytecode-visible bodies, helpers, and bridges (source: assumption §7)

## Component Interactions
- [id: i1] `checker call resolver` -> `ETSCompiler` — selected signature and implementation target for each call expression (source: spec §15.11)
- [id: i2] `overload lowerings` -> `ETSCompiler` — emitted argument layout for rest/spread/default-shape calls (source: assumption §3)
- [id: i3] `overload lowerings` -> `ETSFunctionEmitter` — emission role for implementation, helper, bridge, async wrapper, and declaration stub (source: ref:kotlin)
- [id: i4] `ETSGen` -> `ETSEmitter` — bytecode-visible function names used for dependency recording (source: assumption §7)

## Rationale
Compiler core is affected because it is the last boundary before Panda bytecode and currently owns ETS call emission, constructor emission, function filtering, and dependency recording. The component should remain a consumer: it emits selected targets and requested helpers, while parser, binder, checker, and lowering own overload syntax, grouping, validation, resolution, and structural preparation.

## Skip Rationale
Not skipped.

# Component Design: Lexer And Tokens
Component ID: lexer
Decision: skip

## Summary
The approved architecture does not define a concrete lexer-owned change for `_override_` or `_overload_`. It assigns syntax preservation to `parser/ETSparser*` and semantic ownership to binder, checker, and lowering contracts.

## Top-Level Alignment
Lexer participation remains limited to existing tokenization of ArkTS source text. The architecture requires parser-level preservation of overload and override syntax, but does not require new token kinds, token ordering rules, or lexer diagnostics.

## Cross-Cutting Constraints
- Lexer must remain syntax-neutral for overload/override semantics — semantic decisions belong to binder/checker/lowering boundaries (source: assumption §3)

## Data And Control Flow
- Source text tokenization — lexer -> parser — lexer provides tokens only; parser interprets overload/override declaration grammar (source: assumption §3)

## Component Interactions
- [id: i1] `lexer` -> `parser/ETSparser*` — token stream remains the handoff; overload-list and override syntax interpretation is parser-owned (source: assumption §3)

## Rationale
The approved top-level architecture materially affects parser, IR, binder/scopes, checker, lowering, public metadata, and tests. It does not identify a missing lexer-level representation or diagnostic responsibility, so a detailed lexer task list would invent component work not justified by the approved design.

## Skip Rationale
Skipped because no concrete add/change/remove is required in Lexer And Tokens by the approved top-level architecture.

# Component Design: AST Verifier
Component ID: ast_verifier
Decision: skip

## Summary
The approved architecture does not require a concrete AST Verifier change. `_override_` and `_overload_` semantics move to parser, binder/scopes, checker, and lowering metadata contracts, while AST Verifier remains a structural invariant checker for AST shape after parsing and lowering.

## Top-Level Alignment
AST Verifier participates only as an existing safety net for structural AST correctness. The architecture does not introduce a new AST node kind, AST rewrite pattern, or verifier-visible invariant for this component.

## Cross-Cutting Constraints
- Preserve existing verifier checks — AST Verifier must not disable structural checks while overload/override work moves through other components (source: assumption §Core Engineering Rules)
- Keep semantic decisions out of AST Verifier — override validity and overload resolution belong to checker-owned metadata, not AST structural validation (source: spec §15.9-15.11)

## Data And Control Flow
- Parser/lowering AST output is verified structurally — AST Verifier runs after configured phases and checks parent, source range, scope, type, modifier, getter/setter, and declaration invariants with existing checks (source: assumption §AST Verifier Agent Guide)
- Checker side records are not verifier input — `OverloadSet`, `ResolvedOverloadCall`, and override metadata remain checker/lowering contract data, not AST invariants (source: ref:kotlin-fir-descriptor-override-overload)

## Component Interactions
- [id: i1] `parser/lowering` -> `ast_verifier` — existing AST shape checks continue to guard produced trees; no new overload/override-specific verifier contract is required (source: assumption §AST Verifier Agent Guide)
- [id: i2] `checker` -> `lowering` — checker-owned overload/override metadata bypasses AST Verifier because it is semantic state, not AST structure (source: ref:typescript)

## Rationale
AST Verifier is affected only if overload/override rework creates new AST node kinds, new lowering-generated AST structures, or a known invalid AST shape that current invariants miss. The approved top-level architecture explicitly uses semantic side records and checked metadata, so the required component-local change is not clear and no missing AST Verifier functionality is established.

## Skip Rationale
Skipped because the approved architecture does not materially affect `ast_verifier` through a concrete component-local add/change/remove. Existing invariants already cover AST structural integrity, while all overload/override behavior changes are owned by parser/IR preservation, binder/scopes grouping, checker validation/resolution, lowering metadata consumption, and tests.

No concrete new driver option, public entrypoint, IDL surface, or exported metadata contract is specified for this component, so a detailed implementation task list would invent work beyond the approved architecture.

# Component Design: Tests Tooling And Documentation
Component ID: tests_tooling_docs
Decision: detailed

## Summary
Tests, tooling, and documentation are materially affected because the approved architecture changes observable overload/override diagnostics, call selection, lowering-facing metadata validation, and performance gates. This component owns the spec ledger, behavior inventory artifacts, focused test matrices, runner manifests, and required validation counters.

## Top-Level Alignment
This component verifies that parser, binder, checker, resolver, and lowering changes remain spec-aligned without making semantic decisions itself. It turns Tasks 1-12 into reviewable documentation, targeted diagnostics tests, runnable ETS tests, scale fixtures, and final validation reports.

## Tasks

### Task 1: Spec Ledger Record Rules
Request Tasks: Task 1, Task 9, Task 10
Description: The spec ledger is the documentation anchor for `_override_` and `_overload_` behavior in tests and review. It records ArkTS TP rule sections, release-feed deltas, expected diagnostic ownership, and explicit ambiguity markers.
Dependancies: none
Detailed Design: Add a rule ledger template covering overload declarations, first-valid resolution, inherited overload sets, constructors, accessors, visibility, staticness, generics, optional/rest parameters, and diagnostics. Change existing ad-hoc test rationale into ledger references. Remove test justification based only on legacy behavior when it conflicts with the ledger. The ledger hands rule ids to AST negative tests, runtime positive tests, migration checklists, and validation reports.
Acceptance Criteria: Every new overload/override test references a ledger rule id or an ambiguity marker. The ledger includes spec sections for Tasks 5 and 6 diagnostics, including no applicable overload, ambiguous overload or deferred ambiguity, type-argument arity, generic inference failure, and lambda/context-sensitive argument failure where spec-defined.
Workload: 0.8 MM

### Task 2: Behavior Inventory Matrix
Request Tasks: Task 2, Task 7, Task 10
Description: The inventory matrix documents current overload/override behavior by compiler phase so tests can distinguish preserved behavior from migrated behavior. It is local to docs/tooling and does not prescribe implementation changes in parser, binder, checker, or lowering.
Dependancies: Spec Ledger Record Rules
Detailed Design: Add an inventory matrix with rows for syntax preservation, scope grouping, checker override validation, call resolution, lowering helper generation, async overload handling, interface/property bridge behavior, and public overload metadata emission. Change migration notes to point at concrete inventory rows instead of broad component names. Remove unresolved “current behavior unknown” placeholders once inventory evidence is captured. The matrix feeds the migration checklist and marks which existing tests are authoritative, divergent, or pending.
Acceptance Criteria: The inventory has a phase owner, observed behavior, ledger rule, divergence status, and test coverage column for every overload/override surface named in the approved architecture. Async, bridge/interface, and public metadata paths are explicitly inventoried or marked not applicable with a ledger-backed reason.
Workload: 0.7 MM

### Task 3: AST Diagnostic Matrix
Request Tasks: Task 5, Task 6, Task 9, Task 11
Description: The AST diagnostic matrix owns negative compile-time coverage for spec-defined failures. It prevents checker and binder diagnostics from drifting into ad-hoc errors unrelated to the ledger.
Dependancies: Spec Ledger Record Rules, Behavior Inventory Matrix
Detailed Design: Add focused negative-test categories for duplicate overload-equivalent signatures, invalid overload lists, missing override target, illegal override target, visibility narrowing, static/instance mismatch, accessor/field/property shape mismatch, constructor misuse, inherited collisions, no applicable overload, ambiguous overload or spec ambiguity, type-argument arity, generic inference failure, and lambda/context-sensitive argument rejection. Change existing broad fixtures into minimal one-root-cause cases where practical. Remove expectation files whose only purpose is to preserve non-spec legacy behavior, replacing them with divergence entries when needed. The matrix maps each case to parser, binder, or checker diagnostic ownership.
Acceptance Criteria: Each diagnostic category has at least one minimal negative case or a ledger-backed deferred marker. No applicable overload, ambiguity/spec ambiguity, type-argument/generic failures, and lambda/context-sensitive failures are present as first-class matrix entries.
Workload: 1.4 MM

### Task 4: Runtime Dispatch Matrix
Request Tasks: Task 6, Task 7, Task 11
Description: The runtime matrix owns positive runnable coverage for first-valid overload selection and lowering metadata consumption. It validates emitted behavior without letting lowering choose semantic winners.
Dependancies: Spec Ledger Record Rules, Behavior Inventory Matrix
Detailed Design: Add runnable cases for explicit-list order, implicit overloads, inherited overloads, constructors, `super` calls, static/member calls, generics, optional/rest parameters, inaccessible candidate skipping when spec-defined, implementation-signature leakage prevention, async overloads, interface property/accessor bridge behavior, and selected callable metadata consumption. Change runtime expectations to assert the selected callable directly through observable results. Remove tests that pass only because implementation signatures are callable outside the overload surface unless the ledger says that is valid. The matrix receives selected-call facts from checker metadata indirectly through emitted behavior and helper/bridge output.
Acceptance Criteria: Runtime tests prove first-valid dispatch and fail if lowering reselects a different overload. Async overloads, bridge/interface/property behavior, public metadata decision effects, and implementation-signature leakage prevention are covered or marked not applicable with ledger-backed rationale.
Workload: 1.6 MM

### Task 5: Scale Fixture Generator
Request Tasks: Task 8, Task 11, Task 12
Description: Scale fixtures exercise performance-sensitive overload and override shapes without hand-maintaining large source files. They provide reproducible inputs for large overload sets, deep inheritance, diamond interfaces, and repeated generic/lambda calls.
Dependancies: AST Diagnostic Matrix, Runtime Dispatch Matrix
Detailed Design: Add a generator for parameterized ETS fixtures with configurable overload count, hierarchy depth, interface diamond width, constructor overload count, and repeated call sites. Change benchmark inputs to come from deterministic generator parameters recorded in manifests. Remove manually duplicated scale fixtures once equivalent generated cases exist. The generated programs feed targeted compile tests, runtime smoke where applicable, and counter validation.
Acceptance Criteria: The generator can produce at least one fixture for each approved scale shape: large overload sets, deep class chains, diamond interfaces, repeated generic calls, and repeated lambda/context-sensitive calls. Generated fixture manifests record parameters, expected diagnostic/runtime outcome, and related ledger rule ids.
Workload: 1.2 MM

### Task 6: Counter Validation Contract
Request Tasks: Task 8, Task 12
Description: The counter contract makes performance validation a required final output rather than an optional observation. It defines the checker/lowering-facing metrics that final migration must report.
Dependancies: Scale Fixture Generator
Detailed Design: Add a validation manifest requiring overload-set builds, inherited-index builds, candidate scans, relation-cache hit rate, diagnostic candidate render count, compile-time median, and peak RSS. Change pre-counter migration phases to report “counter unavailable” only with a blocking follow-up entry and a temporary phase label. Remove optional wording from final validation criteria. The manifest consumes scale fixtures and runner output, then produces pass/fail data against the approved thresholds.
Acceptance Criteria: Final validation cannot pass without required counters and thresholds: no more than 5% median compile-time regression and no more than 10% peak RSS regression unless explicitly justified. Pre-counter phases are clearly marked temporary and cannot be used as final acceptance.
Workload: 0.9 MM

### Task 7: Migration Checklist Gates
Request Tasks: Task 7, Task 10, Task 12
Description: The migration checklist coordinates docs and tests across semantic model, binder grouping, checker override checks, resolver selection, and lowering adapter phases. It keeps rollback boundaries visible without creating implementation phases inside this component.
Dependancies: Behavior Inventory Matrix, AST Diagnostic Matrix, Runtime Dispatch Matrix, Counter Validation Contract
Detailed Design: Add checklist gates for spec ledger completion, inventory completion, semantic side-table visibility to tests, binder grouping diagnostics, checker override diagnostics, call resolver metadata, lowering adapter consumption, async/bridge/public metadata validation, and performance counter reporting. Change review templates to require the relevant gate evidence for every overload/override patch. Remove generic “run tests” checklist entries and replace them with named targeted suites and manifests. The checklist consumes all prior task artifacts and publishes the final validation packet.
Acceptance Criteria: Each gate names the required test matrix rows, runner manifest, counter manifest, and ledger references. Lowering-contract gates explicitly verify async overloads, interface/property bridge behavior, selected callable consumption, and public metadata decision coverage.
Workload: 0.8 MM

## Cross-Cutting Constraints
- Every test expectation must trace to a ledger rule or ambiguity marker — this enforces the spec-first policy across diagnostics and runtime behavior (source: spec §§15.9-15.11).
- Negative diagnostics live in AST compile-time coverage, while runnable dispatch lives in ETS runtime coverage — this follows the repository test placement policy (source: assumption §Test Placement).
- Final performance validation must include counters and thresholds — this preserves the approved architecture’s falsifiable validation plan (source: ref:kotlin, ref:typescript).

## Data And Control Flow
- Spec ledger entries — docs matrix and test manifests — ledger ids are created before diagnostics or runtime expectations are accepted (source: spec §§15.9-15.11).
- Inventory rows — migration checklist — current behavior is classified before a gate claims behavior was preserved or changed (source: assumption §Target Repo Validation Hooks).
- Generated scale fixtures — counter validation manifest — fixture parameters are stable inputs for compile-time, RSS, and semantic counter reports (source: ref:kotlin).

## Component Interactions
- [id: i1] `spec ledger` -> `AST diagnostic matrix` — diagnostic tests cite rule ids and ownership categories (source: spec §§15.9-15.11).
- [id: i2] `runtime dispatch matrix` -> `lowering adapter validation` — emitted behavior proves selected callable metadata is consumed rather than recomputed (source: ref:kotlin).
- [id: i3] `scale fixture generator` -> `counter validation contract` — generated overload and inheritance programs provide required final performance inputs (source: ref:typescript).

## Rationale
This component is affected because the approved architecture is only reviewable if its rules, diagnostics, runtime behavior, lowering contract, and performance claims are encoded in durable tests and validation artifacts. The design keeps semantic ownership in parser/binder/checker/lowering components while making tests and tooling enforce the contract.

## Skip Rationale
Not skipped.

content.text:
I looked through `~/overloads/*.md`.

Overall: **good high-level direction, but too big and too overload-centric**. I would use it as a checklist/source of ideas, not as an implementation plan.

## What is good

It gets several important principles right:

- Parser should stay syntax-only.
- Binder/scopes should provide structural facts, not final semantics.
- Checker should own overload resolution and override validation.
- Lowering should consume checked decisions, not rediscover overload/override semantics.
- Explicit overload aliases should expand real candidates.
- Overload resolution should be ordered / first-valid, not TypeScript-style hidden implementation-signature logic.
- AST should not be rewritten just to model overload semantics.
- Public API changes should be avoided unless proven necessary.

These align with our direction.

## Biggest issue

The design is mostly an **overload-set architecture**. It does not really solve the hardest override/default-method problems.

It talks about:

```text
ExplicitOverloadList
ImplicitOverloadEntity
OverloadSet
ResolvedOverloadCall
TypedSignatureFacts
InheritedMemberIndex
OverloadSetView
OverrideValidator
FirstValidResolver
```

But it does not give a precise algorithm for:

- class/superclass method dominance over interface defaults;
- subinterface default dominance over superinterface defaults;
- inherited selected defaults;
- verifier-safe default emission;
- duplicate override-of-same-base detection;
- stable method target identity under generic substitution;
- private interface defaults;
- `this` return viewpoint;
- generic supertype path substitution.

So it solves the **shape** of overload handling better than it solves the **semantics** of overriding/default implementation.

## What is over-engineered

I would not implement these literally:

1. Full `TypedSignatureFacts` infrastructure first.
2. Full `InheritedMemberIndex` as a mandatory cache.
3. Full `OverloadSetView` framework across all call kinds immediately.
4. Full binder-side frozen group system.
5. New AST `SyntaxIdentity` boundary everywhere.
6. Complete lowering metadata adapter for all overload/override-sensitive phases.
7. Compiler-core argument-layout rewrite.
8. Required performance counters and scale-fixture generator as part of first implementation.
9. Complete public metadata audit before fixing core semantics.
10. Physical full bridge lowering rewrite.

That is a large frontend re-architecture, not a focused feature implementation.

## Main semantic gaps

### 1. Default interface methods are underdesigned

The docs mention “interface obligations” and “selected implementation identity”, but not the real algorithm we need:

```text
ResolveInterfaceImplementation(classType, MethodKey)
```

with outcomes like:

```text
class method
superclass method
selected interface default
inherited selected default
none
conflict
```

Without this, the current active bug family remains unsolved.

### 2. Generic views are too vague

It says “generic substitution” and “substituted signature id”, but does not define something like:

```cpp
SupertypeView
MethodView
MethodTargetKey
```

This is dangerous for repeated generic interfaces and inherited defaults.

### 3. Stable target identity is missing

It relies heavily on ids/signature ids but does not define a safe key for:

```text
same original method through different substituted views
same default through multiple paths
duplicate override of same base
```

This is central for correctness.

### 4. Binder is given too much infrastructure

Binder should probably not grow a large frozen overload-group architecture before checker needs it. For first implementation, binder can provide enough declaration/group facts, while checker relation queries do semantic grouping lazily.

### 5. Lowering target is too strict

“Lowering consumes metadata only” is correct direction, but making every lowering phase assert full metadata coverage immediately is too much.

For bridges, simpler first target:

```text
existing bridge phases may stay split,
but both use shared overridden-target discovery and descriptor dedup
```

No need for a complete bridge-planning framework immediately.

## What I would keep from it

Keep these ideas:

- `ResolvedOverloadCall` / selected call target metadata.
- Checker-owned overload candidate construction.
- First-valid overload resolution.
- Explicit overload expansion.
- Lowering should not choose overload winners.
- Bridge lowering should not independently rediscover override targets.
- Parser/IR should preserve syntax/source order, not own semantics.
- Tests should separate parser/binder/checker/lowering ownership.

## What I would replace with our simpler model

Instead of the full architecture, use one internal checker component:

```cpp
class SemanticRelations {
public:
    Signature *ViewSignature(...);

    OverrideDecision IsOverride(const MethodView &base,
                                const MethodView &derived);

    ArenaVector<OverrideTarget> OverriddenTargets(...);

    ImplementationResolution ResolveInterfaceImplementation(...);

    OverloadSet GetMethodOverloadSet(...);

    OverloadSet ExpandExplicitOverload(...);

    void Clear();
};
```

That covers the real needs without committing to many separate systems.

## Verdict

The other design is **directionally good but too broad**.

It is useful as:

- architecture vocabulary;
- migration checklist;
- reminder to keep lowering semantic-free;
- overload-set design inspiration.

But I would not follow it literally. It risks turning the work into a large frontend rewrite while still missing the hardest correctness pieces around interface defaults and generic override views.

For our implementation, I would keep the simpler target:

```text
generic method views
+ shared override compatibility
+ stable target keys
+ group-based interface/default implementation resolution
+ verifier-safe selected-default emission
+ explicit overload expansion
+ selected call targets
+ shared bridge target discovery
```

Everything else should be optional cleanup/future architecture.

The subset defined via type mapping is referred to as *effective type*.
*Effective type* mapping satisfies the following properties:

- For arbitrary types ``A`` and ``B``, if ``A`` is a subtype of ``B``, then an
  ``EffectiveType(A)`` is a subtype of ``EffectiveType(B)``

- For arbitrary types ``A`` and ``B``, ``EffectiveType(A | B)`` is identical to
  ``EffectiveType(A) | EffectiveType(B)``

- For an arbitrary type ``A``, ``A | undefined`` is a subtype of ``EffectiveType(A | undefined)``

  - In particular, for an arbitrary type ``A``, ``undefined`` is a subtype of ``EffectiveType(A)``

An original type and an *effective type* can have relationships of two kinds:

-  If *Effective type* of ``T`` is identical to ``T``, then type ``T`` is *preserved by type erasure*;
-  Otherwise, the type is considered as *affected by type erasure*.

If ``T | undefined`` is *preserved by type erasure*, then type ``T`` is *preserved
up to undefined*.

This property limits the possible applications of type-checking expressions:

-  :ref:`instanceof Expression`;
-  :ref:`Cast Expression`.

.. index::
   type erasure
   instanceof expression
   cast expression
   execution
   operation
   type
   generic
   semantics
   effective type
   type mapping
   supertype

Type mapping determines *effective types* as follows (the ``undefined`` union
member is excluded in the right-hand-side column for brevity):

.. list-table::
   :width: 100%
   :widths: 45 55
   :header-rows: 1

   * - **Original Type**
     - **Effective Type (undefined member excluded)**
   * - ``Any``
     - ``Any``
   * - ``never``
     - ``never``
   * - ``undefined``
     - ``undefined``
   * - ``null``
     - ``null``
   * - *Generic types* (see :ref:`Generics`)
     - Instantiation of the same generic type
       (see :ref:`Explicit Generic Instantiations`) with type arguments selected
       in accordance with :ref:`Type Parameter Variance`:

       - *Covariant* type parameters are instantiated with the constraint type;
       - *Contravariant* type parameters are instantiated with type ``never``;
       - *Invariant* type parameters are instantiated with a *Wildcard Type*
   * - :ref:`Type Parameters`
     - :ref:`Type Parameter Constraint`
   * - :ref:`Union Types` in the form ``T1 | T2 ... Tn``
     - Union of effective types of each constituent type of ``T1 ... Tn``.
   * - :ref:`Array Types` in the form ``T[]``
     - Same as for a generic type ``Array<T>``.
   * - :ref:`Fixed-Size Array Types` (``FixedArray<T>``)
     - Instantiations of ``FixedArray<T>`` (i.e., the effective type of type
       argument ``T`` is preserved).
   * - :ref:`Function Types` in the form ``(P1, P2, Pn) => R``
     - Instantiation of an internal generic *function* type with respect to the
       number of parameter types *n*. Parameter
       types ``P1, P2 ... Pn`` are instantiated with ``Any``. Return type ``R``
       is instantiated with type ``never``.
   * - :ref:`Function Types` in the form ``(P1, P2, Pn, ...PR) => R``
     - Instantiation of an internal generic *rest-parametrized function* type
       with respect to the number of parameter types *n*.
       Internal generic *rest-parametrized function* of *n* parameters is a supertype
       of the internal generic *function* type of *n* parameters. Parameter
       types ``P1, P2 ... Pn`` and rest parameter type ``PR`` are instantiated
       with ``Any``. Return type ``R`` is instantiated with type ``never``.
   * - :ref:`Tuple Types` in the form ``[T1, T2 ..., Tn]``

possibly include return backend/runtime constraints

These questions should not be answered by the same helper.

Finding #4

Effective signature type is not explicit

The spec gives effective type mapping rules. The implementation needs an actual helper that represents this mapping, otherwise the checker will keep using approximations such as ordinary subtyping or assembler type strings.

Type *EffectiveType(Type *type);
Type *EffectiveSignatureType(Type *type);
EffectiveSignature EffectiveSignatureOf(Signature *sig);
  • Use this helper for overload-equivalence.
  • Use it for “not override-compatible but erasure-compatible” diagnostics.
  • Use it later for bridge necessity decisions.

This reduces the risk that different subsystems implement slightly different erasure semantics.

Finding #5

Explicit overload declarations mishandle groups

Spec allows a listed name inside an explicit overload declaration to denote an implicit overload group. Current code can reject this or keep only the first signature.

function foo(x: number) {}
function foo(x: string) {}

overload callFoo { foo }
// should include both foo(number) and foo(string)

Current risk

Using CallSignatures().front() silently drops overload candidates.

Required behavior

Expand all call signatures of the listed overload group in declaration order.

Finding #6

Overload-set formation is too implicit

The checker should be able to answer “what is the overload set for this name and static receiver type?” without triggering a complex property lookup with synthetic variables and special flags.

OverloadSet BuildFunctionOverloadSet(scope, name);
OverloadSet BuildStaticMethodOverloadSet(classType, name);
OverloadSet BuildInstanceMethodOverloadSet(objectType, name);
OverloadSet BuildInterfaceMethodOverloadSet(interfaceType, name);
OverloadSet BuildConstructorOverloadSet(classType);

Once overload-set formation is explicit, ordering and inherited candidate skipping become testable.

edits.oldText:
## 4. Effective signature type is not first-class

The spec depends on effective signature type for overload-equivalence and erasure collision diagnostics.

Current implementation often uses:

- normal type relation;
- `ToAssemblerTypeWithRank`;
- ad-hoc erasure-like behavior.

This does not clearly implement the spec-defined effective type mapping.

edits.newText:
### Desired change

Do not introduce a new frontend type entity for effective signature types. Instead, fix/audit `GetApparentType()` and expose small semantic wrappers around it:

```cpp
Type *EffectiveType(Type *type)              // delegates to GetApparentType()
Type *EffectiveSignatureType(Type *type)     // delegates to EffectiveType(), with any spec signature exceptions
EffectiveSignatureKey EffectiveSignatureKeyOf(Signature *sig)
```

These helpers should return/use ordinary `Type *` values and stable keys; they should not mutate signatures to store apparent/effective types.

Then use the wrappers, not raw local erasure logic, in:

- overload-equivalence;
- override erasure-conflict diagnostics;
- bridge necessity checks;
- `MethodKey` / effective parameter keys.

Do not spread raw `GetApparentType()` blindly into every relation check. Source override compatibility, overload applicability, generic inference, and diagnostics that need original types must still use original/substituted source types.

## Phase 4: audit `GetApparentType` and expose effective-signature wrappers

Do not create a parallel effective-type representation. Use `GetApparentType()` as the implementation point, but first audit it against the spec effective-type table, especially generic type variance, arrays, fixed arrays, function/tuple types, string literals, utility types, and cache lifetime.

Add thin source-semantic wrappers:

```cpp
Type *EffectiveType(Type *type);              // delegates to GetApparentType()
Type *EffectiveSignatureType(Type *type);     // signature-specific wrapper
EffectiveSignatureKey EffectiveSignatureKeyOf(Signature *sig);
```

Apply gradually through these wrappers:

1. overload-equivalence;
2. override erasure-conflict diagnostics;
3. `MethodKey` effective parameter keys;
4. bridge necessity checks.

Do not replace ordinary source type relation checks with apparent/effective types unless the spec rule explicitly asks for effective signature types.

+1198 ### Reuse existing instantiation/substitution infrastructure
+1199 
+1200 Generic view support should reuse the existing checker machinery instead of creating a parallel substitution system.
+1201 
+1202 Relevant existing pieces:
+1203 
+1204 - `checker::InstantiationContext` validates explicit type arguments, applies defaults, checks constraints, and produces instantiated `ETSObjectType` objects;
+1205 - `ETSObjectType::Substitute()` creates instantiated object types, substitutes supertypes/interfaces, and records effective substitution data;
+1206 - instantiated `ETSObjectType` property maps can already contain substituted method signatures;
+1207 - `Signature::Substitute()` can create a substituted signature view from an existing substitution.
+1208 
+1209 Recommended use:
+1210 
+1211 - use `InstantiationContext` when resolving explicit generic type references or when a new instantiated object type must be created and validated;
+1212 - for override/overload/default relation queries, prefer already-instantiated `SuperType()` / `Interfaces()` path objects and existing `ETSObjectType::Substitute()` / `Signature::Substitute()` behavior;
+1213 - if a relation query needs a substitution, derive it from the instantiated supertype view or expose a small accessor/helper for the existing effective substitution, rather than maintaining another substitution map type;
+1214 - traverse real superclass/interface paths, not only transitive original-base-type sets, because repeated generic interfaces can have different instantiations along different paths.
+1215 
+1216 Do not call `InstantiationContext` blindly inside relation queries just to view an inherited method: it performs validation, can log diagnostics, needs source positions, mutates checker caches, and is oriented toward constructing type instantiations from type arguments. Relation queries usually need a diagnostic-free view of already-checked instantiated supertypes.

Generics-specific design

Reuse InstantiationContext infrastructure

Do not build a parallel generic substitution system for relation queries.

Reuse

  • InstantiationContext for explicit generic type instantiation and validation.
  • ETSObjectType::Substitute() for instantiated object/supertype/interface views.
  • Signature::Substitute() for substituted method signature views.
  • Existing instantiated SuperType()/Interfaces() path objects.

Avoid

  • Calling InstantiationContext inside every override query just to view a method.
  • Duplicating substitution maps when existing effective substitution data can be exposed.
  • Using transitive original-base-type sets when path-specific generic instantiations matter.
  • Re-running type-argument diagnostics from relation-cache queries.

Relation queries should normally consume already-checked instantiated supertypes and derive a diagnostic-free signature view from that path.

Updated target design

It **almost counts**, but only as a **seed** for the proposed helper, not as the helper itself.

Current one:

```cpp
static bool AreOverrideCompatible(ETSChecker *checker, Signature *s1, Signature *s2)
{
    if (s1->Function()->Id()->Name() != s2->Function()->Id()->Name()) {
        return false;
    }

    SavedTypeRelationFlagsContext savedFlagsCtx(checker->Relation(),
                                                TypeRelationFlag::OVERRIDING_CONTEXT);
    return checker->Relation()->SignatureIsSupertypeOf(s1, s2);
}
```

## Why it is not enough today

### 1. It is file-local and not the shared source of truth

It lives in `checker/ets/object.cpp` as a `static` helper. Other places still use other logic, e.g. `IsMethodOverridesOther()` in `checker/ets/function.cpp`, bridge lowering, interface checks, etc.

The proposed helper means:

> all override consumers use the same pairwise compatibility predicate.

Current `AreOverrideCompatible()` is not that.

---

### 2. It is signature-only, not view-based

For generics, the important comparison is:

```text
base original: B.foo(T): T
base view from D: B.foo(string): string
derived: D.foo(string): string
```

Current helper assumes caller already passed the right substituted signature. It has no `MethodView`, no `declaringType`, no `viewOwner`, no supertype path.

So it can be correct only if the caller prepared the right signature view.

---

### 3. It hides directionality

`AreOverrideCompatible(s1, s2)` sounds symmetric, but:

```cpp
SignatureIsSupertypeOf(s1, s2)
```

is directional.

The proposed helper should make direction explicit:

```cpp
IsOverrideCompatible(baseView, derivedView)
```

or:

```cpp
CheckOverrideCompatible(base, derived)
```

---

### 4. It does not define candidate filtering

It does not handle the whole override-candidate contract:

- constructors excluded;
- static vs instance separation;
- private/accessibility filtering;
- getter vs setter vs method distinction;
- synthetic bridge/default-forwarder exclusion;
- explicit overload alias exclusion.

Some of this is done around it in callers, but not consistently.

---

### 5. It returns only `bool`

For migration and diagnostics we probably need at least internally:

```cpp
enum class OverrideDecision {
    OVERRIDES,
    NOT_SAME_NAME,
    NOT_CANDIDATE_KIND,
    INCOMPATIBLE_PARAMETERS,
    INCOMPATIBLE_RETURN,
    INCOMPATIBLE_TYPE_PARAMS,
};
```

Maybe not full public API, but debugging/tests need more than true/false.

---

### 6. It does not own type-parameter constraint checks

Current override checking elsewhere does:

```cpp
CheckTypeParameterConstraints(...)
AdjustForTypeParameters(...)
```

`AreOverrideCompatible()` does not encode that policy. So using it alone may accept/reject differently from other override paths.

---

### 7. It is “pure-ish”, but not a stable semantic primitive

It does not mutate AST directly, so it is much better than `IsMethodOverridesOther()`, which calls:

```cpp
derived->Function()->SetOverride();
```

But it still depends on mutable `TypeRelation` flags/cache. That is acceptable if wrapped, but the helper contract should be explicit:

```text
no diagnostics
no AST mutation
no Signature mutation
only TypeRelation cache effects allowed
```

---

## So what should we do?

Do **not** invent unrelated logic.

Refactor current `AreOverrideCompatible()` into the proposed helper.

Something like:

```cpp
OverrideDecision IsOverrideCompatible(ETSChecker *checker,
                                      const MethodView &base,
                                      const MethodView &derived)
{
    if (base.key.name != derived.key.name) {
        return OverrideDecision::NOT_SAME_NAME;
    }

    if (!IsOverrideCandidate(base, derived)) {
        return OverrideDecision::NOT_CANDIDATE;
    }

    SavedTypeRelationFlagsContext ctx(checker->Relation(),
                                      TypeRelationFlag::OVERRIDING_CONTEXT);

    if (!checker->Relation()->SignatureIsSupertypeOf(base.viewSignature,
                                                     derived.viewSignature)) {
        return OverrideDecision::INCOMPATIBLE_SIGNATURE;
    }

    return OverrideDecision::OVERRIDES;
}
```

Then current `AreOverrideCompatible()` can become a compatibility shim or disappear.

## Bottom line

Current `AreOverrideCompatible()` is not wrong to reuse.

But it currently answers only:

> Are these two already-prepared signatures compatible under `OVERRIDING_CONTEXT`?

The proposed helper must answer:

> Does this derived method view override this base method view according to source semantics, with explicit candidate filtering and no side effects?

So: **reuse its core `TypeRelation` check, but wrap it in a proper view-based, side-effect-free, shared helper.**
add this into docs (including draft of IsOverrideCompatible)

# Documentation Agent Guide

Use this file for work under `docs/` together with the repository-level `AGENTS.md`.

## Core Metadata

| Attribute | Value |
|-----------|--------|
| **Name** | Documentation |
| **Purpose** | Contributor-facing docs for frontend architecture, rules, workflows, and onboarding. |
| **Primary Language** | Markdown |

## Scope

- Keep docs aligned with current specification-first policy.
- Keep commands, paths, and options accurate for the current tree/build flow.
- Use concise, actionable guidance with runnable command examples.
- Keep docs aligned with the latest technical preview release feed: <https://gitcode.com/igelhaus/arkcompiler_runtime_core/releases/>.

## Rules

- Do not document behavior that is not in the latest technical preview spec.
- When implementation and spec diverge, call out the mismatch explicitly.
- Do not remove hard review constraints from docs (tests required, no assertion removal, no speculative features).
- Prefer repository-relative paths in links.

## When Updating Docs

- Update `docs/README.md` when adding or renaming major docs.
- Keep onboarding guidance consistent with root `AGENTS.md`.

• An epoch/generation counter can be added later as a debug guard or for fine-grained LSP/plugin incremental invalidation.
  • This is similar in spirit to TypeRelation: relation answers are cached, but not permanently stored on every AST/type node.
    • Updated target design

    Override query group in detail

    enum class MethodKind { METHOD, GETTER, SETTER };
enum class MemberDispatchKind { INSTANCE, STATIC };

struct MethodKey {
    util::StringView name;
    MethodKind kind;
    MemberDispatchKind dispatchKind;
    EffectiveParameterSignature parameters;
};

struct MethodView {
    Signature *originalSignature;
    Signature *viewSignature;
    ETSObjectType *declaringType;
    ETSObjectType *viewOwner;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    MethodKey key;
    bool isAbstract;
    bool isPrivate;
};

// May be methods on SemanticRelations rather than a separate class.
OverrideDecision IsOverride(const MethodView &base,
                            const MethodView &derived);

ArenaVector<OverrideTarget> OverriddenTargets(ETSObjectType *owner,
                                              const MethodView &derived);

    Class/interface validation still asks all necessary questions, so diagnostics are complete. The difference is that answers are computed lazily and cached, not stored as permanent override state.

    // Usage: duplicate override-of-same-base validation
for (auto derived : EffectiveInstanceMethodViews(type)) {
    for (auto target : relations.OverriddenTargets(type, derived)) {
        overridingMethods[target.StableKey()].push_back(derived);
    }
}

if (overridingMethods[baseKey].size() > 1) {
    LogDuplicateOverrideOfSameBase(type, baseKey);
}

    Cache keys must be stable for substituted views. Do not rely on raw Signature* identity unless view signatures are canonicalized.

    Updated target design

    Implementation-resolution query

    enum class ImplementationKind {
    NONE,
    CLASS_METHOD,
    SUPERCLASS_METHOD,
    INTERFACE_DEFAULT,
    INHERITED_SELECTED_DEFAULT,
    CONFLICT,
};

struct ImplementationTarget {
    ImplementationKind kind;
    Signature *signature;
    ir::AstNode *declaration;
    ETSObjectType *declaringType;

[909 more lines in file. Use offset=860 to continue.]

Migration phase 1

Classify suppressed overriding failures

Do not turn the default-interface example into a one-off patch. The ignored CTS tests show several nearby bug families, so first map each failure to the shared relation query that must own it.

Bug familyOwning query group
Duplicate override of same base methodshared override queries
Class/superclass implementation dominates defaultsoverride queries + implementation resolution
Subinterface default overrides superinterface defaultimplementation resolution using override dominance
Generic default/override viewsgeneric-view helpers
Verifier-safe default emissionimplementation resolution + lowering consumer
Migration phase 2

Extract pure semantic helpers

The next step is to make semantic relations explicit and side-effect-free. A predicate should not mutate the AST or mark a method as overriding while answering a yes/no question.

bool IsOverrideCompatible(Signature *base, Signature *derived);
bool AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature *a, Signature *b);
bool IsConcreteImplementationOf(Signature *impl, Signature *requirement);

Before

Compatibility checks can call SetOverride() as a side effect.

After

First compute compatibility. Then consumers use the shared relation query result without predicate side effects.

Migration phase 3

Separate overload-equivalence from ABI collision

This is a cleanup with behavior impact. It prevents source-language diagnostics from depending on backend descriptor behavior.

// Source-language rule
bool AreOverloadEquivalent(Signature *a, Signature *b);

// Backend/helper/bridge rule
bool HaveSameAssemblySignature(Signature *a, Signature *b, bool includeReturn);

// Ambient/helper-specific rule
bool NeedHelperOverload(...);

Apply the language-level helper consistently to functions, methods, interfaces, and constructors.

Migration phase 4

Audit GetApparentType and add wrappers

Do not create a parallel effective-type representation. Use GetApparentType() as the implementation point, but expose source-semantic wrappers and migrate one consumer at a time.

  1. Audit/fix GetApparentType() against the spec effective-type table.
  2. Add EffectiveType, EffectiveSignatureType, and effective signature key helpers as thin wrappers.
  3. Use them in AreOverloadEquivalent and MethodKey.
  4. Add erasure-collision override diagnostics.
  5. Use them in bridge necessity checks through shared override-target queries.

Do not spread raw GetApparentType() into ordinary source type-relation checks. Effective signature type and assembler descriptors are related but different semantic layers.

Cache keys must be stable for substituted views. Do not rely on raw Signature* identity unless view signatures are canonicalized.

Override helper cleanup

Current AreOverrideCompatible is a seed

The existing file-local helper already uses the right core idea: name check + TypeRelationFlag::OVERRIDING_CONTEXT + SignatureIsSupertypeOf. Reuse that core, but do not stop there.

Why not enough

  • file-local, not shared by all consumers;
  • signature-only, not generic-view based;
  • direction is hidden by a symmetric-looking name;
  • candidate filtering and type-parameter checks live elsewhere;
  • returns only bool, so diagnostics lose reason codes.

Target contract

  • base/derived direction explicit;
  • takes MethodView with substituted view signatures;
  • no diagnostics, no SetOverride(), no signature mutation;
  • returns a decision usable by diagnostics/tests.

OverrideDecision CheckOverrideCompatibility(ETSChecker *checker,
                                            const MethodView &base,
                                            const MethodView &derived)
{
    if (base.key.name != derived.key.name) return NOT_SAME_NAME;
    if (!IsOverrideCandidatePair(base, derived)) return NOT_CANDIDATE_KIND;
    if (!HaveCompatibleMethodTypeParameters(checker, base, derived)) return INCOMPATIBLE_TYPE_PARAMS;

    SavedTypeRelationFlagsContext ctx(checker->Relation(), TypeRelationFlag::OVERRIDING_CONTEXT);
    return checker->Relation()->SignatureIsSupertypeOf(base.viewSignature, derived.viewSignature)
        ? OVERRIDES : INCOMPATIBLE_SIGNATURE;
}

bool IsOverrideCompatible(ETSChecker *checker, const MethodView &base, const MethodView &derived)
{
    return CheckOverrideCompatibility(checker, base, derived).Overrides();
}

OverrideDecision CheckOverrideCompatibility(ETSChecker *checker,
                                            const MethodView &base,
                                            const MethodView &derived)
{
    if (base.key.name != derived.key.name) return NOT_SAME_NAME;
    if (!IsOverrideCandidatePair(base, derived)) return NOT_CANDIDATE_KIND;
    if (!HaveCompatibleMethodTypeParameters(checker, base, derived)) return INCOMPATIBLE_TYPE_PARAMS;

    SavedTypeRelationFlagsContext ctx(checker->Relation(), TypeRelationFlag::OVERRIDING_CONTEXT);
    return checker->Relation()->SignatureIsSupertypeOf(base.viewSignature, derived.viewSignature)
        ? OVERRIDES : INCOMPATIBLE_SIGNATURE;
}

bool IsOverrideCompatible(ETSChecker *checker, const MethodView &base, const MethodView &derived)
{
    return CheckOverrideCompatibility(checker, base, derived).Overrides();
}

OverrideDecision CheckOverrideCompatibility(ETSChecker *checker,
                                            const MethodView &base,
                                            const MethodView &derived)
{
    if (base.key.name != derived.key.name) return {NOT_SAME_NAME};
    if (!IsOverrideCandidatePair(base, derived)) return {NOT_CANDIDATE_KIND};
    if (!HaveCompatibleMethodTypeParameters(checker, base, derived)) return {INCOMPATIBLE_TYPE_PARAMS};

    SavedTypeRelationFlagsContext ctx(checker->Relation(), TypeRelationFlag::OVERRIDING_CONTEXT);
    return checker->Relation()->SignatureIsSupertypeOf(base.viewSignature, derived.viewSignature)
        ? OverrideDecision {OVERRIDES} : OverrideDecision {INCOMPATIBLE_SIGNATURE};
}

bool IsOverrideCompatible(ETSChecker *checker, const MethodView &base, const MethodView &derived)
{
    return CheckOverrideCompatibility(checker, base, derived).Overrides();
}
